courses.title: Ch 1 · Relations and Functions
courses.summary: Types of relations, equivalence relations and classes, one-one/onto/bijective functions, composition and inverses — with proofs written the way examiners want.
outcomes: Learners can test a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity
Learners can prove a relation is an equivalence relation and list its classes
Learners can decide whether a function is one-one, onto or bijective
Learners can compose functions and find inverses of bijections

lessons.title: Relations and their types

scenes.text: Warden Rao lists which students share a room. 'Is a room-mate of' is a relation on the set of hostel students.
Is everyone their own room-mate? If A shares with B, does B share with A? These questions are exactly reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

steps.title: What is a relation?
steps.body:
A **relation R from A to B** is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R we write a R b. A relation **on A** is a subset of A × A.

- **Empty relation**: R = ∅ (no pair is related).
- **Universal relation**: R = A × A (every pair is related).

If |A| = n, then A × A has n² pairs, so the number of relations on A is 2^(n²).

steps.title: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive
steps.body:
For a relation R on A:

- **Reflexive**: (a, a) ∈ R for **every** a ∈ A.
- **Symmetric**: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R.
- **Transitive**: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.

To prove a property, argue for arbitrary elements. To disprove it, one counter-example is enough.

steps.title: Solved: R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b} on ℝ
steps.body:
Step 1 (reflexive): a ≤ a for all real a, so (a, a) ∈ R. ✔

Step 2 (symmetric): (1, 2) ∈ R since 1 ≤ 2, but 2 ≤ 1 is false, so (2, 1) ∉ R. ✘

Step 3 (transitive): a ≤ b and b ≤ c give a ≤ c. ✔

Conclusion: reflexive and transitive, **not** symmetric.

steps.title: Solved: R on A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)}
steps.body:
Step 1: (1, 1) ∉ R, so not reflexive.

Step 2: (1, 2) and (2, 1) both present, so symmetric. ✔

Step 3: (1, 2), (2, 1) ∈ R would need (1, 1) ∈ R for transitivity. It is missing, so **not transitive**.

Lesson: transitivity must be checked even when a = c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a relation reflexive because *some* elements are related to themselves — it needs **all** elements of A.
- Forgetting that the empty relation on a non-empty set is symmetric and transitive (vacuously) but not reflexive.
- Using a numerical example as a 'proof' — examples can only disprove a 'for all' statement.

steps.title: Exam habit
steps.body: Write each property as a separate heading with ✔ or ✘ and a one-line reason. Examiners award marks per property.

statements.s: Every relation on a non-empty set A is a subset of A × A.
The empty relation on {1, 2} is reflexive.
R = {(a, b): a − b is even} on ℤ is symmetric.
statements.why: If a − b is even, then b − a = −(a − b) is even.

statements.s: 'Is a brother of' on the set of all people is symmetric.
statements.why: A boy can be the brother of a girl, but the girl is not his brother.

quiz.q: If A has 3 elements, how many relations can be defined on A?
quiz.why: A × A has 3 × 3 = 9 ordered pairs, and each subset of A × A is a relation. So there are 2⁹ = 512 relations.

quiz.q: R = {(a, b): a divides b} on ℕ is
quiz.why: Divisibility is reflexive (a divides a) and transitive (a | b and b | c give a | c). It is not symmetric, since 2 | 4 but 4 does not divide 2.

quiz.q: A relation that is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive on A = {1, 2, 3} is
quiz.why: {(1,1)} is symmetric and transitive, but (2,2) and (3,3) are missing, so it is not reflexive on A.

quiz.q: The universal relation on A is
quiz.why: The universal relation A × A contains every pair, so it has all three properties: reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

quiz.q: To show R is NOT transitive you need
quiz.why: Transitivity is a 'for all' statement, so one counter-example (a, b), (b, c) in R with (a, c) not in R shows it fails.

lessons.title: Equivalence relations and classes

scenes.text: In a maths club, numbers are grouped by their remainder when divided by 3.
Every integer falls into exactly one basket: remainder 0, 1 or 2. These baskets are equivalence classes.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive** is an **equivalence relation**.

The **equivalence class** of a is [a] = {x ∈ A : x R a}. Two classes are either identical or disjoint, and together they cover A — they form a **partition** of A.

steps.title: Solved: R = {(a, b): 3 divides a − b} on ℤ
steps.body:
Step 1: a − a = 0 is divisible by 3 ⇒ reflexive.

Step 2: if 3 | (a − b) then 3 | (b − a) = −(a − b) ⇒ symmetric.

Step 3: if 3 | (a − b) and 3 | (b − c), then 3 | [(a − b) + (b − c)] = a − c ⇒ transitive.

Hence an equivalence relation. Classes: [0] = {…, −3, 0, 3, 6, …}, [1] = {…, −2, 1, 4, …}, [2] = {…, −1, 2, 5, …}.

steps.title: Solved: lines in a plane
steps.body:
R = {(L₁, L₂): L₁ ∥ L₂} on the set of lines in a plane (taking each line parallel to itself).

Reflexive ✔, symmetric ✔, transitive ✔ ⇒ equivalence. The class of the line y = 2x + 4 is the set of all lines y = 2x + c, c ∈ ℝ.

steps.title: Solved: set A = {1, 2, …, 12}, R = {(a, b): |a − b| is a multiple of 4}
steps.body:
Equivalence relation (same argument as 'divisible by 4').

Class of 1: {1, 5, 9}. Class of 2: {2, 6, 10}. The four classes partition A into sets of 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Is perpendicular to' is **not** an equivalence relation: it is symmetric but not reflexive or transitive.
- Listing an equivalence class with elements outside the given set A.
- Forgetting that each element must belong to its own class (reflexivity).

steps.title: Where it appears
steps.body: Clock arithmetic (mod 12), grouping students by section, file types on a computer — all are partitions created by equivalence relations.

activity.prompt: Which relations are equivalence relations?

items.text: a R b if a − b is divisible by 5, on ℤ
a R b if a < b, on ℝ
triangles T₁ R T₂ if T₁ is similar to T₂
lines L₁ R L₂ if L₁ ⊥ L₂
a R b if a and b have the same birthday month
a R b if a + b is odd, on ℤ

quiz.q: Equivalence classes of an equivalence relation on A are
quiz.why: The equivalence classes are non-empty, pairwise disjoint and together make up A, so they form a partition of A.

quiz.q: For R = {(a,b): 2 | a − b} on ℤ, the class [1] is
quiz.why: x is related to 1 when x − 1 is even, which means x is odd. So the class of 1 is the set of odd integers.

quiz.q: Number of equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3} containing (1, 2) and (2, 1)
quiz.why: Since 1 and 2 must be in the same class, the partition is either {1,2},{3} or {1,2,3}. So there are 2 such relations.

quiz.q: Similarity of triangles is
quiz.why: Every triangle is similar to itself, if one is similar to another the reverse holds, and similarity carries over a chain. So it is an equivalence relation.

quiz.q: If R is an equivalence relation and a R b, then
quiz.why: If a R b, then anything related to a is related to b by symmetry and transitivity, so [a] = [b].

lessons.title: One-one, onto and bijective functions

scenes.text: Each roll number is assigned exactly one seat — that makes the assignment a function.
If no two students share a seat it is one-one; if no seat is empty it is onto. A perfect seating is a bijection.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Let f : A → B.

- **One-one (injective)**: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ x₁ = x₂.
- **Onto (surjective)**: every y ∈ B has some x ∈ A with f(x) = y, i.e. range = codomain.
- **Bijective**: both one-one and onto.

For finite A and B with |A| = |B|, one-one ⇔ onto.

steps.title: Solved: f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 3 − 4x
steps.body:
One-one: 3 − 4x₁ = 3 − 4x₂ ⇒ x₁ = x₂ ✔.

Onto: for any y, put x = (3 − y)/4 ∈ ℝ; then f(x) = y ✔.

Hence bijective.

steps.title: Solved: f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x²
steps.body:
Not one-one: f(−2) = f(2) = 4.

Not onto: −1 has no pre-image because x² ≥ 0.

But g : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞), g(x) = x² is bijective — the domain and codomain matter!

steps.title: Solved: f : ℕ → ℕ, f(n) = n + 1 if n odd, n − 1 if n even
steps.body:
f(1) = 2, f(2) = 1, f(3) = 4, f(4) = 3, … It swaps 1↔2, 3↔4, …

One-one: different inputs land on different outputs (check odd/odd, even/even, odd/even cases — parities of outputs differ in the mixed case).

Onto: an odd m is f(m + 1), an even m is f(m − 1). So bijective.

steps.title: Counting
steps.body: If |A| = m and |B| = n: number of functions A → B is nᵐ; number of one-one functions is n!/(n − m)! (m ≤ n); number of bijections from A to A with |A| = n is n!.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking onto without stating the codomain.
- Showing one-one with a couple of numbers instead of the algebraic argument.
- Forgetting the pre-image must lie in the domain (e.g. x = y/2 is not in ℤ for odd y, so f(x) = 2x on ℤ → ℤ is not onto).

activity.prompt: Classify f : ℝ → ℝ

quiz.q: f : ℤ → ℤ, f(x) = 2x is
quiz.why: f(x) = 2x gives different outputs for different inputs, so it is one-one. Odd integers are never obtained, so it is not onto.

quiz.q: Number of functions from {1,2,3} to {a,b}
quiz.why: Each of the 3 elements can be mapped to either of 2 values, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 functions.

quiz.q: Number of bijections on a set with 4 elements
quiz.why: A bijection on 4 elements is a rearrangement of them, and there are 4! = 24.

quiz.q: f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = x³ is
quiz.why: x³ is strictly increasing, so it is one-one, and it takes every real value, so it is onto. Hence it is bijective.

quiz.q: For finite sets with |A| = |B|, a one-one map A → B is
quiz.why: For finite sets of the same size, n distinct images fill all n elements of the codomain, so a one-one map is also onto.

lessons.title: Composition and invertible functions

scenes.text: An app converts dollars to rupees, then adds 18% GST. Two functions applied one after another — a composition.
To get back the original dollars, you undo GST first, then undo conversion: the inverse of a composition reverses the order.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body:
For f : A → B and g : B → C, **g∘f : A → C** is (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)). Usually g∘f ≠ f∘g.

*Board note*: some current board syllabi keep only the definitions of one-one/onto; composition and inverses remain important for JEE and later chapters (inverse trig). Check your board's syllabus.

steps.title: Invertible function
steps.body:
f : A → B is **invertible** if there is g : B → A with g∘f = I_A and f∘g = I_B. Then g = f⁻¹.

**Theorem**: f is invertible ⇔ f is bijective. Also (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x²
steps.body:
(g∘f)(x) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.

(f∘g)(x) = 2x² + 1.

Different, so composition is not commutative.

steps.title: Solved: inverse of f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 4x + 3
steps.body:
Step 1: f is bijective (linear, non-zero slope).

Step 2: put y = 4x + 3 ⇒ x = (y − 3)/4.

Step 3: f⁻¹(y) = (y − 3)/4. Check: f(f⁻¹(y)) = 4·(y − 3)/4 + 3 = y ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x). The inverse function is **not** the reciprocal.
- Computing (g∘f) as g first, then f — the right-hand function acts first.
- Finding a formula for f⁻¹ without first checking f is bijective on the given domain.

activity.prompt: Find the inverse.

quiz.q: If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 3x, then (g∘f)(2) =
A function is invertible iff it is
quiz.why: A function has an inverse only if it is both one-one and onto, which means bijective.

quiz.q: (g∘f)⁻¹ equals
quiz.why: To undo g∘f, undo g first and then f, so (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.

quiz.q: If f(x) = x³ on ℝ, f⁻¹(8) =
quiz.why: f⁻¹(8) is the number whose cube is 8, which is 2.

quiz.q: f∘f for f(x) = 1 − x is
quiz.why: f(f(x)) = 1 − (1 − x) = x, so f∘f is the identity and f is its own inverse.

questions.q: A relation on A = {1, 2, 3} is a subset of
questions.why: By definition a relation on A is a subset of the Cartesian product A × A.

questions.q: The identity relation on A is
questions.why: The identity relation {(a, a)} is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.

questions.q: Which is an equivalence relation on ℤ?
options: a R b ⇔ a − b even
questions.why: Same parity is reflexive, symmetric, transitive. (ab > 0 fails reflexivity at 0.)

questions.q: f : ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = 5x − 2 is
questions.why: 5x − 2 is linear with non-zero slope, so it is one-one, and every real y has the pre-image (y + 2)/5, so it is onto. Hence it is bijective.

questions.q: Number of relations on a set of 2 elements
questions.why: A × A has 2 × 2 = 4 pairs and each subset is a relation, so there are 2⁴ = 16 relations.

questions.q: Assertion (A): f : ℕ → ℕ, f(x) = x² is one-one. Reason (R): f(x) = x² is onto ℕ.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: on ℕ, different numbers have different squares, so f is one-one. R is false: 2, for example, is not a perfect square, so f is not onto.
All (a, a) are present, so R is reflexive. (1,2) is there but (2,1) is not, so it is not symmetric. Transitivity holds, so it is reflexive and transitive, not symmetric.

questions.q: Number of one-one functions from {1,2} to {a,b,c}
questions.why: The first element has 3 choices and the second has 2 remaining, so there are 3 × 2 = 6 one-one functions.

questions.q: Case: In a class, R = {(x, y) : x and y were born in the same month}. The number of equivalence classes at most is
questions.why: People born in the same month are related, so there is one class per month. A year has 12 months, so at most 12 equivalence classes exist.

questions.q: f : ℝ − {0} → ℝ, f(x) = 1/x is
questions.why: 1/x gives different outputs for different inputs, so it is one-one. It never equals 0, so 0 in ℝ has no pre-image and it is not onto.

questions.q: Minimum number of ordered pairs to add to R = {(1,2),(2,3)} on {1,2,3} to make it reflexive and transitive
questions.why: For reflexivity add (1,1), (2,2), (3,3). Since (1,2) and (2,3) are in R, transitivity needs (1,3). That is 4 pairs at least.
Substituting f(x) into itself: numerator 3(3x+2)+2(5x−3) = 19x and denominator 5(3x+2)−3(5x−3) = 19, so f(f(x)) = 19x/19 = x.
On [0, ∞), x² − 1 is strictly increasing, so it is one-one. Its values cover all of [−1, ∞), so it is onto.

questions.q: Number of equivalence relations on {1, 2, 3}
questions.why: Each equivalence relation matches a partition of the set. A 3-element set has 5 partitions: {1,2,3}; three of the form {a,b},{c}; and {1},{2},{3}.

questions.q: If f : A → B is bijective with |A| = 5, the number of bijections from A to B is
questions.why: Since the function is bijective, |B| = 5 as well. The number of bijections from a 5-element set to a 5-element set is 5! = 120.

questions.q: f(x) = |x| on ℝ → ℝ is
questions.why: |x| is not one-one, since f(1) = f(−1) = 1. It is not onto ℝ either, as negative numbers are never outputs. So it is neither.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Inverse Trigonometric Functions
courses.summary: Principal value branches, domains and ranges, graphs by reflection, and the standard identities used in calculus.
outcomes: Learners can state domain and principal range of all six inverse trig functions
Learners can find principal values of positive and negative arguments
Learners can sketch and read the graphs
Learners can simplify expressions using complementary identities

lessons.title: Why principal value branches?

scenes.text: An engineer knows a ramp rises 1 m for every 2 m along the slope, so sin θ = 1/2. Many angles have sine 1/2 — which one is meant?
Restricting sine to [−π/2, π/2] gives a single answer: θ = π/6. That restriction is the principal value branch.

steps.title: The idea
steps.body:
sin, cos, tan … are not one-one on ℝ (they repeat), so they have no inverse on ℝ. We **restrict the domain** to an interval where the function is one-one and onto its range, then invert.

sin⁻¹x means the angle in the principal branch whose sine is x. It is **not** 1/sin x.

steps.title: Solved: principal value of sin⁻¹(−1/2)
steps.body:
Step 1: we need θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2] with sin θ = −1/2.

Step 2: sin(π/6) = 1/2 and sine is odd, so sin(−π/6) = −1/2.

Answer: −π/6.

steps.title: Solved: principal value of cos⁻¹(−√3/2)
steps.body:
Step 1: θ ∈ [0, π] with cos θ = −√3/2.

Step 2: cos(π/6) = √3/2; cos(π − θ) = −cos θ, so θ = π − π/6 = 5π/6.

Answer: 5π/6 (not −π/6, which is outside [0, π]).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving a negative answer for cos⁻¹ or cot⁻¹ — their ranges are inside [0, π].
- Writing sin⁻¹(2): it is undefined because the domain is [−1, 1].
- Confusing sin⁻¹x with (sin x)⁻¹.

steps.title: Quick rule for negatives
steps.body: sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x, tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹x, cosec⁻¹(−x) = −cosec⁻¹x, but cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x, cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹x, sec⁻¹(−x) = π − sec⁻¹x.

activity.prompt: Match each function with its principal range

quiz.q: Principal value of tan⁻¹(−1)
quiz.why: The principal value of tan⁻¹ lies in (−π/2, π/2). Since tan(−π/4) = −1, tan⁻¹(−1) = −π/4.

quiz.q: Domain of cos⁻¹x
quiz.why: cos⁻¹x is defined only when x is a possible cosine value, so its domain is [−1, 1].

quiz.q: Principal value of cot⁻¹(−√3)
quiz.why: cot⁻¹ has range (0, π). cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹x, so cot⁻¹(−√3) = π − π/6 = 5π/6.

quiz.q: Principal value of sec⁻¹(2)
quiz.why: sec⁻¹(2) is the angle in [0, π] with sec = 2, so cos = 1/2, which gives π/3.

quiz.q: sin⁻¹(3/2) is
quiz.why: sin⁻¹ is defined only for values in [−1, 1]. Since 3/2 is greater than 1, sin⁻¹(3/2) is undefined.

lessons.title: Graphs of inverse trigonometric functions

story.title: Mirror on the line y = x

scenes.text: Riya folds her graph paper along y = x. The sine curve on [−π/2, π/2] lands exactly on the graph of sin⁻¹x.
Every inverse function's graph is the mirror image of the original (restricted) graph in y = x.

steps.title: Reflection principle
steps.body: If (a, b) lies on y = f(x), then (b, a) lies on y = f⁻¹(x). So the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

steps.title: Shapes described in words
steps.body:
- **y = sin⁻¹x**: from (−1, −π/2) through (0, 0) to (1, π/2); increasing, an S-like arc, steep at the ends.
- **y = cos⁻¹x**: from (−1, π) through (0, π/2) to (1, 0); decreasing.
- **y = tan⁻¹x**: defined for all x, increasing, passes through (0, 0), with horizontal asymptotes y = ±π/2.
- **y = cot⁻¹x**: decreasing, from near π (x → −∞) to near 0 (x → ∞), value π/2 at x = 0.

steps.title: Solved: read values from the graph of sin⁻¹
steps.body: At x = 1/2 the curve is at height π/6 ≈ 0.52; at x = −√3/2 it is at −π/3 ≈ −1.05. These match sin(π/6) = 1/2 and sin(−π/3) = −√3/2.

steps.title: Solved: domain of f(x) = sin⁻¹(2x − 1)
steps.body:
Step 1: need −1 ≤ 2x − 1 ≤ 1.

Step 2: add 1: 0 ≤ 2x ≤ 2 ⇒ 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.

Domain: [0, 1].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing tan⁻¹x crossing y = π/2: it only approaches the asymptote.
- Drawing cos⁻¹x increasing — it decreases from π to 0.
- Forgetting the closed endpoints for sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ at x = ±1.

statements.s: The graph of tan⁻¹x has horizontal asymptotes y = π/2 and y = −π/2.
y = cos⁻¹x is an increasing function.
The graph of sin⁻¹x passes through the origin.
The domain of sin⁻¹(x/3) is [−3, 3].

quiz.q: Graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of graph of f in
quiz.why: The graph of an inverse function swaps the x and y coordinates of every point, which reflects it in the line y = x.

quiz.q: Domain of cos⁻¹(3x)
quiz.why: cos⁻¹(3x) needs −1 ≤ 3x ≤ 1, so −1/3 ≤ x ≤ 1/3.

quiz.q: Value of cot⁻¹x at x = 0
quiz.why: cot⁻¹x has range (0, π), and cot(π/2) = 0, so cot⁻¹(0) = π/2.

quiz.q: Range of tan⁻¹x includes π/2?
quiz.why: The range of tan⁻¹x is the open interval (−π/2, π/2), so π/2 is not included.

quiz.q: Domain of sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x
quiz.why: Both sin⁻¹x and cos⁻¹x need x in [−1, 1], so their sum is defined on the common domain [−1, 1].

lessons.title: Useful identities and evaluating expressions

scenes.text: A navigation puzzle asks for sin⁻¹(0.6) + cos⁻¹(0.6). Without a calculator, Kabir answers π/2 instantly.
He used the complementary identity — a tool that turns hard-looking expressions into one-liners.

steps.title: Identities (valid in the stated domains)
steps.body:
- sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2, x ∈ [−1, 1]
- tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2, x ∈ ℝ
- sec⁻¹x + cosec⁻¹x = π/2, |x| ≥ 1
- sin⁻¹(1/x) = cosec⁻¹x, |x| ≥ 1; cos⁻¹(1/x) = sec⁻¹x; tan⁻¹(1/x) = cot⁻¹x for x > 0
- sin(sin⁻¹x) = x for x ∈ [−1, 1], but sin⁻¹(sin θ) = θ only for θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2].

*Board note*: the current CBSE syllabus emphasises definitions, ranges and graphs; these identities are standard for JEE and help in calculus.

steps.title: Solved: sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3)
steps.body:
Step 1: 2π/3 is not in [−π/2, π/2], so the answer is not 2π/3.

Step 2: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − 2π/3) = sin(π/3), and π/3 is in the branch.

Answer: π/3.

steps.title: Solved: cos(sin⁻¹(3/5))
steps.body:
Let θ = sin⁻¹(3/5), so sin θ = 3/5 with θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2] ⇒ cos θ ≥ 0.

cos θ = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cancelling sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for every x.
- Taking the negative root for cos(sin⁻¹x): in the principal branch cosine is ≥ 0.
- Mixing degrees and radians in one answer.

lessons.title: What a matrix is: order and types

scenes.text: Anu's stationery shop sells pens, pencils and erasers in two branches. She writes the stock as a 2 × 3 table.
That rectangular table of numbers is a matrix — and it lets her add, scale and multiply whole tables at once.

steps.title: Definition and order
steps.body: A **matrix** is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with m rows and n columns has **order m × n** and mn elements. The element in row i, column j is written aᵢⱼ, and A = [aᵢⱼ]ₘₓₙ.

steps.title: Types of matrices
steps.body:
- **Row matrix** 1 × n; **column matrix** m × 1.
- **Square matrix**: m = n. Its diagonal is a₁₁, a₂₂, …
- **Diagonal**: square, all off-diagonal entries 0.
- **Scalar**: diagonal with all diagonal entries equal.
- **Identity Iₙ**: scalar with diagonal entries 1.
- **Zero matrix O**: all entries 0.
- **Equal matrices**: same order and every corresponding entry equal.

steps.title: Solved: construct A = [aᵢⱼ]₂ₓ₂ with aᵢⱼ = (i + j)²/2
Solved: possible orders of a matrix with 12 elements
steps.body: We need m × n = 12: 1×12, 12×1, 2×6, 6×2, 3×4, 4×3. **Six** possible orders. (With 7 elements — a prime — only 1×7 and 7×1.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing order as columns × rows. It is always **rows × columns**.
- Calling any square matrix with zeros 'diagonal' — the off-diagonal entries must all be 0.
- Comparing matrices of different orders for equality.

quiz.why: A 2 × 2 matrix has 4 entries, and each can be 0 or 1, so there are 2⁴ = 16 matrices.

quiz.q: Number of possible orders for a matrix with 13 elements
quiz.why: 13 is prime, so it factors only as 1 × 13 or 13 × 1. There are 2 possible orders.

lessons.title: Operations: addition, scalar multiple, multiplication

scenes.text: Anu multiplies her stock matrix by a price column to get each branch's stock value in one step.
She notices: stock × price works, but price × stock does not even have the right shape — matrix multiplication is not commutative.

steps.title: Addition and scalar multiplication
steps.body:
For A, B of the **same order**, A + B = [aᵢⱼ + bᵢⱼ]. kA = [k·aᵢⱼ].

Properties: A + B = B + A, (A + B) + C = A + (B + C), k(A + B) = kA + kB, A + O = A.

steps.title: Multiplication
steps.body:
If A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p with (AB)ᵢₖ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ bⱼₖ (row i of A · column k of B).

Properties: (AB)C = A(BC), A(B + C) = AB + AC, AI = IA = A. In general **AB ≠ BA**, and AB = O does not force A = O or B = O.

steps.title: Solved: AB = O with non-zero matrices
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying entry-by-entry (that is not matrix multiplication).
- Expanding (A + B)² as A² + 2AB + B². Correct: A² + AB + BA + B² (equal only if AB = BA).
- Forgetting to check that columns of A = rows of B before multiplying.

steps.title: Real use
steps.body: Computer graphics rotate and scale images with matrix products; recommendation systems store user × item ratings as matrices.

lessons.title: Transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices

scenes.text: Anu's assistant writes the stock table sideways — branches as columns. That sideways table is the transpose.
Some tables look the same after flipping. Those are symmetric matrices, like a distance chart between cities.

steps.title: Transpose and its properties
steps.body:
A′ (or Aᵀ) is obtained by turning rows into columns: if A = [aᵢⱼ]ₘₓₙ, A′ = [aⱼᵢ]ₙₓₘ.

- (A′)′ = A
- (kA)′ = kA′
- (A + B)′ = A′ + B′
- **(AB)′ = B′A′** (order reverses)

steps.title: Symmetric and skew-symmetric
steps.body:
Square A is **symmetric** if A′ = A (aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ), **skew-symmetric** if A′ = −A (aᵢⱼ = −aⱼᵢ; so every diagonal entry is 0).

**Theorem**: every square matrix is uniquely P + Q with P = ½(A + A′) symmetric and Q = ½(A − A′) skew-symmetric.

steps.title: Solved: express A = [[2, 4], [6, 8]] as P + Q
Solved: for any square A, A + A′ is symmetric
steps.body: (A + A′)′ = A′ + (A′)′ = A′ + A = A + A′. Similarly (A − A′)′ = A′ − A = −(A − A′), so A − A′ is skew-symmetric.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (AB)′ = A′B′.
- Putting non-zero diagonal entries in a skew-symmetric matrix.
- Forgetting the ½ in the decomposition.

statements.s: The diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix are all zero.
(AB)′ = A′B′ for all compatible A, B.
A matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric must be the zero matrix.
AA′ is always symmetric.

quiz.why: The transpose swaps rows and columns, so a 3 × 5 matrix becomes 5 × 3.

quiz.why: A skew-symmetric matrix has a zero diagonal, since aᵢᵢ = −aᵢᵢ. So the sum of its diagonal entries is 0.

lessons.title: Invertible matrices

scenes.text: Two friends encode messages by multiplying number-blocks by a matrix A.
To decode they multiply by A⁻¹. If A had no inverse, the message could never be recovered.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A square matrix A is **invertible** if there is B with **AB = BA = I**. Then B = A⁻¹, and it is unique.

Properties: (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A, (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, (A′)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)′. A non-square matrix has no inverse.

*Note*: The quick way to find inverses uses determinants (next chapter). For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] with ad − bc ≠ 0, the inverse is (1/(ad − bc))·[[d, −b], [−c, a]].

steps.title: Solved: verify B is the inverse of A by multiplication
Solved: if A² − 5A + 7I = O, find A⁻¹ in terms of A
steps.body: Multiply by A⁻¹: A − 5I + 7A⁻¹ = O ⇒ A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹.
- Inverting entry by entry (1/aᵢⱼ) — that is wrong.
- Trying to invert a matrix whose ad − bc = 0 (it is singular).

quiz.why: The inverse of a product reverses the order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

quiz.q: Inverse of [[3, 0], [0, 2]]
quiz.why: The inverse of a diagonal matrix has the reciprocals of the diagonal entries: diag(1/3, 1/2).

quiz.q: Which matrix has no inverse?
quiz.why: A matrix has no inverse when its determinant is 0. For [[1,2],[2,4]], 1·4 − 2·2 = 0.

quiz.q: If A² = I, then A⁻¹ =
quiz.why: If A·A = I, then A is its own inverse, so A⁻¹ = A.

lessons.title: Evaluating determinants

story.title: A number that judges a matrix

scenes.text: Every square matrix carries one special number — its determinant — that decides whether the matrix can be inverted.
Geometrically, a 2 × 2 determinant measures how much a shape's area is scaled by the matrix.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For A = [[a, b], [c, d]]: |A| = ad − bc.

For a 3 × 3 matrix, expand along any row or column using signs + − + / − + − / + − +:
|A| = a₁₁(a₂₂a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₂) − a₁₂(a₂₁a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₁) + a₁₃(a₂₁a₃₂ − a₂₂a₃₁).

Only **square** matrices have determinants.

steps.title: Solved: |[[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 4], [5, 6, 0]]|
steps.body:
Expand along row 1:

1·(1·0 − 4·6) − 2·(0·0 − 4·5) + 3·(0·6 − 1·5) = −24 + 40 − 15 = **1**.

Tip: expanding along a row/column with most zeros saves time.

steps.title: Key results
steps.body:
- |A′| = |A|
- |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n × n matrix
- |AB| = |A||B|
- If two rows are identical (or proportional), |A| = 0

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the alternating sign on the middle term.
- Writing |3A| = 3|A| for a 3 × 3 matrix — it is 27|A|.
- Confusing determinant bars with absolute value (a determinant can be negative).

quiz.why: For a 2 × 2 determinant ad − bc = 5·4 − 3·2 = 20 − 6 = 14.

quiz.why: For an n × n matrix |kA| = kⁿ|A|. Here |3A| = 3³ × 2 = 27 × 2 = 54.

quiz.why: If two rows are equal, subtracting one from the other gives a zero row without changing the determinant, so |A| = 0.
For a diagonal matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: 1 × 2 × 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Area of a triangle using determinants

scenes.text: A surveyor gives the corners of a triangular field as coordinates (1, 0), (6, 0) and (4, 3) in units of 10 m.
One determinant gives the area — and if it is zero, the three points are on a straight line.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
Area of triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃):

Δ = ½ |[[x₁, y₁, 1], [x₂, y₂, 1], [x₃, y₃, 1]]|, taking the **absolute value** of the result.

Three points are **collinear** ⇔ this determinant is 0.

steps.title: Solved: vertices (1, 0), (6, 0), (4, 3)
steps.body:
Expand: 1(0 − 3) − 0(6 − 4) + 1(18 − 0) = −3 + 18 = 15.

Δ = ½·15 = **7.5 square units**. With 1 unit = 10 m, one square unit is 100 m², so the field is 750 m².

Solved: k when area is 4 with vertices (k, 0), (4, 0), (0, 2)

- Forgetting **both** values of k when area is given (the ± case).
- Missing the ½.

lessons.title: Minors, cofactors, adjoint and inverse

scenes.text: A locksmith app needs A⁻¹ for a 3 × 3 code matrix. Guessing is impossible.
Minors → cofactors → adjoint → divide by |A|: a recipe that always works when |A| ≠ 0.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Minor Mᵢⱼ**: determinant left after deleting row i and column j.
- **Cofactor Aᵢⱼ** = (−1)^(i+j) Mᵢⱼ.
- **adj A** = transpose of the cofactor matrix.
- **A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I**, so if |A| ≠ 0, **A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|**.
- A is **singular** if |A| = 0, non-singular otherwise. Invertible ⇔ non-singular.

steps.title: Useful results (n × n)
steps.body:
- |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹
- |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|
- adj(AB) = (adj B)(adj A)
- For 2 × 2 [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].

steps.title: Solved: |adj A| when A is 3 × 3 with |A| = 5
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to **transpose** the cofactor matrix.
- Sign slips in cofactors: use the checkerboard + − +.
- Writing |adj A| = |A|ⁿ instead of |A|ⁿ⁻¹.

lessons.title: Solving linear equations by the matrix method

scenes.text: Three customers buy different mixes of apples, bananas and mangoes and pay ₹6, ₹5 and ₹11 (in tens). The prices are unknown.
Writing the purchases as AX = B and computing X = A⁻¹B gives all three prices at once.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Write the system as **AX = B**.

- If |A| ≠ 0: unique solution X = A⁻¹B (consistent).
- If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O: no solution (inconsistent).
- If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O: the system may have infinitely many solutions or none — check further.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing BA⁻¹ instead of A⁻¹B.
- Concluding 'infinitely many solutions' as soon as |A| = 0.
- Arithmetic slips — always substitute the answer back.

steps.title: Real use
steps.body: Circuit analysis (Kirchhoff's laws), mixing problems and economic input–output models all reduce to AX = B.

activity.prompt: Solve x + y = 7, x − y = 1 by any method. Enter x.

quiz.why: When |A| ≠ 0, A⁻¹ exists and X = A⁻¹B, which gives exactly one solution.

quiz.q: If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O, the system is
quiz.why: If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O, the system has no solution, so it is inconsistent.

quiz.q: x + 2y = 3, 2x + 4y = 6 has
quiz.why: The second equation is twice the first, so they describe the same line. So there are infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: Solution X equals
quiz.why: Multiply AX = B on the left by A⁻¹ to get X = A⁻¹B.

quiz.q: Homogeneous system AX = O with |A| ≠ 0 has
quiz.why: If |A| ≠ 0, then X = A⁻¹O = O, so only the trivial solution exists.

lessons.title: Continuity at a point and on an interval

scenes.text: Teacher: 'If you can draw the graph without lifting your pencil, the function is continuous there.'
Meera asks how to *prove* it without a drawing. The answer: compare the left limit, right limit and the value.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
f is **continuous at x = c** if f(c) is defined and

lim(x→c⁻) f(x) = lim(x→c⁺) f(x) = f(c).

f is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it (one-sided at closed ends).

steps.title: Continuous families
steps.body: Polynomials, sin x, cos x, eˣ, |x| are continuous everywhere; rational functions, tan x, log x are continuous wherever they are defined. Sums, differences, products, quotients (denominator ≠ 0) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous.

steps.title: Solved: find k so f is continuous at x = 5
Solved: is f(x) = x/|x| (x ≠ 0), f(0) = 1 continuous at 0?
steps.body:
For x > 0, f = 1, so RHL = 1. For x < 0, f = −1, so LHL = −1.

LHL ≠ RHL ⇒ the limit does not exist ⇒ **discontinuous** at 0 (a jump).

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = (sin x)/x for x ≠ 0, f(0) = k
steps.body: lim(x→0) sin x / x = 1, so continuity needs **k = 1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking only one side of a piecewise function.
- Saying 1/x is discontinuous at x = 0 'in its domain' — 0 is not in its domain; 1/x is continuous on its domain.
- Forgetting the value f(c) must equal the common limit.

activity.prompt: f(x) = 2x + k for x < 2 and x² for x ≥ 2. Find k for continuity at 2.

quiz.why: |x| has left and right limits of 0 at x = 0, and f(0) = 0, so it is continuous there.

quiz.why: The greatest integer function jumps at every integer, so it is discontinuous at each integer.

quiz.why: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0, so it is discontinuous at x = π/2.

quiz.q: Sum of two continuous functions is
quiz.why: The sum of two continuous functions is continuous at every point.

lessons.title: Differentiability and the chain rule

scenes.text: A car's position s(t) is smooth. Its speed at any instant is the derivative s′(t).
But a path with a sharp corner — like |x| at 0 — has no single slope there: continuous, yet not differentiable.

steps.title: Differentiability
steps.body:
f is differentiable at c if the left-hand derivative lim(h→0⁻)[f(c + h) − f(c)]/h equals the right-hand derivative lim(h→0⁺)[f(c + h) − f(c)]/h.

**Differentiable ⇒ continuous**, but continuous ⇏ differentiable (|x| at 0: LHD = −1, RHD = +1).

steps.title: Chain rule
steps.body: If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x))·g′(x). In Leibniz form, with u = g(x): dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).

steps.title: Solved: d/dx sin(x²)
steps.body: Let u = x². dy/du = cos u, du/dx = 2x. So dy/dx = **2x cos(x²)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inside (writing d/dx sin(x²) = cos(x²)).
- Assuming continuity implies differentiability.
- Treating sin²x as sin(x²): d/dx sin²x = 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x.

activity.prompt: Match the function with its derivative

quiz.q: |x| is differentiable at 0?
quiz.why: At 0 the left derivative of |x| is −1 and the right derivative is +1, so they differ and |x| is not differentiable at 0.

quiz.q: d/dx sin(5x) =
quiz.why: By the chain rule d/dx sin(5x) = cos(5x) × 5 = 5 cos 5x.

quiz.q: d/dx (3x − 1)⁴ =
quiz.why: By the chain rule d/dx (3x − 1)⁴ = 4(3x − 1)³ × 3 = 12(3x − 1)³.

quiz.q: If f is differentiable at c, then f is
quiz.why: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there, but not the other way round.

quiz.q: d/dx cos²x =
quiz.why: d/dx cos²x = 2 cos x × (−sin x) = −2 sin x cos x = −sin 2x.

lessons.title: Implicit functions and inverse trigonometric derivatives

story.title: A circle that won't solve for y

scenes.text: The circle x² + y² = 25 can't be written as one function y = f(x). Yet its slope at (3, 4) is needed for a design.
Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x.

steps.title: Implicit differentiation
steps.body: Differentiate every term with respect to x; whenever you differentiate a term in y, multiply by dy/dx. Then collect dy/dx terms and solve.

steps.title: Inverse trig derivatives
steps.body:
- d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1 − x²)
- d/dx cos⁻¹x = −1/√(1 − x²)
- d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1 + x²)
- d/dx cot⁻¹x = −1/(1 + x²)
- d/dx sec⁻¹x = 1/(|x|√(x² − 1))
- d/dx cosec⁻¹x = −1/(|x|√(x² − 1))

steps.title: Solved: x³ + y³ = 3axy
steps.body: 3x² + 3y² y′ = 3a(y + x y′) ⇒ y′(y² − ax) = ay − x² ⇒ **y′ = (ay − x²)/(y² − ax)**.

steps.title: Solved: d/dx sin⁻¹(2x)
steps.body: Chain rule: 2/√(1 − 4x²), for |x| < 1/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing d/dx(y²) = 2y (forgetting dy/dx).
- Using the product rule wrongly on xy: d/dx(xy) = y + x dy/dx.
- Missing the minus sign for cos⁻¹ and cot⁻¹.

activity.prompt: Complete.

lessons.title: Exponential, logarithmic and logarithmic differentiation

scenes.text: A lab culture grows like N = N₀eᵏᵗ. Its growth rate is proportional to its size.
For tricky powers like xˣ, taking logs first turns a hard derivative into an easy one.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- d/dx eˣ = eˣ;  d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a
- d/dx ln x = 1/x (x > 0);  d/dx logₐx = 1/(x ln a)
- Log laws: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b, ln(aⁿ) = n ln a

steps.title: Logarithmic differentiation
steps.body: Use it for y = [f(x)]^g(x) or messy products/quotients. Take ln of both sides, simplify with log laws, differentiate implicitly, multiply back by y.

steps.title: Solved: y = xˣ (x > 0)
steps.body: ln y = x ln x ⇒ (1/y)y′ = ln x + 1 ⇒ **y′ = xˣ(1 + ln x)**.

steps.title: Solved: y = e^(sin x)
steps.body: y′ = e^(sin x)·cos x.

steps.title: Solved: y = (sin x)^x
steps.body: ln y = x ln sin x ⇒ y′/y = ln sin x + x cot x ⇒ y′ = (sin x)^x [ln sin x + x cot x].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating xˣ with the power rule (x·x^(x−1)) or with the exponential rule only — both are wrong; use logs.
- Writing d/dx 2ˣ = x·2^(x−1). Correct: 2ˣ ln 2.
- Using ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b (false).

statements.s: d/dx 3ˣ = 3ˣ ln 3
d/dx xˣ = x·xˣ⁻¹
statements.why: Use logarithmic differentiation: xˣ(1 + ln x).

statements.s: d/dx ln(5x) = 1/x
ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b

quiz.why: By the chain rule d/dx e^(3x) = e^(3x) × 3 = 3e^(3x).

quiz.why: d/dx ln(cos x) = (−sin x)/cos x = −tan x.

quiz.why: y = xˣ gives y′ = xˣ(1 + ln x). At x = 1 this is 1 × (1 + 0) = 1.

quiz.why: log₁₀x = ln x / ln 10, so its derivative is 1/(x ln 10).

quiz.q: d/dx e^(x²) =
quiz.why: By the chain rule d/dx e^(x²) = e^(x²) × 2x = 2x e^(x²).

lessons.title: Parametric forms and second-order derivatives

story.title: A ball's flight described by time

scenes.text: A football's position is given by x = 20t and y = 15t − 5t². Both depend on time t.
dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) gives the slope of the path at any moment; the second derivative tells how the slope itself changes.

steps.title: Parametric differentiation
steps.body:
If x = f(t), y = g(t) and f′(t) ≠ 0, then **dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)**.

Second derivative: d²y/dx² = d/dx(dy/dx) = [d/dt(dy/dx)] / (dx/dt).

steps.title: Solved: x = a cos θ, y = a sin θ
steps.body: dx/dθ = −a sin θ, dy/dθ = a cos θ ⇒ dy/dx = **−cot θ**.

steps.title: Solved: y = 5 cos x − 3 sin x; show y″ + y = 0
steps.body: y′ = −5 sin x − 3 cos x; y″ = −5 cos x + 3 sin x = −y ⇒ y″ + y = 0 ✔

steps.title: Solved: y = x³ + tan x
steps.body: y′ = 3x² + sec²x; y″ = 6x + 2 sec²x tan x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing d²y/dx² as (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²) — wrong.
- Forgetting to divide by dx/dt again in the second derivative.
- Dropping the chain factor when differentiating sec²x.

courses.summary: Rates of change, increasing/decreasing functions, local maxima and minima by first and second derivative tests, absolute extrema and real optimisation problems.
outcomes: Learners can solve related-rate problems with correct units
Learners can find intervals of increase and decrease

lessons.title: Rate of change of quantities

scenes.text: A stone drops into a pond; the circular ripple's radius grows at 3 cm/s.
How fast is the disturbed area growing when the radius is 10 cm? Differentiate the area with respect to time.

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: If y = f(x), dy/dx is the rate of change of y with respect to x. If both depend on time t: **dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt)**. Always write units (cm²/s, ₹ per unit, …).

steps.title: Solved: ripple area
steps.body: A = πr² ⇒ dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt = 2π(10)(3) = **60π cm²/s**.

steps.title: Solved: cube
steps.body:
Volume of a cube grows at 9 cm³/s. When side x = 10 cm: dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt ⇒ 9 = 300 dx/dt ⇒ dx/dt = 0.03 cm/s.

Surface S = 6x² ⇒ dS/dt = 12x dx/dt = 12·10·0.03 = **3.6 cm²/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Substituting the specific value (r = 10) **before** differentiating.
- Forgetting units or writing cm/s for an area rate.
- Sign errors: a decreasing quantity has a negative rate.

activity.prompt: A balloon's radius increases at 0.5 cm/s. Rate of increase of its surface area (4πr²) when r = 7 cm, in cm²/s, using π = 22/7?

quiz.why: dA/dr = 2πr, so at r = 5 it is 10π.

quiz.q: Area rate units if length is in cm and time in s
quiz.why: A rate of change of area has units of area per time, so cm²/s.

quiz.q: Marginal revenue is
quiz.why: Marginal revenue is the rate of change of total revenue with respect to quantity, R′(x).

quiz.q: Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; dV/dt when r = 3, dr/dt = 1
quiz.why: dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt = 4π(9)(1) = 36π.

quiz.q: A quantity that is decreasing has rate
quiz.why: A decreasing quantity has a negative rate of change.

lessons.title: Increasing and decreasing functions

scenes.text: A startup's monthly profit first rises, then falls. The owner wants the exact months where the trend switches.
The sign of the derivative answers it: f′ > 0 means rising, f′ < 0 means falling.

steps.title: Test
steps.body:
On an interval where f is differentiable:

- f′(x) > 0 ⇒ f strictly increasing
- f′(x) < 0 ⇒ f strictly decreasing
- f′(x) = 0 throughout ⇒ f constant

Method: find f′, solve f′(x) = 0 to get critical points, split the number line, test the sign in each interval.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 36x + 7
steps.body:
f′(x) = 6x² − 6x − 36 = 6(x − 3)(x + 2). Zeros: x = −2, 3.

- x < −2: f′ > 0 → increasing
- −2 < x < 3: f′ < 0 → decreasing
- x > 3: f′ > 0 → increasing

So f increases on (−∞, −2) ∪ (3, ∞) and decreases on (−2, 3).

steps.title: Solved: show f(x) = eˣ is increasing on ℝ
steps.body: f′(x) = eˣ > 0 for every real x ⇒ strictly increasing.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = sin x + cos x on [0, π/2]
steps.body: f′(x) = cos x − sin x. It is positive on [0, π/4) and negative on (π/4, π/2]. Increasing on [0, π/4], decreasing on [π/4, π/2].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking f′(c) = 0 at one point spoils strict increase: x³ is strictly increasing on ℝ even though f′(0) = 0.
- Testing only one point for the whole number line.
- Forgetting to factor f′ fully.

activity.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x: where is it increasing or decreasing?

quiz.q: f(x) = x² is decreasing on
quiz.why: f′(x) = 2x, which is negative for x < 0, so x² is decreasing on (−∞, 0).

quiz.q: f(x) = 3x + 5 is
quiz.why: f′(x) = 3 > 0 everywhere, so the function is increasing.

quiz.q: f(x) = log x is increasing on
quiz.why: f′(x) = 1/x is positive for x > 0, so log x is increasing on its whole domain (0, ∞).

quiz.q: Critical points of f(x) = x³ − 3x
quiz.why: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x² = 1, so the critical points are x = ±1.

quiz.q: f(x) = e^(−x) is
quiz.why: f′(x) = −e^(−x) is always negative, so e^(−x) is decreasing.

lessons.title: Maxima and minima: first and second derivative tests

scenes.text: A hiker's altitude along a trail is a function of distance. At the top, the slope is zero; just before it is positive and just after negative.
That sign change is the first derivative test. The curvature (second derivative) is a quicker check.

steps.title: First derivative test
steps.body:
At a critical point c (f′(c) = 0 or undefined):

- f′ changes + to − ⇒ **local maximum**
- f′ changes − to + ⇒ **local minimum**
- no sign change ⇒ neither (point of inflection, e.g. x³ at 0)

steps.title: Second derivative test
steps.body:
If f′(c) = 0:

- f″(c) < 0 ⇒ local max
- f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local min
- f″(c) = 0 ⇒ test fails; use the first derivative test.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x⁴
steps.body: f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = 0 (test fails). f′ = 4x³ changes − to + at 0 ⇒ local min 0.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x + 1/x, x > 0
steps.body: f′ = 1 − 1/x² = 0 ⇒ x = 1. f″ = 2/x³ > 0 ⇒ local min value 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying f′(c) = 0 guarantees a max or min (x³ is a counter-example).
- Concluding 'no extremum' when f″(c) = 0 — just switch tests.
- Reporting the x-value when the question asks for the maximum **value**.

quiz.why: f′ = 3x² does not change sign at 0 (it is positive on both sides), so x = 0 is neither a maximum nor a minimum.

quiz.q: If f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = −4, c is a
quiz.why: If f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0, the curve is concave down, so c is a local maximum.

quiz.why: −(x − 1)² ≤ 0 with equality at x = 1, so the local maximum value is 0 + 10 = 10.

quiz.q: Minimum of x + 1/x for x > 0
quiz.why: f′ = 1 − 1/x² = 0 gives x = 1, and f″ > 0 there. The minimum value is 1 + 1 = 2.

quiz.q: Critical point of f(x) = x² − 4x + 3
quiz.why: f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2.

lessons.title: Absolute extrema and optimisation problems

story.title: The box from a square sheet

scenes.text: A packaging intern cuts equal squares from the corners of an 18 cm × 18 cm sheet and folds up the sides into an open box.
What cut size gives the biggest box? Optimisation with derivatives finds it exactly: 3 cm.

steps.title: Absolute extrema on [a, b]
steps.body: A continuous f on a closed interval attains an absolute max and min. Find them by evaluating f at **all critical points inside (a, b) and at the end-points a and b**; the largest is the absolute max, the smallest the absolute min.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 2]
steps.body:
f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 ⇒ x = 1 (x = −1 is outside).

f(0) = 0, f(1) = −2, f(2) = 2.

Absolute max **2** at x = 2, absolute min **−2** at x = 1.

steps.title: Solved: the open box
steps.body:
Cut x cm squares: V = x(18 − 2x)², 0 < x < 9.

V′ = (18 − 2x)² − 4x(18 − 2x) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x) = 0 ⇒ x = 3 (x = 9 gives no box).

V″ at 3 is negative (check sign change: V′ > 0 for x < 3, < 0 for 3 < x < 9) ⇒ max. V = 3·12² = **432 cm³**.

steps.title: Solved: maximum area of a rectangle with perimeter 40
steps.body: 2(x + y) = 40 ⇒ y = 20 − x. A = x(20 − x), A′ = 20 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 10, A″ = −2 < 0 ⇒ max. The rectangle is a **10 × 10 square**, area 100.

steps.title: Optimisation recipe
steps.body: 1. Draw and name variables. 2. Write the quantity to optimise. 3. Use the constraint to reduce to one variable. 4. Differentiate, find critical points in the allowed range. 5. Confirm max/min. 6. Answer the question in words with units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting end-points for absolute extrema.
- Keeping two variables in the function.
- Not stating the domain (e.g. 0 < x < 9 for the box).

activity.prompt: Two positive numbers have sum 16. What is the maximum possible product?

quiz.q: Absolute max of f(x) = x² on [−1, 3]
quiz.why: On [−1, 3], compare f at the end points and critical point: f(−1) = 1, f(0) = 0, f(3) = 9. The maximum is 9.

quiz.q: Absolute min of f(x) = x² on [−1, 3]
quiz.why: Among f(−1) = 1, f(0) = 0 and f(3) = 9, the smallest value is 0, at the critical point x = 0.

quiz.q: For fixed perimeter, the rectangle with max area is a
quiz.why: With a fixed perimeter 2(l + b), the area lb is largest when l = b, which makes the rectangle a square.

quiz.q: Max of sin x + cos x
quiz.why: sin x + cos x = √2 sin(x + π/4), so its maximum is √2.

quiz.q: In the box problem with an 18 cm sheet, cut size for max volume
quiz.why: V = x(18 − 2x)². V′ = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x) = 0 gives x = 3 for a maximum, as x = 9 gives zero volume.

lessons.title: Integration as anti-differentiation

scenes.text: Kiran's cycle computer shows speed v(t) at every second but has lost the distance record.
Reversing differentiation — integration — rebuilds the distance function from the speed.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
F is an **antiderivative** of f if F′(x) = f(x). The **indefinite integral** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant (because derivatives of constants are zero).

Properties: ∫[f ± g]dx = ∫f dx ± ∫g dx; ∫k f dx = k∫f dx.

steps.title: Standard integrals
steps.body:
- ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, n ≠ −1;  ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x| + C
- ∫eˣdx = eˣ + C;  ∫aˣdx = aˣ/ln a + C
- ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C;  ∫cos x dx = sin x + C
- ∫sec²x dx = tan x + C;  ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x + C
- ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x + C;  ∫cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C
- ∫dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + C;  ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C

steps.title: Solved: ∫(x³ + 2x − 5)dx
steps.body: x⁴/4 + x² − 5x + C.

steps.title: Solved: ∫(x² + 1)/x dx
steps.body: Split: ∫x dx + ∫(1/x)dx = x²/2 + ln|x| + C.

steps.title: Solved: ∫(2 sin x + 3 sec²x − 4eˣ)dx
steps.body: −2 cos x + 3 tan x − 4eˣ + C.

steps.title: Solved: find f if f′(x) = 4x³ − 3 and f(1) = 5
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting **+ C** in indefinite integrals.
- Using xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) for n = −1 (use ln|x|).
- Integrating a quotient by dividing integrals: ∫(f/g) ≠ ∫f / ∫g.

quiz.q: ∫x⁵dx =
quiz.why: By the power rule ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), so ∫x⁵dx = x⁶/6 + C.
The power rule fails for n = −1. The derivative of ln|x| is 1/x, so ∫(1/x)dx = ln|x| + C.

quiz.q: ∫cosec²x dx =
quiz.why: d/dx cot x = −cosec²x, so ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x + C.

quiz.q: ∫2ˣdx =
quiz.why: ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C, so ∫2ˣ dx = 2ˣ/ln 2 + C.

lessons.title: Integration by substitution and trigonometric identities

scenes.text: Neha sees ∫2x cos(x²)dx and notices 2x is the derivative of x².
Putting t = x² turns it into ∫cos t dt — substitution is the chain rule run backwards.

steps.title: Substitution
steps.body:
If the integrand contains g(x) and g′(x), put t = g(x), dt = g′(x)dx. After integrating in t, substitute back.

Key results: ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C; ∫[f(x)]ⁿf′(x)dx = [f(x)]ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C.

steps.title: Integrals of tan, cot, sec, cosec
steps.body:
- ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C
- ∫cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C
- ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
- ∫cosec x dx = ln|cosec x − cot x| + C

steps.title: Solved: ∫2x cos(x²)dx
steps.body: t = x², dt = 2x dx ⇒ ∫cos t dt = sin t + C = **sin(x²) + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫(ln x)/x dx
steps.body: t = ln x, dt = dx/x ⇒ ∫t dt = t²/2 + C = **(ln x)²/2 + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫sin²x dx (identity)
steps.body: sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 ⇒ ∫ = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C.

steps.title: Solved: ∫e^(tan⁻¹x)/(1 + x²) dx
steps.body: t = tan⁻¹x, dt = dx/(1 + x²) ⇒ ∫eᵗdt = **e^(tan⁻¹x) + C**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing the variable but leaving a stray x in the integral.
- Forgetting to replace dx by dt/g′(x).
- ∫sin²x dx ≠ sin³x/3 — use the half-angle identity.

quiz.why: With t = 3x, dt = 3dx, so ∫cos 3x dx = (1/3) sin 3x + C.

The numerator 2x is the derivative of 1 + x², so ∫f′/f dx = ln(1 + x²) + C.

lessons.title: Special integrals and partial fractions

scenes.text: Rohan's integrals keep looking like 1/(x² + something). He builds a toolkit of six standard forms.
For rational functions with factorable denominators, he breaks them into simpler fractions first.

steps.title: Six special integrals
steps.body:
- ∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + C
- ∫dx/(x² − a²) = (1/2a)ln|(x − a)/(x + a)| + C
- ∫dx/(a² − x²) = (1/2a)ln|(a + x)/(a − x)| + C
- ∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
- ∫dx/√(x² + a²) = ln|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
- ∫dx/√(x² − a²) = ln|x + √(x² − a²)| + C

steps.title: Solved: ∫dx/(x² + 4x + 13)
steps.body:
Complete the square: x² + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)² + 9.

∫dx/((x + 2)² + 3²) = **(1/3)tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C**.

steps.title: Partial fractions
steps.body:
For a **proper** rational function (degree of numerator < denominator):

- (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b)
- (px + q)/(x − a)² = A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²
- (px² + qx + r)/((x − a)(x² + bx + c)) = A/(x − a) + (Bx + C)/(x² + bx + c)

If improper, divide first.

steps.title: Solved: ∫dx/(x² − 9)
steps.body: Using the second formula with a = 3: (1/6)ln|(x − 3)/(x + 3)| + C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using partial fractions on an improper fraction without dividing first.
- Mixing up ∫dx/(x² − a²) and ∫dx/(a² − x²) — the log arguments are reciprocal-like; memorise carefully.
- Forgetting the 1/a factor in the tan⁻¹ formula.

activity.prompt: Match the integral with its result (+ C)

quiz.why: ∫dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + C. With a = 4 this is (1/4)tan⁻¹(x/4) + C.
∫dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. With a = 3 it is sin⁻¹(x/3) + C.

quiz.q: Partial fraction of 1/((x + 1)(x + 2))
quiz.why: Write 1/((x+1)(x+2)) = A/(x+1) + B/(x+2). Cover-up gives A = 1 and B = −1.

quiz.q: x² + 6x + 10 written by completing the square
Before partial fractions, (x³ + 1)/(x² − 1) must be
quiz.why: The numerator has degree 3, higher than the denominator's 2, so the fraction is improper. Divide first, then use partial fractions.

lessons.title: Integration by parts

scenes.text: ∫x eˣ dx has no obvious substitution. Ishaan remembers the product rule for derivatives.
Rearranged, it gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du — integration by parts.

steps.title: Formula and ILATE
steps.body:
∫u·v dx = u∫v dx − ∫[u′·∫v dx]dx.

Choose u (the function to differentiate) by the order **ILATE**: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.

steps.title: Solved: ∫x eˣ dx
steps.body: u = x, v = eˣ: x eˣ − ∫1·eˣdx = **eˣ(x − 1) + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫x cos x dx
steps.body: u = x: x sin x − ∫sin x dx = **x sin x + cos x + C**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫ln x dx
steps.body: Write as ∫ln x·1 dx, u = ln x: x ln x − ∫x·(1/x)dx = **x ln x − x + C**.

steps.title: Two special results
steps.body:
- ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)]dx = eˣf(x) + C. Example: ∫eˣ(sin x + cos x)dx = eˣ sin x + C.
- ∫√(a² − x²)dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
- ∫√(x² + a²)dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2)ln|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
- ∫√(x² − a²)dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2)ln|x + √(x² − a²)| + C

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing u = eˣ in ∫x eˣ dx — the new integral becomes harder.
- Sign slip in the second term (it is **minus** ∫).
- Forgetting that ∫ln x dx needs the hidden factor 1.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to evaluate ∫x sin x dx
items: Choose u = x (algebraic) and v = sin x
Simplify: −x cos x + sin x + C

quiz.q: By ILATE, in ∫x² ln x dx choose u =
quiz.why: By ILATE, a logarithmic function comes before an algebraic one, so u = ln x and dv = x² dx.

quiz.why: By parts with u = x: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = eˣ(x − 1) + C.

quiz.why: ∫eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)]dx = eˣ f(x) + C. Here f = 1/x and f′ = −1/x², so the result is eˣ/x + C.

quiz.q: ∫ln x dx =
quiz.why: By parts with u = ln x and dv = 1·dx: ∫ln x dx = x ln x − ∫1 dx = x ln x − x + C.
The standard formula ∫√(a² − x²)dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C with a = 2 gives (x/2)√(4 − x²) + 2 sin⁻¹(x/2) + C.

lessons.title: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

scenes.text: A rain gauge records rainfall *rate* r(t) mm/hour. The total rain between 2 pm and 5 pm is the area under the rate graph.
The fundamental theorem says: find any antiderivative F, then the total is F(5) − F(2).

steps.title: Fundamental theorems
steps.body:
- **First**: if A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t)dt, then A′(x) = f(x).
- **Second**: if F′ = f on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a).

The constant C cancels, so it is not written. Geometrically, ∫ₐᵇ f dx is the signed area between the curve and the x-axis (as the limit of a sum of thin rectangle areas).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- After substitution, keeping the old x-limits.
- Writing F(a) − F(b) instead of F(b) − F(a).
- Treating a definite integral as always positive: it is a *signed* area.

lessons.title: Properties of definite integrals

scenes.text: Ananya faces ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx in a test. Direct integration looks horrible.
Using ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx, she adds two versions and the answer π/4 drops out in three lines.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- P0: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t)dt
- P1: ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦₐ f;  ∫ₐₐ f = 0
- P2: ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫꜀ᵇ f
- P3: ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x)dx
- P4: ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x)dx
- P5: ∫₀²ᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f(2a − x) = f(x); = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x)
- P6: ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f if f is even; = 0 if f is odd

steps.title: Solved: I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx
steps.body:
By P4, I = ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx.

Add: 2I = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2 ⇒ **I = π/4**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx and ∫₋₁¹ x² dx
steps.body: x³ is odd ⇒ 0. x² is even ⇒ 2∫₀¹ x² dx = 2/3.

steps.title: Solved: ∫₋₁² |x| dx (P2)
steps.body: Split at 0: ∫₋₁⁰ (−x)dx + ∫₀² x dx = 1/2 + 2 = **5/2**.

steps.title: Solved: ∫₋π/2^π/2 sin⁷x dx
steps.body: sin⁷x is odd ⇒ **0** (no integration needed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying P6 without checking even/odd correctly (e.g. x³ + 1 is neither).
- Forgetting to split at the point where |f| changes sign.
- Using P4 on limits that don't start at 0 — use P3 instead.

lessons.title: Area under a simple curve

scenes.text: A muralist paints the region under an arch shaped like y = 4 − x² above the floor (x-axis).
To buy the right amount of paint she needs the exact area — a definite integral of thin vertical strips.

steps.title: Vertical and horizontal strips
steps.body:
Area bounded by y = f(x) ≥ 0, the x-axis and x = a, x = b: **A = ∫ₐᵇ y dx**.

Area bounded by x = g(y) ≥ 0, the y-axis and y = c, y = d: **A = ∫꜀ᵈ x dy**.

If the curve lies **below** the axis, the integral is negative — take its absolute value. If it crosses the axis, split the integral.

steps.title: Solved: area under the arch y = 4 − x² above the x-axis
steps.body: Roots: x = ±2. A = ∫₋₂² (4 − x²)dx = 2∫₀² (4 − x²)dx = 2[4x − x³/3]₀² = 2(8 − 8/3) = **32/3 sq units**.

steps.title: Solved: area between x = y², the y-axis, y = 0 to y = 2
steps.body: Horizontal strips: A = ∫₀² y² dy = **8/3 sq units**.

steps.title: Solved: area bounded by y = sin x and the x-axis from 0 to 2π
steps.body: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2 and ∫_π^2π sin x dx = −2. Area = 2 + |−2| = **4 sq units** (not 0).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Integrating straight across a sign change and getting a cancelled (too small) area.
- Using dx when the region is described by x = g(y).
- Forgetting units: 'sq units'.

steps.title: Always sketch
steps.body: A rough sketch shows which strip to use, the limits and whether symmetry can halve the work.

Upper half y = (b/a)√(a² − x²).

courses.title: Ch 9 · Differential Equations
courses.summary: Order and degree, general and particular solutions, and solving first-order equations by separation of variables, the homogeneous substitution and the integrating factor.
outcomes: Learners can find order and degree (or say it is undefined)
Learners can verify solutions and find particular solutions
Learners can solve separable and homogeneous DEs
Learners can solve linear first-order DEs with an integrating factor

lessons.title: Order, degree and solutions

scenes.text: A cup of tea cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter it is than the room. That sentence is a differential equation.
Before solving one, we classify it: order, degree, and what counts as a solution.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- A **differential equation (DE)** involves derivatives of an unknown function.
- **Order** = order of the highest derivative present.
- **Degree** = power of the highest-order derivative, *only when the DE is a polynomial in its derivatives*; otherwise degree is **not defined**.
- **General solution**: contains as many arbitrary constants as the order. **Particular solution**: constants fixed by given conditions.

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- y‴ + 2y″ + y′ = 0 → order 3, degree 1.
- (y″)² + (y′)³ = x → order 2, degree 2.
- y″ + sin(y′) = 0 → order 2, degree **not defined** (sin of a derivative is not polynomial).
- (dy/dx)⁴ + 3y = 0 → order 1, degree 4.

steps.title: Solved: verify y = eˣ + 1 solves y″ − y′ = 0
steps.body: y′ = eˣ, y″ = eˣ ⇒ y″ − y′ = 0 ✔

steps.title: Solved: verify y = A cos x + B sin x solves y″ + y = 0
steps.body: y″ = −A cos x − B sin x = −y ⇒ y″ + y = 0 ✔. Two constants for a 2nd-order DE — a general solution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the degree from a lower-order derivative's power.
- Giving a degree when the DE contains sin(y′), e^(y′), etc.
- Confusing order with the number of terms.

activity.prompt: Match each DE with its order and degree

quiz.q: Order of y″ + 5(y′)⁴ = 0
quiz.why: The highest derivative in y″ + 5(y′)⁴ = 0 is y″, so the order is 2.

quiz.q: Degree of (y″)² + y′ = 0
quiz.why: The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative. y″ is squared, so the degree is 2.

quiz.q: Number of arbitrary constants in the general solution of a 3rd-order DE
quiz.why: The general solution of an n-th order DE has n independent arbitrary constants, so a 3rd-order one has 3.

quiz.q: Degree of y′ + e^(y′) = x
quiz.why: The equation y′ + e^(y′) = x is not a polynomial in y′, so its degree is not defined.

quiz.q: y = Ce^(2x) is the general solution of
quiz.why: From y = Ce^(2x), y′ = 2Ce^(2x) = 2y. So y = Ce^(2x) solves y′ = 2y.

sources: NCERT (topic)

lessons.title: Variables separable method

scenes.text: A colony grows at a rate proportional to its size: dN/dt = kN.
Money in an account with continuous interest obeys the same law. Separating N and t solves both.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: If dy/dx = f(x)g(y), separate: dy/g(y) = f(x)dx, then integrate both sides: ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx + C.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²)
steps.body: dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²) ⇒ **tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + C**.

steps.title: Solved: dN/dt = kN
steps.body: dN/N = k dt ⇒ ln|N| = kt + C ⇒ **N = N₀eᵏᵗ** (N₀ = value at t = 0).

steps.title: Doubling time
steps.body: Money at 5% p.a. compounded continuously: dP/dt = 0.05P ⇒ P = P₀e^(0.05t). It doubles when e^(0.05t) = 2, t = ln 2/0.05 ≈ **13.9 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the constant C, or adding a constant on both sides separately (one is enough).
- Dividing by g(y) without noting g(y) ≠ 0.
- Writing ln|y| = x² + C then y = eˣ² + C (wrong) — exponentiate everything: y = Ae^(x²).

activity.prompt: Money doubles under continuous growth at 10% per year. Using ln 2 ≈ 0.693, how many years?

quiz.q: Solution of dy/dx = y
quiz.why: Separate: dy/y = dx, so ln|y| = x + c and y = Ceˣ.

quiz.q: Solution of dy/dx = x/y
quiz.why: Separating variables gives y dy = x dx. Integrating, y²/2 = x²/2 + c, so y² − x² = C.

quiz.q: dy/dx = eˣ⁺ʸ separates as
quiz.why: e^(x+y) = eˣ eʸ, so dy/dx = eˣeʸ. Separating, e⁻ʸ dy = eˣ dx.

quiz.q: Solution of dy/dx = sec²x
quiz.why: Integrate directly: ∫sec²x dx = tan x, so y = tan x + C.

quiz.q: Particular solution of dy/dx = 2x, y(0) = 3
quiz.why: Integrating gives y = x² + C. With y(0) = 3, C = 3, so y = x² + 3.

lessons.title: Homogeneous differential equations

scenes.text: Some equations look the same whether you measure in metres or centimetres — only the ratio y/x matters.
For these homogeneous equations, putting y = vx turns them into separable ones.

steps.title: Definition and method
steps.body:
F(x, y) is **homogeneous of degree n** if F(λx, λy) = λⁿF(x, y). A DE dy/dx = F(x, y) is homogeneous if F is homogeneous of degree 0 (i.e. a function of y/x).

Method: put **y = vx**, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, separate v and x, integrate, replace v = y/x.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = (x + y)/x
steps.body:
y = vx: v + x v′ = 1 + v ⇒ x dv/dx = 1 ⇒ dv = dx/x ⇒ v = ln|x| + C.

**y = x ln|x| + Cx**.

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx = y/x + tan(y/x)
steps.body: v + x v′ = v + tan v ⇒ cot v dv = dx/x ⇒ ln|sin v| = ln|x| + c ⇒ **sin(y/x) = Cx**.

steps.title: Solved: test homogeneity of F(x, y) = (x² + y²)/(xy)
steps.body: F(λx, λy) = λ²(x² + y²)/(λ²xy) = λ⁰F ⇒ homogeneous of degree 0 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the extra 'v' when writing dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
- Calling (x + y + 1)/x homogeneous — the constant 1 breaks it.
- Leaving the answer in v.

activity.prompt: Is the DE dy/dx = F(x, y) homogeneous?

quiz.q: In a homogeneous DE, substitute
quiz.why: For a homogeneous DE the standard substitution is y = vx, so the equation is in v and x only.

quiz.q: If y = vx, dy/dx =
quiz.why: If y = vx, by the product rule dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.

quiz.q: Degree of homogeneity of x² + xy
quiz.why: Replacing x, y by λx, λy gives λ²x² + λ²xy = λ²(x² + xy), so the degree is 2.

quiz.q: dy/dx = (x + y)/x has solution
quiz.why: Put y = vx: v + x dv/dx = 1 + v, so dv = dx/x and v = ln|x| + C. So y = x ln|x| + Cx.

quiz.q: Is x³ + y² homogeneous?
quiz.why: x³ + y² has terms of degree 3 and 2, so scaling by λ does not give a single power of λ. It is not homogeneous.

lessons.title: Linear differential equations

story.title: The tank with inflow and leak

scenes.text: Salt water flows into a tank while mixed water drains out. The salt amount S obeys dS/dt + kS = q.
This is a first-order linear DE. An integrating factor turns the left side into one neat derivative.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Form: **dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x)**.

1. Integrating factor IF = e^(∫P dx).
2. Solution: y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.

(Similarly dx/dy + P₁(y)x = Q₁(y) uses IF = e^(∫P₁dy).)

steps.title: Solved: dy/dx + y = eˣ
steps.body: IF = eˣ. y eˣ = ∫e²ˣdx = e²ˣ/2 + C ⇒ **y = eˣ/2 + Ce⁻ˣ**.

steps.title: Solved: x dy/dx + 2y = x² (x ≠ 0)
steps.body:
Divide by x: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x. IF = e^(2 ln x) = x².

yx² = ∫x³dx = x⁴/4 + C ⇒ **y = x²/4 + C/x²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not dividing by the coefficient of dy/dx before reading P.
- Writing IF = ∫P dx (forgetting the exponential).
- e^(ln x) = x, e^(−ln x) = 1/x, e^(2 ln x) = x² — simplify carefully.

activity.prompt: Find the integrating factor.

quiz.q: IF of dy/dx + 2y = sin x
quiz.why: For dy/dx + Py = Q the integrating factor is e^(∫P dx). Here P = 2, so IF = e²ˣ.

quiz.q: IF of dy/dx − (1/x)y = x
quiz.why: P = −1/x, so IF = e^(∫−1/x dx) = e^(−ln x) = 1/x.

quiz.q: IF of dy/dx + y tan x = sec x
quiz.why: P = tan x, so IF = e^(∫tan x dx) = e^(ln sec x) = sec x.

quiz.q: Solution form for linear DE
quiz.why: The solution of a linear DE is y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.

quiz.q: dy/dx + y = 1 has solution
quiz.why: IF = eˣ, so y eˣ = ∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C. So y = 1 + Ce⁻ˣ.

questions.why: IF = e⁻ˣ gives y e⁻ˣ = −2e⁻ˣ + C, so y = −2 + Ceˣ. With y(0) = 1, C = 3, so y = 3eˣ − 2.

questions.why: Put y = vx: x dv/dx = tan v, so cot v dv = dx/x. Integrating, ln|sin v| = ln|x| + c, so sin(y/x) = Cx.

questions.why: Dividing by (1 + x²), P = 2x/(1 + x²), so IF = e^(ln(1 + x²)) = 1 + x².

questions.why: Dividing by (1 + x²) gives y′ + [2x/(1 + x²)]y = 1/(1 + x²)². With IF = 1 + x², d/dx[y(1 + x²)] = 1/(1 + x²), so y(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C.

lessons.title: Vectors: basics, types and components

scenes.text: A treasure map says: walk 3 km east, then 4 km north. Distance alone is not enough — direction matters.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
A **vector** has magnitude and direction; a **scalar** has magnitude only. Position vector of P(x, y, z): OP = x î + y ĵ + z k̂, |OP| = √(x² + y² + z²).

Types: **zero** vector, **unit** vector (magnitude 1), **co-initial**, **collinear** (parallel), **equal** (same magnitude and direction), **negative** of a vector.

lessons.title: Addition, scalar multiples and section formula

scenes.text: Two tugboats pull a ship with forces in different directions. The ship moves along their sum.
Vector addition follows the triangle (or parallelogram) law — and the same algebra splits a segment in a given ratio.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Triangle law: AB + BC = AC. Parallelogram law gives the same result.
- a + b = b + a; (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
- In components: add matching components. λa scales the magnitude by |λ| and reverses direction if λ < 0.
- a and b are collinear ⇔ b = λa for some scalar λ (component ratios equal).

steps.title: Section formula
steps.body:
Point R dividing PQ (position vectors a, b) in ratio m : n:

- internally: r = (mb + na)/(m + n)
- externally: r = (mb − na)/(m − n)
- midpoint: (a + b)/2

steps.body: AB = î + ĵ + k̂, AC = 3î + 3ĵ + 3k̂ = 3AB ⇒ parallel with a common point ⇒ **collinear**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Using '+' in external division.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
a · b = |a||b| cos θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π). In components: a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.

- Projection of a on b = (a · b)/|b|; projection vector = ((a · b)/|b|²) b

lessons.title: Cross (vector) product and areas

scenes.text: A mechanic pushes a spanner. The turning effect (torque) points along the bolt — perpendicular to both the spanner and the push.
That perpendicular vector is the cross product, and its size equals the area of a parallelogram.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector perpendicular to both (right-hand rule).

- a × b = −(b × a) (not commutative); a × a = 0
- a ∥ b ⇔ a × b = 0
- î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ
- Determinant form: a × b = |î ĵ k̂; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃|
- Area of parallelogram with sides a, b = |a × b|; triangle = ½|a × b|; parallelogram with diagonals d₁, d₂ = ½|d₁ × d₂|

steps.title: Solved: area of triangle A(1, 1, 1), B(1, 2, 3), C(2, 3, 1)
steps.body:
AB = ĵ + 2k̂, AC = î + 2ĵ.

AB × AC = î(0 − 4) − ĵ(0 − 2) + k̂(0 − 1) = −4î + 2ĵ − k̂, magnitude √21.

Area = **√21/2 sq units**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign on the ĵ-component of the determinant.
- Using a × b = b × a.
- Taking |a × b| as the triangle's area (it is the parallelogram's — halve it).

lessons.title: Direction cosines and direction ratios of a line

scenes.text: A drone flies in a straight line from launch pad P(−2, 4, −5) to rooftop Q(1, 2, 3).
The direction of that path is captured by three numbers — direction ratios — and their normalised versions, direction cosines.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For a line making angles α, β, γ with the x, y, z axes: l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ, with **l² + m² + n² = 1**.

Any numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n are **direction ratios**; then l = ±a/√(a² + b² + c²), etc.

Direction ratios of the line through (x₁, y₁, z₁) and (x₂, y₂, z₂): x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁.

steps.title: Solved: DCs of a line making equal angles with the axes
steps.body: l = m = n and 3l² = 1 ⇒ l = m = n = ±1/√3.

steps.body: DRs of AB: −3, −5, −3. DRs of BC: 6, 10, 6 = −2 × (−3, −5, −3). Proportional with common point B ⇒ collinear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating DRs as DCs without normalising.
- Forgetting l² + m² + n² = 1 when one DC is unknown (two possible signs).
- Thinking 90°, 60°, 30° can be the angles with the three axes (cos² sum ≠ 1).

steps.title: Forms

Through point A (position a), parallel to b = aî + bĵ + ck̂:

- Vector: **r = a + λb**
- Cartesian: **(x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c**

Through two points a and c: r = a + λ(c − a); Cartesian with DRs x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Not making the coefficient of x, y, z equal to 1 before reading DRs (e.g. (2x − 1)/3 → (x − 1/2)/(3/2)).
- Using the point as the direction.

lessons.title: Shortest distance between two lines

scenes.text: Two cable-car wires pass close to each other at different heights without touching. Safety needs their minimum gap.
Lines in space that are neither parallel nor intersecting are skew. The shortest distance runs along their common perpendicular.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**Skew lines** r = a₁ + λb₁, r = a₂ + μb₂:

d = |(a₂ − a₁) · (b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|. (If d = 0, the lines intersect.)

**Parallel lines** r = a₁ + λb, r = a₂ + μb:

d = |b × (a₂ − a₁)| / |b|.

steps.title: Solved: an intuitive case
steps.body:
L₁: the x-axis (a₁ = 0, b₁ = î). L₂: through (0, 0, 3) parallel to the y-axis (a₂ = 3k̂, b₂ = ĵ).

b₁ × b₂ = k̂; (a₂ − a₁) · k̂ = 3 ⇒ **d = 3** — exactly the height gap, as expected.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the skew formula for parallel lines (b₁ × b₂ = 0 there — division by zero).
- Forgetting the modulus.
- Arithmetic slips in the cross product — recheck the ĵ sign.

lessons.title: Formulating a linear programming problem

scenes.text: A carpenter makes tables (profit ₹30 each) and chairs (₹20 each). Wood and labour hours are limited.
How many of each maximises profit? First, translate the story into an objective function and constraints.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **Decision variables**: the quantities we choose (x, y ≥ 0).
- **Objective function**: Z = ax + by to maximise or minimise.
- **Constraints**: linear inequalities from limited resources, plus **non-negativity** x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
- **Feasible region**: points satisfying all constraints; each such point is a feasible solution; the best one is the **optimal solution**.

steps.title: Solved: carpenter
steps.body:
A table needs 2 units of wood and 1 hour; a chair 1 unit of wood and 2 hours. Available: 40 units of wood, 50 hours.

Let x tables, y chairs. Maximise **Z = 30x + 20y** subject to 2x + y ≤ 40, x + 2y ≤ 50, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Solved: diet problem
steps.body:
Food P costs ₹4/unit with 3 units of vitamin A and 1 of B; food Q costs ₹6/unit with 1 of A and 2 of B. Need at least 6 of A and 4 of B.

Minimise **Z = 4x + 6y** subject to 3x + y ≥ 6, x + 2y ≥ 4, x, y ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ≥ for a resource limit (limits are usually ≤; requirements are ≥).
- Forgetting non-negativity constraints.
- Mixing up which coefficient goes with which variable — make a small table first.

steps.title: Make a table
steps.body: Rows = products, columns = resources + profit. Each column of resources becomes one constraint; the profit column becomes Z.

lessons.title: Graphical method: corner point theorem

scenes.text: Shading all the carpenter's constraints on graph paper gives a polygon-shaped feasible region.
The best plan is always at a corner — just test each corner in Z.

steps.title: Corner point theorem
steps.body:
If the feasible region is **bounded**, Z = ax + by has both a maximum and a minimum, and each occurs at a **corner point**.

Method: 1) draw each constraint line, shade the correct side; 2) find corner points (solve pairs of lines); 3) evaluate Z at each; 4) pick the largest/smallest. If two adjacent corners give the same optimum, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.

steps.title: Solved: carpenter (max Z = 30x + 20y)
steps.body:
Lines 2x + y = 40 and x + 2y = 50 meet where x = 10, y = 20.

Corners: (0, 0) → 0; (20, 0) → 600; (0, 25) → 500; (10, 20) → 300 + 400 = **700**.

Make 10 tables and 20 chairs; maximum profit ₹700.

Common mistakes
steps.body:

steps.title: Check

lessons.title: Unbounded regions and minimisation

scenes.text: For the diet problem the feasible region stretches away to infinity — you can always buy more food.
A minimum may still exist, but we must check it with an extra half-plane test.

steps.title: Rule for unbounded regions
steps.body:
Find the candidate value M at the corners.

- For a **minimum** candidate m: draw ax + by < m. If this open half-plane has **no point in common** with the feasible region, m is the minimum; otherwise no minimum.
- For a **maximum** candidate M: draw ax + by > M; if no common point, M is the maximum; otherwise Z has no maximum.

steps.title: Solved: min Z = 3x + 5y, x + 3y ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 2, x, y ≥ 0
steps.body:
Corners: (3, 0) → 9; (0, 2) → 10; intersection of x + 3y = 3 and x + y = 2: y = 1/2, x = 3/2 → 4.5 + 2.5 = **7**.

The region 3x + 5y < 7 lies below the corner (3/2, 1/2) and meets no feasible point ⇒ minimum **7** at (3/2, 1/2).

steps.title: Solved: diet min Z = 4x + 6y, 3x + y ≥ 6, x + 2y ≥ 4
steps.body:
Corners: (0, 6) → 36; (4, 0) → 16; intersection: from 3x + y = 6 and x + 2y = 4: x = 8/5, y = 6/5 → 6.4 + 7.2 = 13.6.

Half-plane 4x + 6y < 13.6 has no feasible point ⇒ minimum cost **₹13.60** at (1.6, 1.2).

steps.title: Solved: max Z = x + y on the same unbounded region
steps.body: Z grows without limit (e.g. (100, 0) is feasible, Z = 100) ⇒ **no maximum**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring the smallest corner value the minimum without the half-plane check.
- Claiming a maximum exists on an unbounded region just because corners give finite values.
- Arithmetic errors at the intersection corner.

lessons.title: Conditional probability

scenes.text: Two coins are tossed to decide batting order. Someone peeks and says 'at least one is a head'.
Now what is the chance both are heads? New information shrinks the sample space — that's conditional probability.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
For events E, F with P(F) > 0: **P(E|F) = P(E ∩ F)/P(F)**.

Properties: P(S|F) = P(F|F) = 1; P(E′|F) = 1 − P(E|F); P(A ∪ B|F) = P(A|F) + P(B|F) − P(A ∩ B|F).

steps.title: Solved: two coins, at least one head
steps.body:

P(E|F) = (1/4)/(3/4) = **1/3** (not 1/2!).

lessons.title: Multiplication theorem and independent events

scenes.text: A jar has 10 black and 5 red marbles. Two are drawn one after another without replacement.

steps.title: Multiplication theorem
steps.body: **P(E ∩ F) = P(E)·P(F|E) = P(F)·P(E|F)**. For three events: P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F|E)P(G|E ∩ F).

steps.title: Independence
steps.body:
E and F are **independent** if P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) (equivalently P(E|F) = P(E)). If E, F are independent, so are E and F′, E′ and F, E′ and F′.

Independent ≠ mutually exclusive: exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are always **dependent**.

steps.title: Solved: two students attempt a problem
steps.body:

P(solved) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − (1/2)(2/3) = **2/3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying probabilities of dependent events without conditioning.
- Assuming 'mutually exclusive' means 'independent'.
- Forgetting the complement trick for 'at least one'.

lessons.title: Total probability and Bayes' theorem

scenes.text: A test for a rare condition (1% of people) is 90% accurate on those who have it, but gives 5% false positives.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
If E₁, …, Eₙ partition S (mutually exclusive, exhaustive, each P(Eᵢ) > 0) and A is any event:

- **Total probability**: P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ)
- **Bayes**: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ)

P(Eᵢ) are **prior** probabilities; P(Eᵢ|A) are **posterior** probabilities.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A **random variable** X assigns a real number to each outcome. Its **probability distribution** lists values xᵢ with pᵢ = P(X = xᵢ), where pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1.

**Mean (expectation)**: μ = E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ.

*Extension*: variance Var(X) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ − μ², standard deviation = √Var(X).

steps.title: Relations & functions
steps.body:
- Number of relations on an n-set: 2^(n²)
- Equivalence = reflexive + symmetric + transitive; classes partition the set
- Functions A → B: nᵐ; one-one (m ≤ n): n!/(n − m)!; bijections on n-set: n!

Matrices & determinants

steps.title: Derivatives
steps.body:
- Chain: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))g′(x)
- d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1 − x²), tan⁻¹x = 1/(1 + x²), sec⁻¹x = 1/(|x|√(x² − 1))
