steps.title: Applications of derivatives
steps.body:
- Related rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt)
- f′ > 0 increasing, f′ < 0 decreasing
- f′(c) = 0, f″(c) < 0 ⇒ local max; f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local min

steps.body:

- By parts (ILATE); ∫eˣ(f + f′) = eˣf

steps.title: Vectors
steps.body:
- |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²); unit â = a/|a|

questions.why: With y′ = 1/√(1 − x²), (1 − x²)y′² = 1. Differentiating and dividing by 2y′ gives (1 − x²)y″ − xy′ = 0.

lessons.title: Electric charge and its properties

scenes.text: On a dry winter evening Riya pulls off her woollen sweater and hears tiny crackles in the dark.
She even sees faint sparks. Her little brother asks: is the sweater full of lightning?
Riya realises friction has moved electrons between the wool and her shirt — the sweater and shirt now carry equal and opposite charge.

steps.title: What charge is
steps.body:
Electric charge is a basic property of matter that makes it feel electric forces. There are two kinds, called **positive** and **negative** (names given by Benjamin Franklin). **Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.**

When two bodies are rubbed, electrons move from one to the other. The body that loses electrons becomes positive; the one that gains becomes negative. Mass changes are negligible (an electron is only 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg). SI unit of charge: **coulomb (C)**.

steps.title: Conductors, insulators and charging by induction
steps.body:
- **Conductors** (metals, the human body, earth) let charge move freely.
- **Insulators** (glass, plastic, rubber) hold charge where it is placed.
- **Charging by induction:** bring a charged rod near a neutral metal sphere, earth the far side, remove the earth connection, then remove the rod. The sphere keeps a charge *opposite* to the rod, with no contact.
- A charged body attracts a neutral light object (paper bits) because it induces opposite charge on the near side.

steps.title: Three basic properties
steps.body:
- **Additivity:** total charge is the algebraic sum: +3 μC, −5 μC and +1 μC together make −1 μC.
- **Conservation:** charge can neither be created nor destroyed in an isolated system, only transferred. (In pair production a γ-photon creates an electron and a positron — net charge still zero.)
- **Quantisation:** every free charge is an integer multiple of e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C: **q = ne**, n = 0, ±1, ±2, …

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** How many electrons must be removed from a neutral body to give it +1 μC?
- n = q/e = 1×10⁻⁶ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹
- n = **6.25×10¹²** electrons.

**Ex 2.** Can a body carry 2.4×10⁻¹⁹ C?
- n = 2.4×10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5
- n must be an integer, so **no**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying protons move during rubbing — only electrons move in solids.
- Forgetting that quantisation is invisible at large scales: 1 μC already contains trillions of e, so charge looks continuous.
- Mixing up induction (no contact, opposite charge) with conduction (contact, same sign charge).

statements.s: A body becomes positively charged by gaining protons.
statements.why: It loses electrons; protons stay locked in nuclei.

statements.s: Charge 4.8×10⁻¹⁹ C is possible on an isolated body.
In charging by induction the body gets the same sign of charge as the inducing rod.
Total charge of an isolated system stays constant.

quiz.q: The SI unit of charge is
quiz.why: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb. 1 C is the charge carried by a current of 1 A in 1 s.

quiz.q: The smallest free charge observed is
quiz.why: Charge comes in whole multiples of e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, the charge of an electron or proton, so this is the smallest free charge.

quiz.q: A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive because
quiz.why: Rubbing transfers electrons. Glass loses electrons to silk, so glass is left positive and silk negative.

quiz.q: Which charge is NOT possible?
quiz.why: Charge must be an integer multiple of e (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C). 8.0×10⁻²⁰ C is half of e, so it is not possible.

quiz.q: A neutral paper bit is attracted by a charged comb because
options: the comb induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper
quiz.why: The charged comb induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper, which is closer than the like charge on the far side. So the attraction is stronger than the repulsion.

lessons.title: Coulomb's law and superposition

scenes.text: In the physics lab two charged balloons hang from threads and push each other apart.
Kabir moves them twice as close; the threads swing out far more — not double, but four times the force.
His teacher says: that is the inverse-square law Coulomb measured in 1785 with a torsion balance.

steps.title: Coulomb's law
steps.body:
The force between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by r in vacuum:

**F = k q₁q₂ / r²**, with k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻²

ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻² is the permittivity of free space. The force acts along the line joining the charges; repulsive for like charges, attractive for unlike.

**Vector form:** F₂₁ (force on q₂ by q₁) = k q₁q₂ r̂₂₁ / r², where r̂₂₁ points from q₁ to q₂. Note F₁₂ = −F₂₁ (Newton's third law).

steps.title: In a medium
steps.body: In a medium of permittivity ε = Kε₀ the force becomes **F = q₁q₂ / (4πε₀K r²)**, i.e. reduced K times. K (dielectric constant or relative permittivity εᵣ) is 1 for vacuum, ≈ 1.0006 for air and about 80 for water.

steps.title: Superposition principle
steps.body:
The force on a charge due to several charges is the **vector sum** of the forces due to each one taken alone — each pair interaction is unaffected by the others.

**F₁ = F₁₂ + F₁₃ + … + F₁ₙ**

Add vectors by components, or use the parallelogram rule: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Charges 2 μC and 3 μC are 30 cm apart in air. Force?
- F = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶)(3×10⁻⁶) / (0.3)²
- = 9×10⁹ × 6×10⁻¹² / 0.09 = **0.6 N (repulsive)**.
- In oil of K = 3 the same pair feels 0.6/3 = **0.2 N**.

**Ex 2.** Three equal charges q sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. Net force on one?
- Each of the other two pushes with F = kq²/a²; the angle between the two forces is 60°.
- R = √(F² + F² + 2F² cos 60°) = √3 F
- **F_net = √3 kq²/a²**, directed along the bisector, away from the triangle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert μC to C (×10⁻⁶) and cm to m.
- Adding forces as numbers instead of vectors.
- Using the medium formula with K multiplied instead of divided.
- Applying Coulomb's law directly to large charged bodies that are not point-like.

steps.title: JEE shortcut
steps.body: For a charge placed between two like charges q₁ and q₂ (distance d apart) to be in equilibrium, it must sit at x = d√q₁/(√q₁ + √q₂) from q₁. For unlike charges the null point lies outside, nearer the smaller charge.

activity.prompt: Two point charges of +4 μC and −2 μC are 20 cm apart in vacuum. Find the magnitude of the force (in newton).

quiz.q: If the distance between two charges is halved, the force becomes
quiz.why: The force varies as 1/r². Halving the distance makes the force (1/(1/2))² = 4 times larger.

quiz.q: The value of 1/(4πε₀) in SI units is about
quiz.why: In Coulomb's law k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻².

quiz.q: Two charges in water (K = 80) compared with vacuum feel a force
quiz.why: In a medium of dielectric constant K, the force is reduced to F/K. For water, K = 80, so the force is 80 times less.

quiz.q: Coulomb force between two charges obeys Newton's third law because
options: they are equal only in vacuum
quiz.why: Coulomb forces on the two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, F₁₂ = −F₂₁, as Newton's third law requires.

quiz.q: The superposition principle says the net force is
options: the vector sum of individual forces
quiz.why: By superposition the net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces due to each of the other charges.

lessons.title: Electric field, field lines and the dipole

scenes.text: Ananya imagines every point around a charge carrying an arrow that says: a positive test charge here would be pushed this way, this hard.
That map of arrows is the electric field.
In a microwave oven, water molecules — tiny dipoles — twist back and forth in such a field, and that motion heats the food.

steps.title: Electric field
steps.body:
**E = F/q₀** (force per unit positive test charge, q₀ → 0). Unit N/C (= V/m).

Field of a point charge: **E = kq/r²**, radially outward for +q, inward for −q. Fields from many charges add as vectors (superposition).

**Field lines:** start on + charges and end on − charges (or infinity); never cross (field has one direction at a point); crowded where the field is strong; never form closed loops in electrostatics; are perpendicular to a conductor's surface.

steps.title: Electric dipole and its field
steps.body:
A dipole is a pair +q and −q separated by 2a. **Dipole moment p = q × 2a**, a vector from −q to +q, unit C m.

**On the axis** at distance r from the centre:
E = kq[1/(r−a)² − 1/(r+a)²] = k(4qar)/(r²−a²)² = 2kpr/(r²−a²)²
For r ≫ a: **E_axial = 2kp/r³**, along p.

**On the equatorial line:** the two fields have equal magnitude kq/(r²+a²); their components along the line cancel and those parallel to the axis add:
E = 2kq·a/(r²+a²)^(3/2) = kp/(r²+a²)^(3/2)
For r ≫ a: **E_eq = kp/r³**, opposite to p. So E_axial = 2 E_eq at equal distances. A dipole field falls as 1/r³.

steps.title: Dipole in a uniform field
steps.body:
The forces +qE and −qE are equal and opposite, so **net force = 0**, but they form a couple:

**τ = pE sin θ**, vector form **τ = p × E**.

The torque turns the dipole to align p with E (θ = 0 is stable equilibrium, θ = 180° unstable). In a non-uniform field there is also a net force.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Field 20 cm from a 4 μC charge:
- E = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁶ / (0.2)² = **9×10⁵ N/C**, away from the charge.

**Ex 2.** Charges ±10 μC are 2 mm apart. (a) p = 10×10⁻⁶ × 2×10⁻³ = **2×10⁻⁸ C m**. (b) Equatorial field at 10 cm: E = kp/r³ = 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁸ / 10⁻³ = **1.8×10⁵ N/C**; axial field at 10 cm = **3.6×10⁵ N/C**. (c) In a uniform field 5×10⁴ N/C at 30°: τ = 2×10⁻⁸ × 5×10⁴ × 0.5 = **5×10⁻⁴ N m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing p from + to −: it points from −q to +q.
- Using 1/r² for a dipole at large distance — it is 1/r³.
- Saying a dipole in a uniform field moves: it only rotates.
- Letting field lines cross or start in empty space.

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its expression (r ≫ a).

quiz.q: The SI unit of electric field is
quiz.why: Electric field is force per unit charge, so its unit is N/C, which is also V/m.

quiz.q: Field lines never cross because
options: the field at a point has a unique direction
quiz.why: If two field lines crossed, the field at the crossing point would have two directions, which is impossible. So they never cross.

quiz.q: The direction of a dipole moment is
quiz.why: By convention the dipole moment p points from the negative charge to the positive charge.

quiz.q: At the same large distance, axial field : equatorial field =
quiz.why: Axial field = 2kp/r³ and equatorial field = kp/r³, so the ratio is 2 : 1.

quiz.q: A dipole in a uniform field experiences
quiz.why: In a uniform field the two forces on a dipole are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple that gives torque pE sin θ.

quiz.q: Torque on a dipole is maximum when the angle between p and E is
quiz.why: Torque = pE sin θ, which is maximum when sin θ = 1, that is at 90°.

lessons.title: Electric flux and Gauss's law

scenes.text: Dev holds a hoop in a steady breeze. Facing the wind, lots of air goes through; turned sideways, none.
Electric flux works the same way — it measures how much field passes through a surface, depending on its tilt.
Gauss found something beautiful: for any closed surface, the total flux depends only on the charge inside.

steps.title: Electric flux
steps.body:
For a small area ΔS with outward normal: **ΔΦ = E·ΔS = E ΔS cos θ**. Total flux Φ = ∮ E·dS. Unit N m² C⁻¹ (= V m). Flux is a scalar.

For a closed surface, outward flux is positive, inward flux negative.

steps.title: Continuous charge distributions
steps.body:
- Linear charge density **λ = dq/dl** (C/m) — wires, rings.
- Surface charge density **σ = dq/dS** (C/m²) — sheets, conductor surfaces.
- Volume charge density **ρ = dq/dV** (C/m³).
The field is found by adding contributions k dq/r² as vectors (integration).

steps.title: Gauss's law
steps.body:
**Φ = ∮ E·dS = q_enclosed / ε₀**

- Charges outside the surface contribute zero net flux (lines entering also leave).
- The surface chosen (a *Gaussian surface*) is imaginary and must not pass through a discrete charge.
- The E in the integral is the field due to *all* charges, but only enclosed charge sets the total flux.
- Gauss's law is most useful when symmetry makes E constant over the surface.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A uniform field E = 200 N/C (along x) passes through a 10 cm × 10 cm square whose normal makes 60° with x.
- Φ = EA cos θ = 200 × 0.01 × 0.5 = **1 N m²/C**.

**Ex 2.** A 1 μC charge is at the centre of a cube.
- Total flux = q/ε₀ = 10⁻⁶ / 8.854×10⁻¹² ≈ **1.13×10⁵ N m²/C**.
- By symmetry each of the 6 faces gets **1.88×10⁴ N m²/C**.
- If the charge were moved off-centre (still inside) the total stays 1.13×10⁵, but face values change.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sin θ instead of cos θ: θ is the angle between E and the *normal*, not the surface.
- Thinking the field on the Gaussian surface is due only to enclosed charge.
- Counting a charge outside the surface in q_enclosed.
- For a charge at a cube corner, the flux through the cube is q/(8ε₀) (only 1/8 is enclosed).

activity.prompt: Complete Gauss's law statements.
activity.text: Total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed divided by ___. A charge outside the surface gives a net flux of ___. A charge at the centre of a cube sends 1/___ of the total flux through each face.

quiz.q: Electric flux is a
quiz.why: Flux is E·S, a dot product, so it is a scalar.

quiz.q: A surface encloses charges +3 μC and −3 μC. The net flux is
quiz.why: By Gauss's law flux = (net enclosed charge)/ε₀. +3 μC and −3 μC add up to zero, so the net flux is zero.

quiz.q: If the radius of a Gaussian sphere around a point charge is doubled, the flux
quiz.why: By Gauss's law, flux depends only on the enclosed charge, not on the size of the surface, so it stays the same.

quiz.q: Unit of electric flux is
quiz.why: Flux = E × area, so its unit is (N/C) × m², which is N m² C⁻¹.

quiz.q: A charge q is at the corner of a cube. Flux through the cube is
quiz.why: Eight such cubes meeting at a point surround the charge completely, so each cube gets one eighth of q/ε₀, that is q/8ε₀.

lessons.title: Applications of Gauss's law

story.title: Why the car is safe in lightning

scenes.text: Ishaan's family is driving through a thunderstorm when lightning strikes nearby.
His father calmly says the metal body of a car shields them.
Gauss's law explains it: charge on a closed conductor sits on the outside, and the field inside the cavity is zero.

steps.title: Infinite straight line charge (λ)
steps.body:
Take a coaxial cylinder of radius r and length l. E is radial, so flux through the flat ends is zero; curved surface: E·2πrl.

E·2πrl = λl/ε₀ ⇒ **E = λ/(2πε₀ r) = 2kλ/r**, radial. E ∝ 1/r.

steps.title: Infinite plane sheet (σ)
steps.body:
Take a cylinder (pillbox) of cross-section A piercing the sheet. Flux through the curved side is zero; each flat face gives EA.

2EA = σA/ε₀ ⇒ **E = σ/(2ε₀)**, independent of distance.

Two parallel sheets with +σ and −σ: fields add between them, **E = σ/ε₀**, and cancel outside (this is the parallel-plate capacitor).

steps.title: Thin spherical shell (charge q, radius R)
steps.body:
- **Outside (r > R):** Gaussian sphere of radius r: E·4πr² = q/ε₀ ⇒ **E = kq/r²** — as if all charge were at the centre.
- **On the surface:** E = kq/R² = σ/ε₀.
- **Inside (r < R):** no enclosed charge ⇒ **E = 0**.
The same zero-field result explains electrostatic shielding.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A long wire carries λ = 2 μC/m. Field at 10 cm?
- E = 2kλ/r = 2 × 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶ / 0.1 = **3.6×10⁵ N/C**.

**Ex 2.** A large sheet has σ = 8.85×10⁻¹⁰ C/m².
- E = σ/(2ε₀) = 8.85×10⁻¹⁰ / (2 × 8.85×10⁻¹²) = **50 N/C**.
- Between two such oppositely charged plates: σ/ε₀ = **100 N/C**; outside: 0.

**Ex 3.** A shell of radius 10 cm has 3 μC. Field at 5 cm is **0**; at 20 cm: 9×10⁹ × 3×10⁻⁶/0.04 = **6.75×10⁵ N/C**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ/ε₀ for a single isolated sheet (that is for a conductor surface or two plates).
- Thinking E inside a charged shell is non-zero 'because charge is nearby'.
- Forgetting the 2 in E = λ/(2πε₀r).

steps.title: Where you meet this
steps.body: Sensitive electronics are wrapped in metal cages (Faraday cages); coaxial TV cables use an outer conductor to shield the signal; the plate-charge result underlies every capacitor in your phone.

activity.prompt: How does E vary with distance r?

quiz.q: Field due to an infinite sheet of charge
quiz.why: For an infinite plane sheet E = σ/2ε₀, with no dependence on distance, since the field lines are parallel.

quiz.q: Field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is
quiz.why: A Gaussian surface inside a charged shell encloses no charge, so by Gauss's law the field inside is zero.

quiz.q: For an infinite line charge, if r is tripled, E becomes
quiz.why: For an infinite line charge E ∝ 1/r. If r is tripled, E becomes one third.

quiz.q: Field between two large oppositely charged parallel plates is
quiz.why: Each plate gives σ/2ε₀. Between oppositely charged plates the two fields point the same way and add to σ/ε₀.

quiz.q: Electrostatic shielding is based on
options: field inside a conductor cavity being zero
quiz.why: Inside a conductor's cavity the field is zero, so the region is protected from outside fields. This is electrostatic shielding.

options: Both true; reason does not explain

The field at 1 m on the axis of a short dipole is 4 N/C. Field at 2 m on its equatorial line:
questions.why: Axial field 2kp/r³ = 4 at r = 1 m gives kp = 2. Equatorial at r = 2 m is kp/r³ = 2/8 = 0.25 N/C.

questions.q: Case: An oil drop of mass 3.2×10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary in a field of 1×10⁵ N/C (g = 10 m/s²). The number of excess electrons on it is
questions.why: For balance qE = mg, so q = (3.2×10⁻¹⁵ × 10)/10⁵ = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C. Dividing by e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C gives 2 excess electrons.

questions.why: A charge at the centre has total flux q/ε₀. By symmetry the 6 faces share it equally, so each gets q/6ε₀.

Assertion: The field due to an infinite plane sheet does not depend on distance. Reason: field lines from the sheet are parallel and uniform.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. The field lines of an infinite sheet are parallel and equally spaced, so the field is uniform and independent of distance.

questions.why: At the centroid the three fields have equal magnitude and are 120° apart, so their vector sum is zero.

questions.q: A uniform field E = 3î + 4ĵ N/C passes through a 2 m² area lying in the y–z plane. Flux:
questions.why: The area in the y–z plane has its normal along x, so only Eₓ counts: Φ = 3 × 2 = 6 N m²/C.

questions.q: Two identical small spheres carry 6 μC and −2 μC. They touch and are returned to the same separation. The ratio new force/old force is
questions.why: On touching, the charges share equally: (6 − 2)/2 = +2 μC each. F′/F = (2 × 2)/(6 × 2) = 1/3, and the force is now repulsive.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
courses.summary: Electric potential and potential difference, potential of a point charge, dipole and system of charges, equipotential surfaces, potential energy, conductors and dielectrics, capacitors and their combinations, and energy stored — with derivations and numericals. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can calculate potential due to point charges, dipoles and systems of charges.
Learners can relate E and V (E = −dV/dr) and describe equipotential surfaces.
Learners can derive C = ε₀A/d and the effect of a dielectric.
Learners can solve series/parallel capacitor networks and energy-sharing problems.

lessons.title: Electric potential and potential difference

scenes.text: Meher pushes a shopping cart up a ramp; it gains gravitational potential energy.
Pushing a positive charge towards another positive charge is similar: you do work against the repulsion, and energy is stored.
'Volts' on a battery measure exactly this — work done per unit charge.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Electrostatic force is **conservative**: the work done in moving a charge between two points does not depend on the path.

**Potential at a point:** V = W/q — the work done by an external agent in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point *without acceleration*. Unit **volt** (1 V = 1 J/C). Scalar.

**Potential difference:** V_B − V_A = W_AB/q.

steps.title: Potential due to a point charge
steps.body:
Bring a unit charge from ∞ to r against the field kq/r'²:
V = −∫(∞→r) kq/r'² dr' = **kq/r**.
Positive for +q, negative for −q; falls as 1/r (field falls as 1/r²).

steps.title: Dipole and system of charges
steps.body:
**Dipole:** at distance r (r ≫ a) at angle θ from the axis, **V = kp cos θ / r²**.
- On the axis (θ = 0): V = kp/r².
- On the equatorial line (θ = 90°): **V = 0** (but E ≠ 0!).

**System of charges:** potentials add as scalars: V = k Σ qᵢ/rᵢ.

**Uniformly charged shell:** V = kq/r outside, and V = kq/R (constant) everywhere inside.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Potential 9 cm from a 4×10⁻⁷ C charge, and work to bring 2×10⁻⁹ C there from infinity.
- V = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁷ / 0.09 = **4×10⁴ V**.
- W = qV = 2×10⁻⁹ × 4×10⁴ = **8×10⁻⁵ J**.

**Ex 2.** +4 μC and −1 μC are 15 cm apart. Where on the line is V = 0?
- Between them, x from +4 μC: 4/x = 1/(15 − x) ⇒ x = **12 cm**.
- Outside, beyond −1 μC: 4/x = 1/(x − 15) ⇒ x = **20 cm** (5 cm beyond the smaller charge).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding potentials as vectors — potential is a scalar; keep the sign of each charge.
- Thinking V = 0 means E = 0 (dipole equatorial line: V = 0, E ≠ 0).
- Thinking E = 0 means V = 0 (inside a shell: E = 0, V = kq/R).

activity.prompt: Find the potential (in volts) at the centre of a square of side 2√2 m with charges +2 μC, +2 μC, −1 μC and +1 μC at its corners. (Each corner is 2 m from the centre.)

quiz.q: Electric potential is a
quiz.why: Potential is work per unit charge, which is a scalar.

quiz.q: 1 volt equals
quiz.why: A volt is a joule per coulomb, since potential is energy per unit charge.

quiz.q: Potential on the equatorial line of a dipole is
quiz.why: On the equatorial line the potentials of +q and −q cancel, so the potential is zero.

quiz.q: Potential due to a point charge varies as
quiz.why: For a point charge V = kq/r, so potential varies as 1/r.

quiz.q: Inside a charged conducting sphere the potential is
options: constant, equal to the surface value
quiz.why: The field inside a conductor is zero, so there is no potential difference there, and the potential stays constant at the surface value.

lessons.title: Equipotential surfaces and potential energy

story.title: Contour lines on a hill map

scenes.text: On a trekking map, Arjun sees contour lines joining points of equal height.
Walking along a contour costs no effort against gravity; climbing straight across contours is steepest.
Equipotential surfaces are the contour lines of electricity, and the field always points 'straight downhill'.

steps.title: Equipotential surfaces
steps.body:
A surface on which V is the same everywhere.
- No work is done in moving a charge along it.
- **E is always perpendicular** to an equipotential surface.
- Point charge: concentric spheres. Uniform field: parallel planes perpendicular to E.
- Closely spaced surfaces mean a strong field.
- Two equipotentials never intersect.

steps.title: Relation between E and V
steps.body: **E = −dV/dr** — the field points in the direction of steepest *decrease* of potential, and its magnitude is the potential gradient. For a uniform field: **E = V/d**. Unit V/m = N/C.

steps.title: Potential energy of charges
steps.body:
- **Two charges:** U = kq₁q₂/r₁₂ (work to assemble them from infinity). Negative for unlike charges (bound system).
- **Three charges:** U = k(q₁q₂/r₁₂ + q₂q₃/r₂₃ + q₁q₃/r₁₃).
- **Single charge in external potential V:** U = qV.
- **Dipole in a uniform field:** U(θ) = −pE cos θ (zero at θ = 90°). Work to rotate from θ₁ to θ₂: W = pE(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂). From 0° to 180°: W = 2pE.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** U for +2 μC and −3 μC at 10 cm:
- U = 9×10⁹ × (2×10⁻⁶)(−3×10⁻⁶)/0.1 = **−0.54 J** (0.54 J must be supplied to separate them fully).

**Ex 2.** A dipole p = 2×10⁻⁸ C m is in E = 5×10⁴ N/C. Work to turn it from aligned to anti-aligned:
- W = pE(cos 0° − cos 180°) = 2pE = **2×10⁻³ J**.

**Ex 3.** V = 5x² volts (x in m). Field at x = 2 m:
- E = −dV/dx = −10x = **−20 V/m** (points towards −x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the minus sign in E = −dV/dr.
- Counting each pair twice in the three-charge energy formula.
- Writing U = pE cos θ (the sign is negative; minimum energy is at θ = 0).

statements.s: Electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.
statements.why: Otherwise work would be done moving along the surface.

statements.s: Work is needed to move a charge along an equipotential surface.
A dipole has minimum potential energy when aligned with the field.
Two equipotential surfaces can intersect.
statements.why: A point cannot have two values of potential.

quiz.q: E and V are related by
quiz.why: The electric field is the negative gradient of potential: E = −dV/dr.

quiz.q: Equipotential surfaces of a point charge are
quiz.why: V = kq/r depends only on distance from the charge, so surfaces of equal V are concentric spheres.

quiz.q: Potential energy of two unlike charges is
quiz.why: Potential energy U = kq₁q₂/r. For unlike charges q₁q₂ is negative, so U is negative.

quiz.q: Work done to rotate a dipole from 0° to 180° in field E is
quiz.why: Energy is U = −pE cos θ. Going from 0° to 180° changes it from −pE to +pE, so the work done is 2pE.

quiz.q: A uniform field of 500 V/m exists between plates 4 mm apart. The p.d. is
quiz.why: For a uniform field V = Ed = 500 × 0.004 = 2 V.

lessons.title: Conductors and dielectrics in electric fields

scenes.text: Zoya rubs a ruler and holds it near a stream of tap water; the stream bends towards it.
Water molecules are permanent dipoles; they line up and get pulled into the stronger field.
Materials respond to fields in two very different ways — conductors move charge freely, dielectrics only polarise.

steps.title: Electrostatics of conductors
steps.body:
1. **E = 0 inside** the material of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
2. Just outside, **E is normal** to the surface and E = σ/ε₀.
3. **Excess charge resides only on the surface.**
4. **Potential is constant** throughout the volume and on the surface.
5. Charge density is higher at sharp points (this is why lightning conductors are pointed).
6. **Electrostatic shielding:** a cavity inside a conductor (with no charge in it) has zero field.

steps.title: Dielectrics and polarisation
steps.body:
Dielectrics are insulators that get **polarised** in a field.
- **Non-polar molecules** (O₂, H₂, CO₂): centres of + and − charge coincide; a field *induces* dipoles.
- **Polar molecules** (H₂O, HCl): permanent dipoles, randomly oriented, which *align* in a field.

**Polarisation P** = dipole moment per unit volume = χₑ E (for linear isotropic dielectrics). Bound surface charges reduce the field inside: **E = E₀/K**, with **K = 1 + χₑ** (in suitable units).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm has 2 μC. (a) Field at the centre: **0**. (b) Potential at the centre: kq/R = 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶/0.1 = **1.8×10⁵ V**. (c) Surface charge density: σ = q/4πR² = 2×10⁻⁶/(4π × 0.01) ≈ **1.6×10⁻⁵ C/m²**.

**Ex 2.** A field of 1000 V/m acts across a slab of K = 4 placed between plates (no air gap). Field inside the slab: E = 1000/4 = **250 V/m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the field inside a conductor is zero even while current flows — the result is for electrostatics only.
- Thinking dielectrics conduct; they only shift charge slightly within molecules.
- Forgetting that the potential inside a conductor is not zero, only constant.

steps.title: Real-world links
steps.body: Pointed lightning rods, earthing of appliances, the antistatic bags electronics ship in, and the high-K ceramics used in tiny capacitors all come from these ideas.

activity.prompt: Sort each molecule: polar or non-polar?

quiz.q: Excess charge on a conductor resides
quiz.why: Like charges repel each other and move as far apart as they can, so the excess charge sits on the outer surface of a conductor.

quiz.q: Field just outside a charged conductor is
quiz.why: Just outside a charged conductor the field is σ/ε₀ and normal to the surface. A tangential component would make surface charges move.

quiz.q: A dielectric placed in a field reduces the field inside to
quiz.why: Bound charges in the dielectric set up an opposing field, so the net field inside is reduced to E₀/K.

quiz.q: Which molecule is non-polar?
quiz.why: CO₂ is linear and symmetric, so the dipole moments of its two C=O bonds cancel and it is non-polar. H₂O, NH₃ and HCl are polar.

quiz.q: Charge density on an irregular conductor is greatest at
quiz.why: Charge density is higher where the radius of curvature is smaller, which is at sharp points.

lessons.title: Capacitors and their combinations

scenes.text: Nisha's old camera whines for a few seconds before the flash is ready.
During the whine a capacitor slowly fills with charge from the small battery.
Then it dumps all that energy in a millisecond — a burst no battery could give directly.

steps.title: Capacitance
steps.body: A capacitor = two conductors separated by an insulator. **C = Q/V**. Unit **farad** (1 F = 1 C/V); practical units μF, nF, pF. C depends only on geometry and the medium, not on Q or V.

steps.title: Parallel-plate capacitor (derivation)
steps.body:
Plates of area A, separation d, charges ±Q, σ = Q/A.
- Field between plates: E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A) (fields outside cancel).
- p.d.: V = Ed = Qd/(ε₀A).
- **C = Q/V = ε₀A/d**.

With a dielectric filling the gap: **C = Kε₀A/d = KC₀**.
With a slab of thickness t (< d): **C = ε₀A/(d − t + t/K)**; a metal slab (K → ∞) gives ε₀A/(d − t).

steps.title: Combinations
steps.body:
- **Series** (same Q on each): V = V₁ + V₂ + … ⇒ **1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …** (result smaller than the smallest).
- **Parallel** (same V across each): Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + … ⇒ **C = C₁ + C₂ + …**
For two in series: C = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A = 6×10⁻³ m², d = 3 mm (air).
- C = 8.85×10⁻¹² × 6×10⁻³ / 3×10⁻³ = **1.77×10⁻¹¹ F ≈ 17.7 pF**.
- With mica (K = 6) filling the gap: **106 pF**.

**Ex 2.** 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF across 12 V.
- Series: 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 ⇒ **C = 1 μF**; Q = 12 μC on each; V across 2 μF = 6 V, 3 μF = 4 V, 6 μF = 2 V.
- Parallel: C = **11 μF**; total Q = 132 μC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the resistor formulas the wrong way round: capacitors in *parallel* add directly.
- Assuming equal voltage on series capacitors — it is equal *charge*.
- Forgetting to convert mm to m and cm² to m² in C = ε₀A/d.

steps.title: Battery connected or not?
steps.body: When a dielectric is inserted: **battery connected** ⇒ V fixed, C, Q and U increase K times. **Battery disconnected** ⇒ Q fixed, C up K times, V and U fall K times.

activity.prompt: Capacitors of 4 μF and 12 μF are in series, and this pair is in parallel with a 5 μF capacitor. Equivalent capacitance in μF?

quiz.q: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is
quiz.why: For a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d, from E = σ/ε₀ and V = Ed.

quiz.q: If plate separation is doubled (battery removed), capacitance
quiz.why: C = ε₀A/d, so C ∝ 1/d, and doubling the separation halves the capacitance.

quiz.q: Equivalent of two 6 μF capacitors in series is
quiz.why: In series 1/C = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3, so C = 3 μF.

quiz.q: In a series combination each capacitor has the same
quiz.why: In series the same charge flows through every capacitor, so each carries the same charge.

quiz.q: Filling the gap with a dielectric K = 5 changes C₀ to
quiz.why: A dielectric of constant K multiplies the capacitance by K, so C = 5C₀.

quiz.q: A metal slab of thickness d/2 is inserted into a parallel-plate capacitor of gap d. C becomes
quiz.why: A metal slab of thickness t makes the effective gap d − t = d/2, so C = ε₀A/(d/2) = 2C₀.

lessons.title: Energy stored in a capacitor

scenes.text: Kunal connects a full water tank to an empty one with a pipe; water flows until the levels match.
Some energy is lost as the water sloshes and churns.
Connecting a charged capacitor to an uncharged one is the same — charge shares and some energy is lost as heat.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
While charging, at an instant the charge is q and p.d. q/C. Work to add dq: dW = (q/C) dq.
W = ∫₀^Q (q/C) dq = Q²/2C.

**U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV**.

steps.title: Energy density
steps.body:
For a parallel-plate capacitor: U = ½CV² = ½(ε₀A/d)(Ed)² = ½ε₀E² × (Ad).
Volume between plates = Ad, so the **energy density u = ½ε₀E²** (J/m³). In a dielectric: u = ½Kε₀E². Energy is stored *in the field*.

steps.title: Sharing of charge
steps.body:
Two capacitors C₁ (at V₁) and C₂ (at V₂) joined positive to positive:
- Common potential **V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂)** (charge conserved).
- **Energy lost = C₁C₂(V₁ − V₂)² / 2(C₁ + C₂)** — dissipated as heat and radiation in the wires. Energy is never gained.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 12 pF capacitor is charged to 50 V.
- U = ½ × 12×10⁻¹² × 50² = **1.5×10⁻⁸ J**.

**Ex 2.** A 2 μF capacitor charged to 100 V is connected to an uncharged 2 μF capacitor.
- Common V = (2×100 + 0)/4 = **50 V**.
- Initial U = ½ × 2×10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.01 J; final U = ½ × 4×10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 0.005 J.
- **Loss = 0.005 J** (half!). Check with formula: (2×2/2×4) × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.005 J ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using U = ½QV with the final V but initial Q.
- Expecting energy to be conserved when capacitors share charge.
- For a capacitor charged by a battery, the battery supplies QV but only ½QV is stored — the other half is lost in the circuit resistance.

bands.text: Up to 20 V: U = ½CV² ≤ 2 mJ — tiny.
At 50 V: U = 12.5 mJ. Doubling V quadruples energy.
At 100 V: U = 50 mJ — 25 times the 20 V value, because U ∝ V².

quiz.why: The energy stored is U = ½CV², which equals Q²/2C and ½QV.

quiz.q: Energy density of an electric field in vacuum is
quiz.why: The energy per unit volume of an electric field in vacuum is ½ε₀E².

quiz.q: Doubling the charge on a capacitor makes its energy
quiz.why: U = Q²/2C, so U ∝ Q². Doubling the charge makes the energy four times.

quiz.q: When two capacitors share charge, total energy
quiz.why: When two capacitors share charge, current flows between them and some energy is lost as heat, so the total energy decreases.

lessons.title: Current, drift velocity and mobility

scenes.text: Aarav flips a switch and the bulb glows instantly, yet he reads that electrons in the wire crawl at less than a millimetre per second.
His teacher compares it to a packed metro tube: push one person in at one end and someone pops out at the other at once.
The signal (the field) travels near light speed; the electrons themselves just drift.

steps.title: Electric current
steps.body:
**I = dq/dt**; unit ampere (A) = C/s. Current is a scalar (it obeys algebraic, not vector, addition) even though it has a direction convention: conventional current flows from + to −, opposite to electron flow.

**Current density j = I/A** (A/m²), a vector along E.

steps.title: Drift velocity — derivation
steps.body:
Free electrons move randomly (≈10⁵ m/s) with zero average velocity. Apply a field E: each electron accelerates a = −eE/m between collisions. The average time between collisions is the **relaxation time τ**.

**v_d = −eEτ/m** (opposite to E).

In time Δt, electrons in a length v_dΔt of the wire (cross-section A, n electrons per m³) cross a section:
Δq = neAv_dΔt ⇒ **I = neAv_d**.

steps.title: Ohm's law from the microscopic picture
steps.body:
j = I/A = nev_d = ne(eEτ/m) = (ne²τ/m)E.
So **j = σE** with conductivity **σ = ne²τ/m** and resistivity **ρ = m/(ne²τ)**. Since E = V/l and j = I/A, this gives V = (ρl/A) I = IR — Ohm's law.

**Mobility μ = v_d/E = eτ/m** (m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A copper wire of cross-section 1.0×10⁻⁷ m² carries 1.5 A; n = 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³.
- v_d = I/(neA) = 1.5 / (8.5×10²⁸ × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 1.0×10⁻⁷)
- = 1.5/1360 ≈ **1.1×10⁻³ m/s** (about 1 mm/s).

**Ex 2.** Relaxation time in copper (ρ = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω m):
- τ = m/(ne²ρ) = 9.1×10⁻³¹ / (8.5×10²⁸ × 2.56×10⁻³⁸ × 1.7×10⁻⁸)
- ≈ **2.5×10⁻¹⁴ s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing drift speed (~mm/s) with thermal speed (~10⁵ m/s) or signal speed (~10⁸ m/s).
- Calling current a vector because it has a direction.
- Forgetting that for a given current, v_d is larger where the wire is thinner (v_d ∝ 1/A).

activity.prompt: A wire of cross-section 2×10⁻⁶ m² carries 3.2 A. If n = 1×10²⁹ m⁻³, find the drift speed in mm/s.

quiz.q: Drift velocity of electrons is
quiz.why: Electrons are negatively charged, so they drift opposite to the electric field.

quiz.q: I = neAv_d. If the area is halved for the same current, v_d
quiz.why: I = neAv_d, so for the same current v_d ∝ 1/A. Halving the area doubles the drift velocity.

quiz.q: Resistivity depends on
quiz.why: ρ = m/(ne²τ), so resistivity depends on the number density of electrons and the relaxation time, not on length or area.

quiz.q: Mobility is defined as
quiz.why: Mobility μ = v_d/E, the drift velocity per unit electric field.

quiz.q: Electric current is a scalar because
options: it does not follow vector addition laws
quiz.why: Current has direction along the wire, but it does not obey the vector addition rule. Currents at a junction add algebraically, so it is a scalar.

lessons.title: Ohm's law, resistivity and temperature

scenes.text: Kavya's toaster draws a big current for the first second, then settles down.
As the nichrome coil heats up its resistance rises, so the current falls a little.
Resistance depends on temperature — and in some materials it even drops on heating.

steps.title: Ohm's law and resistance
steps.body:
At constant temperature and physical conditions, **V = IR**. Unit ohm (Ω).

**R = ρl/A** where ρ (Ω m) is resistivity — a property of the material. Conductivity σ = 1/ρ.

**Non-ohmic devices** (diodes, thyristors, water voltameter, gallium arsenide) show non-linear or one-way V–I graphs, or more than one V for the same I.

steps.title: Effect of stretching a wire
steps.body: Volume stays constant (Al = constant). If length becomes n times, area becomes 1/n times, so **R becomes n² times**. If radius is halved (same volume), length is 4 times and R becomes 16 times.

steps.title: Temperature dependence
steps.body:
For metals: **ρ_T = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]**, α > 0 (τ falls as ions vibrate more). Nichrome has a very small α and high ρ — ideal for heaters; manganin and constantan for standard resistors.

For **semiconductors** α < 0: ρ falls with temperature because n increases faster than τ decreases. Insulators: ρ very high.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A coil has 2.1 Ω at 27 °C and 2.7 Ω at 100 °C. Find α.
- α = (R₂ − R₁)/(R₁ΔT) = 0.6/(2.1 × 73)
- ≈ **3.9×10⁻³ °C⁻¹**.

**Ex 2.** A 1 m wire of 4 Ω is stretched to 3 m (volume constant).
- R' = n²R = 9 × 4 = **36 Ω**; resistivity is unchanged (same material).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking resistivity changes when a wire is stretched — resistance changes, resistivity does not.
- Treating every device as ohmic.
- Using α in R = R₀(1 + αΔT) with ΔT in kelvin vs °C — any is fine since it is a *difference*.

statements.s: Resistivity of copper increases on heating.
Doubling the length of a wire by stretching doubles its resistance.
statements.why: Area also halves, so R becomes 4 times.

statements.s: Resistivity of silicon decreases with temperature.
A diode obeys Ohm's law.
statements.why: Its V–I graph is non-linear and one-directional.

quiz.q: Resistivity of a wire depends on
quiz.why: Resistivity is a property of the material and changes with temperature, but not with length or area.

quiz.q: A wire's length is tripled by stretching. Its resistance becomes
quiz.why: Stretching to 3 times the length makes the area 1/3. So R ∝ l/A rises by 3 × 3 = 9 times.

quiz.q: Nichrome is used in heaters because it has
options: high resistivity and high melting point
quiz.why: Nichrome has high resistivity and a high melting point, so it gets very hot without melting or oxidising.

quiz.q: For semiconductors the temperature coefficient of resistivity is
quiz.why: In semiconductors more charge carriers are freed as temperature rises, so resistivity falls, giving a negative temperature coefficient.

quiz.q: The SI unit of resistivity is
quiz.why: ρ = RA/l, so the unit is ohm × m²/m = ohm metre (Ω m).

lessons.title: Combinations of resistors and electrical power

scenes.text: When Sahil switches off his room's fan, the kitchen light stays on.
Home appliances are connected in parallel so each gets the full 230 V and works independently.
And the electricity bill counts kilowatt-hours — energy, not power.

steps.title: Series and parallel
steps.body:
- **Series:** same current; **R = R₁ + R₂ + …**
- **Parallel:** same voltage; **1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …**; two in parallel: R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
- n equal resistors R: series nR, parallel R/n.

steps.title: Electrical power and energy
steps.body:
Energy dissipated when charge q falls through V: W = qV = VIt.

**P = VI = I²R = V²/R** (watt). In series (same I) the larger R dissipates more power; in parallel (same V) the smaller R dissipates more.

1 kWh (1 'unit') = 3.6×10⁶ J. Power loss in transmission lines, I²R, is reduced by transmitting at high voltage (low current).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A bulb is rated 100 W, 220 V.
- R = V²/P = 220²/100 = **484 Ω**.
- On 110 V: P = 110²/484 = **25 W** (a quarter — P ∝ V² for fixed R).

**Ex 2.** 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel across 6 V.
- 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1 ⇒ **R = 1 Ω**; total I = 6 A.
- Currents: 3 A, 2 A, 1 A; powers 18 W, 12 W, 6 W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P = I²R and P = V²/R and concluding opposite things — check which quantity is common.
- Forgetting that a bulb's rated values give its resistance, which stays (roughly) the same on other voltages.
- Adding parallel resistances directly.

steps.title: Two bulbs in series
steps.body: Two bulbs 60 W and 100 W (same rated voltage) in series: the **60 W bulb glows brighter** because it has the larger resistance and the same current flows through both.

activity.prompt: A 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω is connected to 12 V. Find the current from the source (A).

quiz.q: Equivalent of three 9 Ω resistors in parallel is
quiz.why: n equal resistors in parallel give R/n = 9/3 = 3 Ω.

quiz.q: A heater of 1000 W runs for 2 hours. Energy used:
quiz.why: Energy = power × time = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh.

quiz.q: In a parallel combination, which resistor dissipates the most power?
quiz.why: In parallel all have the same voltage, so P = V²/R is largest for the smallest resistance.

quiz.q: 1 kWh equals
Power lines use high voltage to
quiz.why: For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current, which reduces the I²R heat loss in the lines.

lessons.title: Cells, emf and internal resistance

story.title: The car that would not start

scenes.text: On a cold morning, Rohan's dad turns the key; the dashboard lights dim sharply and the engine just clicks.
The battery's emf is still about 12 V, but its internal resistance has grown in the cold.
When the starter motor demands a huge current, most of the voltage is lost inside the battery itself.

steps.title: emf and terminal voltage
steps.body:
**emf (ε)**: the p.d. across a cell's terminals when no current flows — work done by the cell per unit charge.

With current I through external R and internal resistance r:
- **I = ε/(R + r)**
- Terminal voltage **V = ε − Ir** (discharging); **V = ε + Ir** while being charged.
- Short circuit (R = 0): I_max = ε/r.

steps.title: Combinations of cells
steps.body:
- **n identical cells in series:** ε_eq = nε, r_eq = nr ⇒ I = nε/(R + nr).
- **Two cells in parallel:** ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂), r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂).
- **n identical cells in parallel:** ε_eq = ε, r_eq = r/n.
- A cell connected the wrong way in series subtracts its emf but still adds its r.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking terminal voltage equal to emf when current flows.
- Forgetting the internal resistance of reversed cells.
- Using V = ε − Ir while the battery is being *charged* (it is ε + Ir).

steps.title: Graph trick
steps.body: A V–I graph for a cell is a straight line: the **y-intercept = ε** and the **slope = −r**. The x-intercept is the short-circuit current ε/r.

activity.prompt: A cell's terminal voltage is 2.2 V when no current flows and 1.8 V when it supplies current through a 5 Ω resistor. Find its internal resistance (Ω).

quiz.q: When a cell is being charged, terminal voltage is
quiz.why: While charging, current flows into the positive terminal against the emf, so the terminal voltage is V = ε + Ir.

quiz.q: Short-circuit current of a cell is
quiz.why: With R = 0 the whole emf drives current through the internal resistance: I = ε/r.

quiz.q: n identical cells in parallel have internal resistance
quiz.why: Identical cells in parallel combine like parallel resistors, so r_eq = r/n.

quiz.q: On a V–I graph of a cell, the slope gives
quiz.why: V = ε − Ir, so a graph of V against I has slope −r.

quiz.q: emf of a cell is measured best when
quiz.why: When no current flows, there is no drop across the internal resistance, so the terminal voltage equals the emf.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone bridge

scenes.text: Mehak is repairing a toy whose circuit has two batteries and loops that cannot be split into simple series and parallel parts.
She writes two rules on paper: what flows into a point flows out, and around any loop the voltage rises and drops cancel.
With three equations she finds every current — Kirchhoff's rules work for any circuit.

steps.title: Kirchhoff's rules
steps.body:
1. **Junction rule (KCL):** ΣI at a junction = 0 (current in = current out) — conservation of charge.
2. **Loop rule (KVL):** Σ(ΔV) around any closed loop = 0 — conservation of energy.

**Sign conventions:** going across a resistor *with* the assumed current: −IR; against: +IR. Going across a cell from − to +: +ε; from + to −: −ε. If a current comes out negative, its true direction is opposite to the assumed one.

steps.title: Wheatstone bridge
steps.body:
Four resistors P, Q (one arm), R, S (other arm), a galvanometer across the middle and a cell across the ends. When the galvanometer shows no deflection, the bridge is **balanced**:

**P/Q = R/S**

Derivation: with I_g = 0, the same current I₁ flows in P and Q, and I₂ in R and S; the two midpoints are at equal potential, so I₁P = I₂R and I₁Q = I₂S. Dividing gives the condition. The galvanometer and the cell can be swapped without disturbing balance. The meter bridge is a practical form of this circuit.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A loop has a 12 V cell, a 4 V cell opposing it, and resistors 2 Ω and 6 Ω in series (ignore internal resistances).
- KVL: 12 − 4 − 2I − 6I = 0 ⇒ **I = 1 A**.

**Ex 2.** At a junction 3 A and 2 A enter, 4 A leaves along one wire. The fourth wire carries **1 A out**.

**Ex 3.** Bridge: P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω, R = 15 Ω. Balance needs S = QR/P = **30 Ω**. In a balanced bridge the galvanometer branch can be removed, so equivalent resistance = (10 + 20) ∥ (15 + 30) = 30×45/75 = **18 Ω**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing sign conventions halfway through a loop.
- Thinking a negative current answer means a mistake — it just means the direction was assumed wrongly.
- Forgetting that a balanced bridge's middle resistor carries no current and can be ignored.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to solve a circuit with Kirchhoff's rules.
items: Mark an assumed current direction in every branch
Apply the junction rule at enough junctions
Apply the loop rule with consistent signs
Interpret negative answers as reversed currents

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule follows from conservation of
quiz.why: The junction rule says charge entering a junction equals charge leaving it, which is conservation of charge.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule follows from conservation of
quiz.why: The loop rule says the net work done on a charge around a closed loop is zero, which is conservation of energy.

quiz.q: Balanced Wheatstone bridge condition:
quiz.why: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when P/Q = R/S, when the two midpoints are at the same potential.

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge the current through the galvanometer is
quiz.why: At balance the two midpoints are at equal potential, so no current flows through the galvanometer.

quiz.q: Four 2 Ω resistors form a balanced bridge with a 2 Ω galvanometer branch. Equivalent resistance between the ends:
quiz.why: The bridge is balanced, so the galvanometer branch carries no current. Two (2 + 2) = 4 Ω paths in parallel give 2 Ω.

questions.q: The SI unit of current density is
questions.why: Current density j = I/A, so its unit is A/m².

questions.q: Drift speed of electrons in a typical wire is of the order of
questions.why: Electrons drift very slowly, only about a millimetre per second or less (10⁻³ to 10⁻⁴ m/s).

questions.q: A 60 W and a 100 W bulb (both 220 V) are in series on 220 V. Which glows brighter?
questions.why: The 60 W bulb has the larger resistance (R = V²/P). In series the current is the same, so P = I²R is greater for the 60 W bulb, which glows brighter.

questions.q: Assertion: Resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature. Reason: relaxation time decreases as temperature rises.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A rise in temperature shortens the relaxation time τ, and since ρ = m/(ne²τ), resistivity and hence resistance rise.

Five identical resistors of R in parallel have equivalent
questions.why: Five identical resistors in parallel give R/5.

questions.q: A wire of resistance 10 Ω is bent into a circle. Resistance between two diametrically opposite points:
questions.why: The two diametrically opposite points divide the circle into two halves of 5 Ω each. In parallel they give 2.5 Ω.

questions.q: The resistance of a wire is R. Its radius is halved by stretching (volume constant). New resistance:
questions.why: Halving the radius quarters the area. Volume is constant, so the length becomes 4 times. R ∝ l/A rises by 4 × 4 = 16.

questions.q: Case: A battery of 6 identical cells (each 2 V, 0.5 Ω) in series feeds a 9 Ω resistor. Current:
questions.why: Total emf = 6 × 2 = 12 V and total internal resistance = 6 × 0.5 = 3 Ω. I = 12/(9 + 3) = 1 A.

questions.q: Two cells (ε, r) in series with one reversed, across R. Current:
questions.why: With one cell reversed, the emfs oppose and cancel, so the net emf is zero and so is the current.

questions.q: A copper wire of 2 mm² carries 4 A. With n = 8×10²⁸ m⁻³, drift speed is about
A 220 V, 1000 W heater is used on 200 V. Power drawn (constant R):
questions.why: R is constant, so P ∝ V². P = 1000 × (200/220)² ≈ 826 W.

questions.q: In a Wheatstone bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 8 Ω, R = 6 Ω, S = 12 Ω and the galvanometer has 10 Ω. Current through the galvanometer when 6 V is applied:
questions.why: P/Q = 4/8 = 1/2 and R/S = 6/12 = 1/2, so the bridge is balanced and the galvanometer carries no current.

questions.q: A battery gives 0.5 A through 12 Ω and 0.25 A through 25 Ω. Its internal resistance:
Case: A coil has R = 10 Ω at 20 °C and α = 4×10⁻³ °C⁻¹. At what temperature is R = 12 Ω?
questions.why: R = R₀(1 + αΔT): 12 = 10(1 + 0.004ΔT), so ΔT = 50 °C and the temperature is 20 + 50 = 70 °C.

questions.q: Assertion: Terminal voltage of a cell can exceed its emf. Reason: while being charged, V = ε + Ir.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. During charging current is forced into the cell, so V = ε + Ir, which is greater than ε.

questions.q: Twelve identical cells (ε, r) are arranged as 3 parallel rows of 4 in series each, across R. For maximum power delivered to R, R should equal
questions.why: Three rows of 4 cells in series: each row has emf 4ε and resistance 4r. Three rows in parallel give r_eq = 4r/3. Maximum power is delivered when R equals the internal resistance, 4r/3.

questions.q: Case: In the loop rule problem, a 10 V cell (r = 1 Ω) and a 4 V cell (r = 1 Ω) are connected + to + with a 4 Ω resistor in the loop. Current:
questions.why: The cells are connected with opposing emfs, so net emf = 10 − 4 = 6 V. Total resistance = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 Ω, so I = 1 A.

lessons.title: Magnetic force and the motion of charges

scenes.text: On a rare night, sky-watchers in Ladakh photograph a faint red glow — an aurora.
Charged particles from the Sun spiral along Earth's magnetic field lines towards the poles.
A magnetic force bends a moving charge but never speeds it up — that is why the particles corkscrew instead of crashing straight in.

steps.title: Lorentz force
steps.body:
For a charge q moving with velocity v in fields E and B:

**F = q[E + v × B]**

Magnetic part: **F = qvB sin θ**, perpendicular to both v and B (right-hand rule; reverse it for negative charges).
- No force if v = 0 or v ∥ B.
- Being perpendicular to v, the magnetic force **does no work**: speed and kinetic energy stay constant.
- Unit of B: **tesla** (1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹); 1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ T.

steps.title: Circular and helical motion
steps.body:
If v ⊥ B: qvB = mv²/r ⇒ **r = mv/(qB)**, **ω = qB/m**, **T = 2πm/(qB)** — the period does not depend on speed.

If v makes angle θ with B: the component v cos θ is unaffected, v sin θ gives circular motion ⇒ a **helix** with radius r = mv sin θ/(qB) and **pitch p = v cos θ × T = 2πmv cos θ/(qB)**.

steps.title: Velocity selector
steps.body: Cross E and B at right angles, both perpendicular to v. Electric force qE and magnetic force qvB oppose. Particles pass undeflected when **v = E/B**, regardless of charge or mass.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A proton (m = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 2×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to B = 0.1 T.
- r = mv/(qB) = (1.67×10⁻²⁷ × 2×10⁶)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) ≈ **0.21 m**.

**Ex 2.** An electron at 3×10⁷ m/s moves at 30° to B = 6×10⁻⁴ T.
- F = evB sin θ = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 3×10⁷ × 6×10⁻⁴ × 0.5 = **1.44×10⁻¹⁵ N**.

**Ex 3.** E = 3×10⁴ V/m and B = 0.02 T are crossed. Undeflected speed v = E/B = **1.5×10⁶ m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the right-hand rule for an electron without reversing the direction.
- Thinking the magnetic force can change the speed of a particle.
- Using v instead of v sin θ for the radius of a helix.

activity.prompt: An α-particle (q = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 6.4×10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 1×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T. Find the radius of its path in cm.

quiz.why: F = qvB sin θ, and for motion parallel to B, θ = 0, so the force is zero.

quiz.q: Work done by a magnetic force on a moving charge is
quiz.why: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work on the charge.

quiz.q: Time period of a charged particle in a uniform B is
quiz.why: T = 2πm/qB, which does not depend on the speed or radius of the circular path.

quiz.q: 1 tesla equals
quiz.why: 1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ tesla, so 1 tesla = 10⁴ gauss.

quiz.q: In a velocity selector undeflected particles have v =
quiz.why: Particles go straight when the electric and magnetic forces balance: qE = qvB, so v = E/B.

quiz.why: r = mv/qB, so r ∝ v. Doubling the speed doubles the radius.

lessons.title: Biot–Savart law and the circular loop

scenes.text: Tanvi opens an old doorbell and finds a coil of copper wire wound round an iron core.
Every tiny piece of the wire makes a small magnetic field; added together they make a strong field at the centre.
Biot and Savart worked out how much each little piece contributes.

steps.title: Biot–Savart law
steps.body:
The field dB at a point at distance r from a current element I dl:

**dB = (μ₀/4π) × I dl sin θ / r²**, vector form dB = (μ₀/4π) I (dl × r̂)/r²

μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ (permeability of free space). dB is perpendicular to both dl and r. Compare: Coulomb's law has a source scalar q; Biot–Savart has a vector source I dl, and the field is zero along the line of the element (θ = 0).

steps.title: Field on the axis of a circular loop (derivation)
steps.body:
Loop radius R, current I, point P on the axis at distance x. Each element dl is ⊥ to the line joining it to P (length √(R² + x²)), so dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl/(R² + x²).

Components perpendicular to the axis cancel in pairs; components along the axis add: dB cos φ with cos φ = R/√(R² + x²).

B = (μ₀ I R/4π(R² + x²)^(3/2)) ∮dl = **μ₀ I R² / [2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]**

- At the centre (x = 0): **B = μ₀I/(2R)**; for N turns, μ₀NI/(2R).
- Direction by the right-hand thumb rule (curl fingers with current; thumb gives B).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A coil of 100 turns, radius 10 cm, carries 1 A.
- B at centre = μ₀NI/(2R) = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 100 × 1/(0.2) = **6.28×10⁻⁴ T**.

**Ex 2.** Same coil, point on the axis at x = R = 10 cm.
- B = μ₀NIR²/[2(2R²)^(3/2)] = B_centre/(2√2) ≈ **2.2×10⁻⁴ T**.

**Ex 3.** A semicircular arc of radius R carrying I: B at centre = μ₀I/(4R) (half of a full loop).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using μ₀I/(2πR) (straight wire) for a loop centre — the loop is μ₀I/(2R).
- Forgetting the 3/2 power on the axis.
- Not multiplying by the number of turns N.

steps.title: A loop is a magnetic dipole
steps.body: Far along the axis (x ≫ R): B ≈ μ₀IR²/(2x³) = (μ₀/4π)(2m/x³) with **m = IπR² = IA** — exactly like the axial field of an electric dipole. The face where current appears anticlockwise acts as a north pole.

activity.prompt: Complete the results.
activity.text: Field at the centre of a loop of radius R is μ₀I/(___R). The permeability of free space is 4π×10^___ T m/A. Along the line of the current element itself the field is ___.

quiz.why: The field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns is B = μ₀NI/2R.

quiz.q: Biot–Savart law gives dB proportional to
quiz.why: In the Biot–Savart law, dB ∝ Idl sin θ/r², so it falls as the inverse square of distance.

quiz.q: If the radius of a loop is doubled at the same current, B at centre
quiz.why: B = μ₀I/2R at the centre, so doubling the radius at the same current halves B.

quiz.q: Far along the axis, a current loop behaves like
quiz.why: Far from the loop, along its axis, B ∝ m/x³ like a bar magnet, so the loop behaves as a magnetic dipole.

quiz.q: The direction of B at the centre of a loop is given by
quiz.why: The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction of B at the centre: curl the fingers in the direction of current and the thumb shows the field.

lessons.title: Ampère's circuital law: wire and solenoid

scenes.text: Grandpa Ravi is nervous before his MRI scan; the technician explains the huge ring is a solenoid.
Superconducting wire carries a large current through thousands of turns, making a strong, uniform field inside.
Ampère's law tells us that field: μ₀ times turns per metre times current.

steps.title: Ampère's circuital law
steps.body:
**∮ B·dl = μ₀ I_enclosed**

The line integral of B around any closed loop (an *Amperian loop*) equals μ₀ times the net current threading it. Sign by the right-hand rule. Like Gauss's law, it is most useful when symmetry makes B constant along the loop.

steps.title: Long straight wire
steps.body:
Take a circle of radius r centred on the wire. B is tangential and constant in magnitude:
B × 2πr = μ₀I ⇒ **B = μ₀I/(2πr)**. Field lines are concentric circles (right-hand thumb rule).

steps.title: Long solenoid
steps.body:
n = N/L turns per metre. Inside, B is uniform and along the axis; outside ≈ 0. Take a rectangular loop with one side l inside:
B l = μ₀ (n l) I ⇒ **B = μ₀nI**.
At the ends of a long solenoid B ≈ μ₀nI/2. With a core of relative permeability μᵣ, B = μ₀μᵣnI.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A long wire carries 35 A. Field at 20 cm:
- B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2×10⁻⁷ × 35/0.2 = **3.5×10⁻⁵ T**.

**Ex 2.** A solenoid 0.5 m long has 500 turns and carries 5 A.
- n = 500/0.5 = 1000 m⁻¹
- B = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 5 = **6.28×10⁻³ T** inside.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total turns N instead of turns per unit length n in B = μ₀nI.
- Including currents outside the Amperian loop.
- Thinking B is zero inside a wire — for a thick wire of radius a it rises as μ₀Ir/(2πa²) inside.

quiz.q: Ampère's law relates ∮B·dl to
quiz.why: Ampère's circuital law states that the line integral of B around a closed loop is μ₀ times the current enclosed.

quiz.why: Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform and equals μ₀nI.

quiz.q: Field at the end of a long solenoid is about
quiz.why: At the end of a long solenoid the field is half that at the centre, μ₀nI/2.

quiz.q: Field due to a long wire at distance r varies as
quiz.why: For a long straight wire B = μ₀I/2πr, so B varies as 1/r.

quiz.q: Field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are
quiz.why: By the right-hand thumb rule the field lines around a straight wire are concentric circles.

lessons.title: Force between currents and torque on a loop

story.title: The electric motor in a mixer

scenes.text: Isha's mixer-grinder whirs into life — inside, coils of wire spin between magnets.
Each side of a current loop is pushed in opposite directions by the magnetic field, creating a turning effect.
That torque on a current loop is the heart of every DC motor and every analogue meter.

steps.title: Force on a conductor
steps.body: A straight conductor of length l carrying I in field B: **F = I(l × B)**, magnitude **BIl sin θ** (Fleming's left-hand rule).

steps.title: Two parallel currents
steps.body:
Wire a produces B_a = μ₀I_a/(2πd) at wire b. Force per unit length on b:
**f = μ₀I_aI_b/(2πd)**
- **Like (parallel) currents attract; opposite currents repel** (opposite of charges!).
- Historically the ampere was defined as the current that gives 2×10⁻⁷ N/m between wires 1 m apart; since 2019 the SI defines the ampere by fixing e = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C, and the old relation remains true in practice.

steps.title: Torque on a rectangular loop
steps.body:
Loop of N turns, area A, current I in uniform B; θ = angle between B and the loop's normal (area vector).
- Net force = 0.
- Torque **τ = NIAB sin θ**, vector form **τ = m × B** with **magnetic moment m = NIA** (A m²).
- Potential energy U = −m·B. Stable equilibrium when m ∥ B.

**Electron orbit as a dipole:** an electron circling at speed v in radius r has μ = evr/2 = (e/2mₑ)L. For the lowest Bohr orbit μ_B ≈ 9.27×10⁻²⁴ A m² (Bohr magneton).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 3 A in the same direction.
- f = 2×10⁻⁷ × 5 × 3/0.1 = **3×10⁻⁵ N/m, attractive**.

**Ex 2.** A coil of 50 turns, area 5×10⁻³ m², carries 2 A in B = 0.2 T with its plane parallel to B (θ = 90° between normal and B).
- τ = NIAB = 50 × 2 × 5×10⁻³ × 0.2 = **0.1 N m** (maximum).
- m = NIA = **0.5 A m²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the angle between B and the *plane* of the coil instead of its *normal* in τ = NIAB sin θ.
- Saying parallel currents repel.
- Expecting a net force on a closed loop in a *uniform* field.

statements.s: Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract.
statements.why: Each lies in the other's field and the force points inward.

statements.s: A current loop in a uniform field feels a net force.
statements.why: Forces on opposite sides cancel; only torque remains.

statements.s: Torque on a coil is maximum when its plane is parallel to B.
statements.why: Then the normal is ⊥ B, sin 90° = 1.

statements.s: Magnetic moment of a coil is NIA.

lessons.title: Moving-coil galvanometer, ammeter and voltmeter

story.title: Building a meter in the lab

scenes.text: In the practical exam, Varun is handed a galvanometer that reads only 3 mA full-scale and is asked to measure 3 A.
He adds a tiny resistance in parallel — a shunt — so most of the current bypasses the coil.
Later, with a large resistance in series, the same galvanometer becomes a voltmeter.

steps.title: How the galvanometer works
steps.body:
A rectangular coil (N turns, area A) hangs in a **radial magnetic field** from curved pole pieces and a soft-iron core, so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B (sin θ = 1).
- Deflecting torque NIAB is balanced by the spring's restoring torque kφ:
**NIAB = kφ ⇒ φ = (NAB/k) I** — a linear scale.
- **Current sensitivity** φ/I = NAB/k.
- **Voltage sensitivity** φ/V = NAB/(kG), G = coil resistance.
Doubling N doubles current sensitivity but also doubles G, so voltage sensitivity is unchanged.

steps.title: Conversion
steps.body:
- **Ammeter:** small **shunt S in parallel**: I_g G = (I − I_g)S ⇒ **S = I_g G/(I − I_g)**. Ammeter resistance is tiny; it is joined in series; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance.
- **Voltmeter:** large **R in series**: V = I_g(G + R) ⇒ **R = V/I_g − G**. Joined in parallel; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
A galvanometer has G = 12 Ω and full-scale current 3 mA.

**Ex 1. Ammeter 0–3 A:**
- S = (3×10⁻³ × 12)/(3 − 0.003) ≈ **0.012 Ω** in parallel.

**Ex 2. Voltmeter 0–18 V:**
- R = 18/(3×10⁻³) − 12 = 6000 − 12 = **5988 Ω** in series.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the shunt in series or the multiplier in parallel.
- Forgetting that a galvanometer alone cannot measure large currents — the coil would burn.
- Thinking higher current sensitivity always means higher voltage sensitivity.

activity.prompt: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full deflection for 2 mA. What series resistance (Ω) converts it into a voltmeter of range 0–10 V?

quiz.q: The radial field in a galvanometer ensures
options: the coil's plane is always parallel to B, so the scale is linear
quiz.why: A radial field keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to B, so the torque depends only on current and the deflection is proportional to current, giving a linear scale.

quiz.q: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, connect
quiz.why: An ammeter has a low-resistance shunt connected in parallel with the galvanometer, so most current bypasses it.

quiz.q: An ideal voltmeter has resistance
quiz.why: An ideal voltmeter draws no current from the circuit, so its resistance is infinite.

quiz.q: Current sensitivity of a galvanometer is
quiz.why: Current sensitivity is deflection per unit current: φ/I = NAB/k.

quiz.q: If N is doubled, voltage sensitivity
quiz.why: Voltage sensitivity = NAB/(kG). Doubling N also doubles the resistance G of the coil, so the ratio is unchanged.

outcomes: Learners can describe field lines of a bar magnet and compute its axial and equatorial fields.

lessons.title: The bar magnet and its field

scenes.text: Little Anaya snaps a fridge magnet in two, hoping to get one north piece and one south piece.
Each half still has both a north and a south pole.
Her sister explains: a magnet behaves like a tiny solenoid — cutting a solenoid just gives two shorter solenoids.

steps.title: Field lines of a bar magnet
steps.body:
- Field lines form **continuous closed loops**: outside from N to S, inside from S to N.
- Tangent at a point gives the direction of B; density gives strength.
- Lines never intersect.
- Isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) have never been found: breaking a magnet always gives two dipoles.

steps.title: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
steps.body:
A finite solenoid's field far away matches a bar magnet's: on its axis B = (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³) with m = NIA. Iron filings show identical patterns. So a bar magnet can be pictured as a solenoid of circulating atomic currents.

**Magnetic dipole fields (far away, r ≫ size):**
- Axial: **B = (μ₀/4π) × 2m/r³**
- Equatorial: **B = (μ₀/4π) × m/r³**, opposite to m
Magnetic moment m points from S to N; unit A m² (or J/T).

steps.title: Dipole in a uniform field
steps.body:
- Torque **τ = m × B**, magnitude mB sin θ.
- Potential energy **U = −m·B = −mB cos θ**: minimum (−mB) when aligned (stable), maximum (+mB) when anti-aligned (unstable).
- A freely suspended magnet (moment of inertia I) given a small twist oscillates with **T = 2π√(I/(mB))** — this is how a compass needle settles.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A short bar magnet has m = 0.4 A m². Field on its axis at 20 cm:
- B = 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 0.4/(0.2)³ = 10⁻⁷ × 0.8/0.008 = **1×10⁻⁵ T**.
- On the equatorial line at 20 cm: **5×10⁻⁶ T**.

**Ex 2.** A magnet of m = 0.32 J/T is at 60° to B = 0.15 T.
- τ = mB sin 60° = 0.32 × 0.15 × 0.866 ≈ **4.2×10⁻² N m**.
- U = −mB cos 60° = **−0.024 J**.
- Work to turn it to anti-aligned from aligned: 2mB = **0.096 J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing field lines inside the magnet from N to S (inside they go S to N).
- Expecting broken pieces to be monopoles.
- Using electric-dipole intuition for U sign: U = −mB cos θ, minimum when aligned.

activity.prompt: A bar magnet of moment 2 A m² is placed at 90° to a uniform field of 0.05 T. Find the torque on it (N m).

quiz.q: Outside a bar magnet, field lines go
quiz.why: Outside a bar magnet field lines go from the north pole to the south pole, and inside they go from S to N.

quiz.q: Magnetic field lines are
quiz.why: Magnetic field lines form closed loops because there are no isolated magnetic poles.

quiz.q: Unit of magnetic moment can be written as
quiz.why: U = −mB, so m has the unit of energy per field: J/T (same as A m²).

quiz.q: A magnet is in stable equilibrium when its moment is
quiz.why: A magnet is in stable equilibrium when its moment is parallel to B, where its potential energy is minimum.

quiz.q: Far away, the axial field of a bar magnet varies as
quiz.why: Far from a bar magnet, on its axis, B ∝ 1/r³ like any dipole.

lessons.title: Gauss's law for magnetism

scenes.text: Physicists have built detectors deep underground just to catch a single magnetic monopole.
None has ever been confirmed.
That experimental fact is written as a law: the total magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero.

steps.title: The law
steps.body:
**∮ B·dS = 0** for every closed surface.

As many field lines leave any closed surface as enter it, because magnetic field lines are closed loops and there are no isolated poles. Compare Gauss's law for electricity, ∮E·dS = q/ε₀, where charges act as sources.

steps.title: Electric vs magnetic dipole
steps.body:
| Feature | Electric dipole | Magnetic dipole |
- Moment: p = q(2a) | m = NIA
- Axial field: (1/4πε₀)(2p/r³) | (μ₀/4π)(2m/r³)
- Torque: p × E | m × B
- Energy: −p·E | −m·B
- Sources: + and − charges exist separately | poles never exist separately
The correspondence is p ↔ m, 1/ε₀ ↔ μ₀.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A closed cube sits in a non-uniform magnetic field. Net flux through it = **0** (always).

**Ex 2.** 5×10⁻⁵ Wb of flux enters a closed surface through its left face. Total flux leaving through all other faces = **5×10⁻⁵ Wb**, so that the net is zero.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the flux through an *open* surface (like a coil) must be zero — the law is for *closed* surfaces only.
- Equating zero net flux with zero field.

activity.prompt: Match the electric quantity to its magnetic analogue.

quiz.q: Gauss's law for magnetism says the net magnetic flux through a closed surface is
quiz.why: Gauss's law for magnetism says the net flux through any closed surface is zero, because magnetic poles do not exist singly.

quiz.q: The law implies that
options: magnetic field lines are closed loops
flux through a coil is zero
quiz.why: Since the net flux through any closed surface is zero, every field line that enters also leaves, so field lines form closed loops.

quiz.why: In the dipole field formulas, μ₀/4π takes the place of 1/4πε₀, so μ₀ is the analogue of 1/ε₀.

lessons.title: Magnetisation, H, susceptibility and permeability

scenes.text: Om winds wire round a nail and picks up 3 paper clips; on a plastic pen, the same coil picks up none.
The iron nail adds its own magnetism to the coil's field — it becomes magnetised.
We describe that extra contribution with magnetisation M and the material's susceptibility.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Magnetisation M** = net magnetic moment per unit volume (A/m).
- **Magnetic intensity H**: the part of the field due to free (conduction) currents. For a solenoid H = nI (A/m).
- Total field: **B = μ₀(H + M)**.
- For linear materials **M = χH**, where χ (magnetic susceptibility) is dimensionless.
- So **B = μ₀(1 + χ)H = μ₀μᵣH = μH**, with relative permeability **μᵣ = 1 + χ** and permeability μ = μ₀μᵣ.

steps.title: Signs and sizes of χ
steps.body:
- Diamagnetic: χ small and **negative** (about −10⁻⁵), μᵣ slightly < 1.
- Paramagnetic: χ small and **positive** (10⁻⁵–10⁻³), μᵣ slightly > 1.
- Ferromagnetic: χ **very large and positive** (10²–10⁵), μᵣ ≫ 1, and not constant (depends on H and history).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A solenoid with n = 1000 turns/m and I = 2 A has an iron core with μᵣ = 400.
- H = nI = **2000 A/m**.
- B = μ₀μᵣH = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 400 × 2000 ≈ **1.0 T**.
- χ = μᵣ − 1 = 399; M = χH ≈ **8.0×10⁵ A/m**.

**Ex 2.** A material has χ = −2×10⁻⁵. μᵣ = 1 − 0.00002 = **0.99998** — diamagnetic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing H (A/m) with B (T).
- Forgetting B = μ₀(H + M), not μ₀H + M.
- Treating χ of iron as a fixed number — for ferromagnets it varies.

activity.text: B = μ₀(H + ___). Relative permeability μᵣ = 1 + ___. For a diamagnetic material χ is ___.

lessons.title: Dia-, para- and ferromagnetism

scenes.text: Ritika sees a famous photo of a live frog levitating inside a very strong magnet.
Water — and therefore the frog — is diamagnetic, weakly pushed out of strong fields.
Most matter is magnetic in one of three ways; strong magnets just make the weakest kind visible.

steps.title: Diamagnetism
steps.body:
Atoms have no net permanent moment. An applied field induces tiny currents that oppose it (Lenz-like behaviour), so the material is **repelled** and moves from strong to weak field.
- Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water, NaCl, nitrogen (at STP).
- **Superconductors** are perfect diamagnets (χ = −1): they expel fields completely (**Meissner effect**) — used in maglev trains.

steps.title: Paramagnetism
steps.body:
Atoms have permanent moments that point randomly. A field partly aligns them, so the material is **weakly attracted** (moves from weak to strong field).
- Examples: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen (at STP), copper chloride.
- **Curie's law:** M = C(B₀/T), i.e. **χ = Cμ₀/T** — susceptibility falls as temperature rises, because thermal agitation fights alignment.

steps.title: Ferromagnetism
steps.body:
Strong interactions line up atomic moments in small regions called **domains** (about 1 mm across, each containing ~10¹¹ atoms). An applied field makes favourable domains grow and others rotate, giving huge M; the material is **strongly attracted**.
- Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, alnico.
- **Hard ferromagnets** (alnico) keep magnetisation → permanent magnets. **Soft** ferromagnets (soft iron) lose it → electromagnet and transformer cores.
- Above the **Curie temperature** T_c a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic; then χ ∝ 1/(T − T_c). T_c for iron is about 1043 K.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A paramagnetic salt has χ = 2.8×10⁻⁴ at 300 K. At 200 K (Curie's law):
- χ₂ = χ₁ × T₁/T₂ = 2.8×10⁻⁴ × 300/200 = **4.2×10⁻⁴**.

**Ex 2.** A paramagnetic sample shows M = 8 A/m at 4 K in a field B₁. At 16 K in a field 2B₁:
- M ∝ B/T ⇒ M₂ = 8 × (2) × (4/16) = **4 A/m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying diamagnetism only occurs in some materials — it is present in *all*, but masked by para/ferro effects.
- Applying Curie's law to ferromagnets below T_c.
- Mixing up hard (permanent magnet) and soft (core) magnetic materials.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Electromagnetic Induction
courses.summary: Faraday's and Henry's experiments, magnetic flux, Faraday's law, Lenz's law and energy conservation, motional emf, self- and mutual inductance with energy stored, and the AC generator — derivations and graded numericals. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can calculate magnetic flux and induced emf with Faraday's law.
Learners can use Lenz's law to find the direction of induced current and link it to energy conservation.

lessons.title: Faraday's law and magnetic flux

scenes.text: Pranav's grandfather still has a bicycle with a little dynamo pressed against the tyre.
Pedal faster and the headlamp glows brighter; stop and it goes dark.
A magnet spinning near a coil changes the magnetic flux through it — and a changing flux makes an emf. That is Faraday's discovery.

steps.title: The experiments
steps.body:
Faraday and Henry (1830s) found:
- Moving a magnet towards or away from a coil makes a galvanometer deflect; faster motion, bigger deflection; no motion, no deflection.
- Moving the coil instead of the magnet gives the same effect — only *relative* motion matters.
- Switching a current ON or OFF in one coil induces a momentary current in a nearby coil (no motion at all).
Common factor: **change in magnetic flux**.

steps.title: Magnetic flux
steps.body: **Φ_B = B·A = BA cos θ** (θ between B and the normal to the area). For non-uniform fields Φ = ∫B·dA. Unit **weber (Wb)** = T m². Flux can change by changing B, A or θ.

steps.title: Faraday's law
steps.body:
**ε = −N dΦ_B/dt**

The induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage (NΦ). The minus sign is Lenz's law. Induced current I = ε/R and induced charge **Δq = NΔΦ/R** — independent of how fast the change happens.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A 100-turn coil's flux per turn falls from 5×10⁻³ Wb to 1×10⁻³ Wb in 0.1 s.
- |ε| = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 4×10⁻³/0.1 = **4 V**.

**Ex 2.** A 10 cm × 10 cm loop (R = 0.5 Ω) is perpendicular to B, which falls at 0.5 T/s.
- ε = A dB/dt = 0.01 × 0.5 = **5×10⁻³ V**.
- I = 5×10⁻³/0.5 = **10 mA**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using B instead of change of flux: a strong *steady* field induces nothing.
- Forgetting cos θ when the coil is tilted.
- Forgetting N for multi-turn coils.

activity.prompt: A 50-turn coil of area 0.02 m² is perpendicular to a field that rises uniformly from 0.1 T to 0.5 T in 0.2 s. Find the induced emf (V).
