lessons.title: Line spectra and de Broglie's explanation

story.title: Standing waves on a sitar string

scenes.text: When Ustad-ji plucks a sitar string, only certain notes ring — those that fit a whole number of half-waves.
De Broglie suggested an electron's wave must wrap around its orbit and join itself smoothly.
Only whole numbers of wavelengths fit — which is exactly Bohr's mysterious rule.

steps.title: de Broglie's explanation of quantisation
steps.body:
For a stable orbit the electron wave must form a **standing wave**: circumference = whole number of wavelengths:
**2πr_n = nλ** and λ = h/(mv) ⇒ **mvr_n = nh/(2π)** — Bohr's second postulate follows naturally.

steps.title: Number of spectral lines
steps.body: An electron in level n can return to the ground state through various jumps. Maximum number of lines emitted = **n(n − 1)/2**. From n = 4: 6 lines.

steps.title: Limitations of Bohr's model
steps.body:
- Works only for hydrogen-like (one-electron) atoms; fails for helium and heavier atoms.
- Cannot explain relative intensities of lines or the fine structure.
- Mixes classical orbits with quantum rules; replaced by quantum mechanics where electrons are described by probability clouds.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Hydrogen atoms are excited to n = 5. Maximum lines = 5 × 4/2 = **10**.

**Ex 2.** In which orbit is the electron's de Broglie wavelength equal to 4 × 0.33 nm (λ₁ ≈ 0.33 nm, n = 1)? Since λ ∝ n (λ = 2πr/n with r ∝ n²): **n = 4**.

**Ex 3.** Does a 12.1 eV photon get absorbed by ground-state hydrogen? E₃ − E₁ = 13.6 − 1.51 = **12.09 eV** ⇒ yes, to n = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the direct jump to ground state when asked for 'possible lines'.
- Assuming any photon above 10.2 eV is absorbed — only exact level differences (or > 13.6 eV for ionisation).

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the wavelength of a hydrogen spectral line.
items: Identify the initial and final levels nᵢ and n_f

quiz.q: de Broglie's condition for a stable orbit is
quiz.why: For a stable orbit the circumference must hold a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths: 2πr = nλ.

quiz.q: Maximum number of lines from n = 4 is
quiz.why: From n = 4 the possible transitions are n(n − 1)/2 = 4 × 3/2 = 6 lines.

quiz.q: Bohr's model fails for
quiz.why: Bohr's model works only for one-electron systems, and fails for multi-electron atoms such as neutral helium.

quiz.q: Photon energy needed to excite H from n = 1 to n = 2 is
De Broglie wavelength of the electron in the nth Bohr orbit is proportional to
quiz.why: λ = h/mv = 2πr/n. In the nth orbit the circumference is n wavelengths, so λ = 2πrₙ/n, and rₙ ∝ n², giving λ ∝ n.

courses.summary: Atomic masses and nuclear composition, isotopes, isobars and isotones, nuclear size and density, mass–energy equivalence, mass defect and binding energy, the binding-energy curve, nuclear force, and nuclear energy from fission and fusion — plus radioactive decay as a JEE/NEET extension. outcomes: Learners can describe nuclear composition and use R = R₀A^(1/3).

lessons.title: Composition and size of the nucleus

scenes.text: Scientists measure atomic masses with mass spectrometers to six or more decimal places.
Chlorine shows two peaks: masses near 35 and 37 — same element, different nuclei.
Nuclei are built from protons and neutrons, and their sizes follow a beautifully simple rule.

steps.title: Atomic mass unit and composition
steps.body:
**1 u** = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = **1.660539×10⁻²⁷ kg**.
- Proton m_p = 1.007276 u; neutron m_n = 1.008665 u (Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932).
- Nucleus ᴬ_Z X: **Z** protons (atomic number), **N = A − Z** neutrons, **A** nucleons (mass number).
- **Isotopes:** same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl).
- **Isobars:** same A, different Z (³H and ³He).
- **Isotones:** same N (¹⁹⁸Hg and ¹⁹⁷Au both have N = 118).

steps.title: Nuclear size and density
steps.body: Scattering experiments show **R = R₀A^(1/3)**, R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m). So volume ∝ A and **nuclear density is the same for all nuclei**: ρ ≈ m_u/((4/3)πR₀³) ≈ **2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³** — about 10¹⁴ times the density of water (similar to neutron stars).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Radius of ²⁷Al: R = 1.2 × 27^(1/3) = 1.2 × 3 = **3.6 fm**.

**Ex 2.** Ratio of radii of ²¹⁶X and ²⁷Al: (216/27)^(1/3) = 8^(1/3) = **2**.

**Ex 3.** Neutrons in ²³⁵₉₂U: N = 235 − 92 = **143**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking heavier nuclei are denser — density is roughly constant.
- Writing R ∝ A instead of A^(1/3).
- Confusing isobars (same A) and isotones (same N).

activity.prompt: Classify each pair.

quiz.q: 1 u is defined as
quiz.why: One atomic mass unit is defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

quiz.q: Nuclear radius varies as
quiz.why: Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), proportional to the cube root of the mass number.

quiz.q: Nuclear density
quiz.why: Volume ∝ A and mass ∝ A, so the density is nearly the same for all nuclei.

quiz.q: Number of neutrons in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe is
quiz.why: Number of neutrons = A − Z = 56 − 26 = 30.

quiz.q: ³H and ³He are
quiz.why: ³H and ³He have the same mass number (3) but different atomic numbers, so they are isobars.

lessons.title: Mass–energy, mass defect and binding energy

scenes.text: Kabir adds the masses of 2 protons and 2 neutrons and compares with a helium-4 nucleus.
The nucleus is lighter by about 0.03 u!
That missing mass became binding energy, via Einstein's E = mc².

steps.title: Mass–energy equivalence
steps.body: **E = mc²**; 1 u × c² = **931.5 MeV**. Mass and energy are interconvertible; in nuclear reactions total (mass + energy) is conserved.

steps.title: Mass defect and binding energy
steps.body:
**ΔM = [Z m_p + (A − Z) m_n] − M_nucleus** (using atomic masses: Z m_H + N m_n − M_atom, the electron masses cancel).

**Binding energy E_b = ΔM c²** — energy needed to split the nucleus into free nucleons (or released when it forms).

**Binding energy per nucleon E_bn = E_b/A** measures stability.

steps.title: The binding-energy curve
steps.body:
Plot E_bn against A:
- Rises steeply for light nuclei, has a broad maximum ≈ **8.75 MeV at A ≈ 56 (Fe)**, and is nearly constant (~8 MeV) for 30 < A < 170 — showing nuclear forces are **short-range and saturate** (each nucleon binds only its neighbours).
- Falls to ~7.6 MeV for A ≈ 238.
- Heavy nuclei splitting into medium ones (**fission**) and light nuclei joining (**fusion**) both move towards higher E_bn and therefore **release energy**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing atomic and nuclear masses (use m_H with atomic mass, or m_p with nuclear mass).
- Thinking higher total binding energy means more stable — compare binding energy *per nucleon*.
- Forgetting the 931.5 factor or using 931 inconsistently.

activity.prompt: A nucleus has a mass defect of 0.0989 u and A = 12. Find binding energy per nucleon in MeV (1 u = 931.5 MeV).

quiz.q: 1 u is equivalent to
quiz.why: 1 u × c² is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy.

quiz.q: Binding energy per nucleon is maximum near
quiz.why: The binding energy per nucleon peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56 (the iron region), the most stable nuclei.

quiz.q: Mass of a nucleus is
quiz.why: The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons. The difference is the mass defect.

quiz.q: Constant E_bn over a wide range of A shows that nuclear force
quiz.why: A nearly constant binding energy per nucleon shows that the nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates, so each nucleon interacts only with near neighbours.

quiz.q: Energy is released in fission because
quiz.why: In fission, heavy nuclei split into medium ones with higher binding energy per nucleon. The extra binding energy is released.

lessons.title: Nuclear force and nuclear energy

scenes.text: The Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium deep in its core at about 1.5×10⁷ K.
India's nuclear power plants, like those at Tarapur and Kudankulam, split uranium nuclei instead.
Opposite processes, same reason: both move nuclei towards the peak of the binding-energy curve.

steps.title: Nuclear force
steps.body:
- **Strongest** of the fundamental forces in its range (much stronger than Coulomb repulsion between protons).
- **Short range** (a few fm); attractive above ~0.8 fm, strongly repulsive below.
- **Charge-independent:** p–p, n–n and p–n forces are about equal.
- Saturating, non-central in general.

steps.title: Fission
steps.body:
A slow neutron is absorbed by ²³⁵U, forming unstable ²³⁶U which splits, e.g.
¹n + ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3 ¹n (other fragment pairs also occur)
Energy released ≈ **200 MeV per fission**. Extra neutrons can sustain a **chain reaction**. In reactors: **moderator** (heavy water, graphite) slows neutrons; **control rods** (cadmium, boron) absorb neutrons to keep the multiplication factor K = 1; coolant carries heat to turbines.

steps.title: Fusion
steps.body:
Light nuclei combine at very high temperatures (thermonuclear fusion) so they can overcome Coulomb repulsion:
¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν + 0.42 MeV, and ultimately 4 ¹H → ⁴He + … releasing about 26.7 MeV in the proton–proton cycle. Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission; controlled fusion on Earth is still under development (e.g. the international ITER project, in which India participates).

steps.title: Q-value
steps.body: **Q = (Σ masses of reactants − Σ masses of products) × 931.5 MeV/u**. Q > 0: energy released (exoergic).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Energy from fissioning 1 g of ²³⁵U at 200 MeV each:
- N = 6.02×10²³/235 ≈ 2.56×10²¹ nuclei
- E = 2.56×10²¹ × 200 MeV = 5.1×10²³ MeV ≈ **8.2×10¹⁰ J** (about 23 MWh).

**Ex 2.** D–T fusion ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n with masses 2.014102, 3.016049, 4.002603 and 1.008665 u.
- Δm = 5.030151 − 5.011268 = 0.018883 u ⇒ **Q ≈ 17.6 MeV**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking control rods slow neutrons — moderators slow; control rods absorb.
- Saying fusion needs high temperature for chemical reasons — it is to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
- Getting the sign of Q wrong (reactants minus products).

activity.prompt: Match reactor parts to their roles.

quiz.q: Energy released per fission of ²³⁵U is about
quiz.why: The correct answer is “200 MeV”. Reasoning: Mostly as fragment kinetic energy. A choice like “2 MeV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Nuclear force is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “short range and strong”. Reasoning: A few fm. A choice like “gravitational” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Control rods are made of
quiz.why: The correct answer is “cadmium or boron”. Reasoning: Good neutron absorbers. A choice like “graphite” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: The Sun's energy comes from
quiz.why: The correct answer is “fusion”. Reasoning: Hydrogen to helium. A choice like “radioactive decay only” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “energy released”. Reasoning: Products are lighter. A choice like “mass increases” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Radioactivity (JEE/NEET extension)

scenes.text: Archaeologists date ancient bones from a site using carbon-14.
Half the ¹⁴C in a sample decays every 5730 years, like clockwork.
The decay law lets them read the clock — the same law medical physicists use for radioactive tracers.

steps.title: Types of decay
steps.body:
- **α-decay:** ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−2) Y + ⁴₂He.
- **β⁻-decay:** n → p + e⁻ + ν̄: Z increases by 1, A unchanged.
- **β⁺-decay:** p → n + e⁺ + ν: Z decreases by 1.
- **γ-decay:** an excited nucleus emits a photon; Z and A unchanged.
Penetrating power: γ > β > α; ionising power: α > β > γ.

steps.title: Decay law
steps.body:
Rate ∝ number present: dN/dt = −λN ⇒ **N = N₀e^(−λt)**.
- **Half-life T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ**; after n half-lives N = N₀/2ⁿ.
- **Mean life τ = 1/λ = 1.44 T½**.
- **Activity R = λN** (becquerel, 1 Bq = 1 decay/s; 1 Ci = 3.7×10¹⁰ Bq).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A sample's half-life is 10 days. Fraction left after 30 days = (1/2)³ = **1/8**.

**Ex 2.** ²³⁸U → ²⁰⁶Pb: number of α and β decays?
- ΔA = 32 ⇒ **8 α**; Z falls by 16 from α, but net fall is 92 − 82 = 10 ⇒ **6 β⁻**.

**Ex 3.** λ = 0.0231 per day ⇒ T½ = 0.693/0.0231 = **30 days**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking that after two half-lives everything has decayed (1/4 remains).
- Forgetting that β⁻ decay leaves A unchanged.
- Mixing mean life and half-life.

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Recent rationalised NCERT editions trimmed radioactivity from this chapter, but it remains important for competitive exams; check your current syllabus.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “1.44 T½”. Reasoning: τ = T½/ln 2. A choice like “0.693 T½” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
courses.summary: Classification of metals, semiconductors and insulators by conductivity and energy bands, intrinsic and extrinsic (n- and p-type) semiconductors, formation of the p-n junction, the diode under forward and reverse bias, and the diode as a half-wave and full-wave rectifier — plus special diodes and logic gates as a JEE extension. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.
outcomes: Learners can classify solids using energy bands and band gap.
Learners can explain doping and use nₑnₕ = nᵢ².
Learners can describe depletion layer, barrier potential and diode V–I characteristics.
Learners can explain half-wave and full-wave rectification and filtering.

lessons.title: Energy bands and intrinsic semiconductors

scenes.text: Zara's phone contains billions of transistors made from silicon.
Silicon comes from ordinary sand, yet with a little help it can be made to conduct exactly as engineers want.
The secret is the energy band gap — just right, not too wide, not too narrow.

steps.title: Classification by conductivity
steps.body:
- **Metals:** ρ ≈ 10⁻²–10⁻⁸ Ω m.
- **Semiconductors:** ρ ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁶ Ω m (Si, Ge; compounds like GaAs, CdS; organic semiconductors).
- **Insulators:** ρ ≈ 10¹¹–10¹⁹ Ω m.

steps.title: Energy bands
steps.body:
In a crystal, atomic energy levels spread into bands. The **valence band** (filled at 0 K) and the **conduction band** are separated by the **band gap E_g**.
- **Metals:** bands overlap or conduction band partly filled — E_g ≈ 0.
- **Insulators:** E_g > 3 eV (diamond ≈ 5.4 eV) — electrons cannot jump at room temperature.
- **Semiconductors:** E_g small — Si ≈ **1.1 eV**, Ge ≈ **0.7 eV**; some electrons are thermally excited at room temperature.

steps.title: Intrinsic semiconductors
steps.body: Pure Si or Ge: each atom shares four covalent bonds. Thermal energy breaks a few bonds, creating a **free electron** and a **hole** (vacancy with effective +e charge). In pure material **nₑ = nₕ = nᵢ**. Current I = Iₑ + Iₕ (holes move as neighbouring electrons fill them). At 0 K an intrinsic semiconductor is an insulator; conductivity rises with temperature.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Can red light (700 nm) create electron–hole pairs in Si (E_g = 1.1 eV)? E = 1240/700 ≈ 1.77 eV > 1.1 eV ⇒ **yes**.

**Ex 2.** Longest wavelength that can excite carriers in Si: λ = 1240/1.1 ≈ **1127 nm** (near infrared).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking holes are positrons — a hole is an absence of an electron.
- Saying semiconductors conduct better when cold — resistance falls when they are heated.
- Confusing band gap of Si (1.1 eV) and Ge (0.7 eV).

activity.prompt: Classify by band gap.

quiz.q: Band gap of silicon is about
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1.1 eV”. Reasoning: Si ≈ 1.1 eV. A choice like “0 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: In an intrinsic semiconductor
quiz.why: The correct answer is “nₑ = nₕ”. Reasoning: Pairs are created together. A choice like “nₑ = 0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: At 0 K a pure semiconductor behaves as
quiz.why: The correct answer is “an insulator”. Reasoning: No thermally excited carriers. A choice like “a superconductor” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A hole behaves like
quiz.why: The correct answer is “a positive charge”. Reasoning: Missing electron. A choice like “a photon” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Resistance of a semiconductor on heating
quiz.why: The correct answer is “decreases”. Reasoning: More carriers. A choice like “becomes infinite” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Extrinsic semiconductors: n-type and p-type

story.title: A pinch of salt in the soup

scenes.text: A cook adds just a pinch of salt to a huge pot and the taste changes completely.
Adding one impurity atom per million silicon atoms raises conductivity enormously.
This controlled impurity — doping — makes n-type and p-type materials.

steps.title: n-type (pentavalent dopant)
steps.body:
Dopants: **P, As, Sb** (group 15). Four electrons bond, the fifth is loosely held (~0.01–0.05 eV) and freed easily ⇒ **donor**.
- **Majority carriers: electrons**; minority: holes.
- The material stays electrically **neutral** (the donor ion is positive and fixed).

steps.title: p-type (trivalent dopant)
steps.body:
Dopants: **B, Al, In, Ga** (group 13). One bond is incomplete ⇒ a hole ⇒ **acceptor**.
- **Majority carriers: holes**; minority: electrons.
- Also electrically neutral overall.

steps.title: Mass-action law
steps.body: In thermal equilibrium: **nₑ nₕ = nᵢ²**. Doping raises one carrier density and lowers the other. Donor and acceptor levels lie just below the conduction band and just above the valence band respectively.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Si with nᵢ = 1.5×10¹⁶ m⁻³ is doped with arsenic at 5×10²² m⁻³.
- nₑ ≈ **5×10²² m⁻³** (each As gives one electron)
- nₕ = nᵢ²/nₑ = 2.25×10³²/5×10²² = **4.5×10⁹ m⁻³**.
- It is **n-type**.

**Ex 2.** Ge doped with indium becomes **p-type** (In is trivalent).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying n-type is negatively charged — it is neutral.
- Mixing up donor (pentavalent) and acceptor (trivalent) elements.
- Adding nᵢ to the donor density (it is negligible).

activity.prompt: Which type results from each dopant in silicon?

quiz.q: Majority carriers in p-type silicon are
quiz.why: The correct answer is “holes”. Reasoning: Acceptor doping. A choice like “protons” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Which dopant makes n-type silicon?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “As”. Reasoning: Pentavalent. A choice like “B” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: An n-type semiconductor is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “electrically neutral”. Reasoning: Every free electron leaves a fixed + ion. A choice like “magnetic” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: The mass-action law is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “nₑnₕ = nᵢ²”. Reasoning: Equilibrium relation. A choice like “nₑ = nₕ²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: If nₑ = 10²² m⁻³ and nᵢ = 10¹⁶ m⁻³, nₕ =
quiz.why: The correct answer is “10¹⁰ m⁻³”. Reasoning: 10³²/10²². A choice like “10¹⁶ m⁻³” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: The p-n junction and the diode

scenes.text: Kabir connects an LED backwards in his school project and it refuses to glow.
He flips it and it lights up instantly.
A p-n junction lets current flow easily one way and blocks it the other way.

steps.title: Formation of the junction
steps.body: When p and n regions are joined: electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n (**diffusion current**). They leave behind fixed ions: + on the n side, − on the p side, forming the **depletion region** (≈ 1 μm wide, no free carriers). Its field drives minority carriers back (**drift current**). Equilibrium: diffusion = drift. The resulting **barrier potential** is ≈ 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge.

steps.title: Forward and reverse bias
steps.body:
- **Forward bias** (p to +, n to −): barrier lowered, depletion layer narrows. Current is very small until the **threshold (knee/cut-in) voltage** (≈ 0.7 V Si, 0.2–0.3 V Ge), then rises steeply (exponentially) — milliamperes.
- **Reverse bias** (p to −, n to +): barrier raised, depletion layer widens; only a tiny **reverse saturation current** (μA) of minority carriers, nearly independent of voltage, until **breakdown** at a large reverse voltage.
- Dynamic resistance r_d = ΔV/ΔI (small in forward bias).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** A Si diode (0.7 V drop) in series with 1 kΩ and a 5.7 V battery, forward biased.
- I = (5.7 − 0.7)/1000 = **5 mA**.
- If reversed: I ≈ **0** (only μA leakage).

**Ex 2.** On the forward curve, V rises from 0.70 V to 0.80 V while I rises from 10 mA to 20 mA.
- r_d = 0.1 V/10 mA = **10 Ω**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a diode conducts at any forward voltage — it needs to exceed the knee voltage.
- Calling the depletion region 'empty space' — it contains fixed ions, just no mobile carriers.
- Saying reverse current is zero — it is tiny but non-zero.

statements.s: In forward bias the depletion layer becomes narrower.
Reverse saturation current is due to majority carriers.
statements.why: It is due to minority carriers.

statements.s: The barrier potential of silicon is about 0.7 V.
In equilibrium, diffusion current is greater than drift current.

quiz.q: The depletion region contains
quiz.why: The correct answer is “immobile ions”. Reasoning: No mobile carriers. A choice like “free electrons” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: In reverse bias the depletion layer
quiz.why: The correct answer is “widens”. Reasoning: Barrier increases. A choice like “stays the same” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Knee voltage of a Si diode is about
quiz.why: The correct answer is “0.7 V”. Reasoning: Si threshold. A choice like “1.1 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Forward current in a diode is mainly due to
quiz.why: The correct answer is “majority carriers (diffusion)”. Reasoning: Lowered barrier. A choice like “minority carriers” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A Si diode with 0.7 V drop, 2 kΩ and 10.7 V forward battery carries
quiz.why: The correct answer is “5 mA”. Reasoning: 10/2000. A choice like “10 mA” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: The diode as a rectifier

scenes.text: The wall socket gives AC that reverses 100 times a second, but Riya's phone battery needs steady DC.
Inside the charger, diodes let only one direction through.
A capacitor smooths the bumps — and out comes DC.

steps.title: Half-wave rectifier
steps.body: One diode in series with the load (via a transformer). During the positive half-cycle the diode is forward biased and conducts; during the negative half it blocks. Output: pulsating DC with **one pulse per cycle** — output frequency = input frequency (50 Hz).

steps.title: Full-wave rectifier (centre-tap)
steps.body: Two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer. In each half-cycle one diode conducts, and current through the load is always in the same direction. Output: **two pulses per cycle** — ripple frequency = **2 × input frequency (100 Hz)**. More efficient than half-wave. (A bridge rectifier with four diodes avoids the centre tap.)

steps.title: Filtering
steps.body: A **capacitor in parallel with the load** charges to near the peak voltage and discharges slowly through the load between peaks, smoothing the output. Larger C (and larger load R) ⇒ smaller ripple; time constant RC should be much greater than the time between peaks.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** Input 50 Hz AC. Ripple frequency: half-wave **50 Hz**, full-wave **100 Hz**.

**Ex 2.** A full-wave rectifier gives a peak output of 12 V (ideal diodes). With a large filter capacitor the DC output is close to **12 V**; without it the average of the pulsating output is 2V_m/π ≈ **7.6 V**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying full-wave output frequency equals input frequency.
- Putting the filter capacitor in series with the load.
- Forgetting that each diode in a centre-tap rectifier conducts only for half the cycle.

activity.prompt: Arrange the stages of a simple DC power supply (charger).

quiz.q: Output frequency of a half-wave rectifier on 50 Hz is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “50 Hz”. Reasoning: One pulse per cycle. A choice like “0 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Output frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “100 Hz”. Reasoning: Two pulses per cycle. A choice like “25 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: The filter capacitor is connected
options: in series with the diode only
quiz.why: The correct answer is “in parallel with the load”. Reasoning: It smooths the voltage across the load. A choice like “in series with the load” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: How many diodes does a centre-tap full-wave rectifier use?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2”. Reasoning: One per half. A choice like “1” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A larger filter capacitor gives
quiz.why: The correct answer is “less ripple”. Reasoning: Slower discharge. A choice like “no output” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Special diodes and logic gates (JEE extension)

scenes.text: Modern traffic signals use LEDs that last for years and use little power.
The calculator on Neha's desk runs on a tiny solar cell.
Inside, logic gates add numbers using only 0s and 1s.

steps.title: Special-purpose diodes
steps.body:
- **Zener diode:** heavily doped, used in **reverse breakdown**; voltage across it stays almost constant ⇒ **voltage regulator**.
- **Photodiode:** reverse-biased; light creates e–h pairs and increases reverse current ⇒ light detection.
- **LED:** forward-biased; electrons and holes recombine and emit light; colour depends on band gap (E_g ≈ hc/λ). Low power, long life.
- **Solar cell:** no external bias; light creates e–h pairs and the junction field separates them, giving an emf (~0.5–0.6 V for Si).

steps.title: Logic gates
steps.body:
Digital signals: 0 (low) and 1 (high).
- **NOT:** Y = Ā.
- **OR:** Y = A + B (1 if any input is 1).
- **AND:** Y = A·B (1 only if both are 1).
- **NAND:** NOT of AND; **NOR:** NOT of OR. NAND and NOR are **universal gates** — any gate can be built from them.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Ex 1.** An LED emits 620 nm light. Approximate band gap: 1240/620 = **2.0 eV**.

**Ex 2.** A NAND gate with both inputs tied together acts as a **NOT gate** (Y = (A·A)′ = Ā).

**Ex 3.** For A = 1, B = 0: AND = 0, OR = 1, NAND = 1, NOR = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a Zener in forward bias as a regulator.
- Confusing photodiode (reverse bias) and LED (forward bias).
- Thinking NOR(1, 0) = 1.

steps.title: Note on syllabus
steps.body: Recent rationalised NCERT editions trimmed special diodes, transistors and logic gates from this chapter, but they still appear in some competitive-exam syllabi; check the latest official syllabus.

activity.prompt: Match the device to its operating mode / use.

quiz.q: A Zener diode is used as a
quiz.why: The correct answer is “voltage regulator”. Reasoning: Constant voltage in breakdown. A choice like “oscillator” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A photodiode is operated in
quiz.why: The correct answer is “reverse bias”. Reasoning: Reverse current depends on light. A choice like “no bias” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: The colour of an LED depends on
options: the band gap of the material
quiz.why: The correct answer is “the band gap of the material”. Reasoning: E_g ≈ hc/λ. A choice like “the current” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Output of a NOR gate is 1 only when
quiz.why: The correct answer is “both inputs are 0”. Reasoning: NOT of OR. A choice like “both inputs are 1” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Which are universal gates?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “NAND and NOR”. Reasoning: Any logic can be built from them. A choice like “XOR and AND” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Band gap of germanium is about
questions.why: The correct answer is “0.7 eV”. Reasoning: Ge ≈ 0.7 eV. A choice like “1.1 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Doping Si with boron makes it
questions.why: The correct answer is “p-type”. Reasoning: Trivalent acceptor. A choice like “intrinsic” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: In an n-type semiconductor, minority carriers are
questions.why: The correct answer is “holes”. Reasoning: Electrons are majority. A choice like “electrons” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: An n-type semiconductor is electrically neutral. Reason: Every free electron comes from a donor atom that becomes a fixed positive ion.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: Charges balance. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: In forward bias, the barrier potential
questions.why: The correct answer is “decreases”. Reasoning: Applied voltage opposes it. A choice like “is unchanged” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The width of the depletion layer increases when
questions.why: The correct answer is “reverse bias increases”. Reasoning: Barrier increases. A choice like “doping increases” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Si (nᵢ = 1.5×10¹⁶ m⁻³) is doped so that nₕ = 4.5×10²² m⁻³. Then nₑ is
questions.why: The correct answer is “5×10⁹ m⁻³”. Reasoning: nᵢ²/nₕ = 2.25×10³²/4.5×10²². A choice like “4.5×10²² m⁻³” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A Si diode (0.7 V) and a 500 Ω resistor are in series with a 3.2 V battery (forward). Current:
questions.why: The correct answer is “5 mA”. Reasoning: (3.2 − 0.7)/500. A choice like “6.4 mA” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Same circuit with the diode reversed. Current is
questions.why: The correct answer is “approximately zero”. Reasoning: Reverse bias blocks. A choice like “infinite” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The maximum wavelength absorbed to create e–h pairs in a material with E_g = 2.48 eV:
questions.why: The correct answer is “500 nm”. Reasoning: 1240/2.48. A choice like “620 nm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: The ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier is twice the input frequency. Reason: Both half-cycles are used to produce output pulses.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: Two pulses per cycle. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: On a diode's forward curve, V changes 0.65 → 0.75 V and I changes 2 → 7 mA. Dynamic resistance:
questions.why: The correct answer is “20 Ω”. Reasoning: 0.1/0.005. A choice like “14 Ω” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Which is NOT true for a p-n junction in equilibrium?
options: Mobile carriers fill the depletion region
Fixed ions sit on both sides
questions.why: The correct answer is “Mobile carriers fill the depletion region”. Reasoning: The depletion region has no mobile carriers. A choice like “Diffusion and drift currents balance” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: Two identical Si diodes D₁ (forward) and D₂ (reverse) are in parallel branches each with 1 kΩ across a 5.7 V source. Total current is about
questions.why: The correct answer is “5 mA”. Reasoning: Only D₁'s branch conducts: (5.7 − 0.7)/1000. A choice like “0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: (Extension) For a NAND gate with inputs A = 1 and B = 1, output is
questions.why: The correct answer is “0”. Reasoning: AND = 1 ⇒ NAND = 0. A choice like “A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: (Extension) A Zener diode of 6 V is used with series R = 100 Ω on a 10 V supply, no load. Current through the Zener is
questions.why: The correct answer is “40 mA”. Reasoning: (10 − 6)/100. A choice like “100 mA” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Resistivity of a semiconductor at room temperature lies around
questions.why: The correct answer is “10⁻⁵–10⁶ Ω m”. Reasoning: Between metals and insulators. A choice like “10¹⁵ Ω m” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 12 Physics
courses.summary: Complete formula sheets for all 14 chapters, exam strategy for boards and JEE/NEET, two mock papers with fully explained answers, and a 25-question final mock test with difficulty spread 1–5. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by any board or exam body.

lessons.title: Formula sheet I: Electrostatics and current electricity

scenes.text: It is the night before the board exam and Rahul has no time to reread 3 chapters.
He opens one sheet with every formula, its unit and when to use it.
Twenty minutes later he is confident — he knows which tool fits which problem.

steps.title: Ch 1 · Charges and fields
steps.body:
- F = kq₁q₂/r², k = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻²; medium: ÷K
- E = kq/r²; dipole p = q(2a); E_axial = 2kp/r³; E_eq = kp/r³
- τ = pE sin θ; flux Φ = EA cos θ; Gauss: Φ = q_enc/ε₀
- Line λ: E = λ/2πε₀r; sheet: σ/2ε₀; between plates σ/ε₀; shell: kq/r² outside, 0 inside

steps.title: Ch 2 · Potential and capacitance
steps.body:
- V = kq/r; dipole V = kp cos θ/r²; E = −dV/dr
- U = kq₁q₂/r; dipole U = −pE cos θ
- C = Q/V; parallel plate C = ε₀A/d; dielectric KC₀; slab ε₀A/(d − t + t/K)
- Series 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ; parallel C = ΣCᵢ
- U = ½CV² = Q²/2C; u = ½ε₀E²; loss on sharing C₁C₂(V₁ − V₂)²/2(C₁ + C₂)

steps.title: Ch 3 · Current electricity
steps.body:
- I = neAv_d; v_d = eEτ/m; ρ = m/ne²τ; μ = v_d/E
- R = ρl/A; stretched n times ⇒ n²R; R_T = R₀(1 + αΔT)
- P = VI = I²R = V²/R; 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J
- V = ε − Ir; series cells nε, nr; parallel ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂)
- Kirchhoff: ΣI = 0, ΣΔV = 0; bridge P/Q = R/S

steps.title: How to use the sheet
steps.body: Before solving, write the *given* quantities with units, choose the formula that links them, and convert to SI first. Most lost marks come from μ, m and c prefixes.

cards.front: Energy lost when capacitors share charge

quiz.q: Field outside a charged spherical shell at distance r is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “kq/r²”. Reasoning: As if at the centre. A choice like “zero” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor with K = 4 filling it is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4C₀”. Reasoning: KC₀. A choice like “C₀” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Resistance of a wire stretched to twice its length becomes
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4R”. Reasoning: n²R. A choice like “R” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is based on conservation of
quiz.why: The correct answer is “energy”. A choice like “charge” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.

quiz.q: Unit of electric dipole moment is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “C m”. Reasoning: q × distance. A choice like “N/C” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Energy stored in a capacitor is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “½CV²”. Reasoning: Standard. A choice like “½QV²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Formula sheet II: Magnetism, EMI, AC and EM waves

scenes.text: Isha notices that magnetism formulas look like electrostatics with p → m and 1/ε₀ → μ₀.
Remembering one family lets her rebuild the other.
Pattern-spotting halves the memorising load.

steps.title: Ch 4–5 · Magnetism
steps.body:
- F = q(v × B); r = mv/qB; T = 2πm/qB; pitch = 2πmv cos θ/qB; v = E/B (selector)
- Loop centre μ₀NI/2R; axis μ₀IR²/2(R² + x²)^(3/2); wire μ₀I/2πr; solenoid μ₀nI
- Parallel wires f = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd; τ = NIAB sin θ; m = NIA
- Ammeter shunt S = I_gG/(I − I_g); voltmeter R = V/I_g − G
- Bar magnet: B_axial = μ₀2m/4πr³; τ = mB sin θ; U = −mB cos θ; T = 2π√(I/mB)
- B = μ₀(H + M); χ = M/H; μᵣ = 1 + χ; Curie χ ∝ 1/T

steps.title: Ch 6–7 · EMI and AC
steps.body:
- Φ = BA cos θ; ε = −N dΦ/dt; Δq = NΔΦ/R; ε = Blv; rotating rod ½Bωl²
- L = μ₀n²Al; M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l; U = ½LI²; u = B²/2μ₀; generator ε₀ = NBAω
- I_rms = i_m/√2; X_L = ωL; X_C = 1/ωC; Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²); tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R
- ω₀ = 1/√(LC); Q = ω₀L/R; P = VI cos φ; cos φ = R/Z
- Transformer Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = Iₚ/Iₛ

steps.title: Ch 8 · EM waves
steps.body:
- i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt; c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀); E₀ = cB₀; p = U/c
- Spectrum (long → short λ): radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X, γ

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- Angle in τ = NIAB sin θ is with the *normal*.
- AC heating uses rms values.
- At resonance Z = R, not zero.

activity.prompt: Match the electric formula with its magnetic twin.

quiz.q: Radius of a charged particle's circular path is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “mv/qB”. Reasoning: Balance qvB = mv²/r. A choice like “v/qB” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Self-inductance of a solenoid depends on n as
quiz.why: The correct answer is “n²”. Reasoning: μ₀n²Al. A choice like “1/n” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Power factor at resonance is
quiz.why: At resonance X_L = X_C, so Z = R and φ = 0. Power factor = cos 0 = 1.

quiz.q: Peak emf of a generator is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “NBAω”. Reasoning: Standard. A choice like “NBA/ω” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: E₀/B₀ for an EM wave equals
quiz.why: The correct answer is “c”. Reasoning: E₀ = cB₀. A choice like “c²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Paramagnetic susceptibility varies with temperature as
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1/T”. Reasoning: Curie's law. A choice like “T²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Formula sheet III: Optics and modern physics

scenes.text: With a week left, Fatima splits her revision: two days optics, two days modern physics, three days of mock papers.
She times every paper and marks errors in red.
By the last mock her score has jumped — practice under time pressure works.

steps.title: Ch 9 · Ray optics
steps.body:
- Mirror 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, m = −v/u, f = R/2
- Snell n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r; apparent depth = real/n; sin i_c = 1/n
- Surface n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R; lens maker 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
- Lens 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u; P = 1/f (m); P = P₁ + P₂
- Prism δ = i + e − A; n = sin((A + D_m)/2)/sin(A/2); thin δ = (n − 1)A
- Simple microscope 1 + D/f; compound (L/f_o)(D/f_e); telescope f_o/f_e, length f_o + f_e

steps.title: Ch 10 · Wave optics
steps.body:
- I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2); I_max/I_min = ((√I₁ + √I₂)/(√I₁ − √I₂))²
- YDSE Δ = xd/D; β = λD/d; in medium β/n
- Single slit minima a sin θ = nλ; central width 2λD/a; Fresnel distance a²/λ
- Malus I = I₀ cos² θ; unpolarised → I₀/2; Brewster tan i_B = n

steps.title: Ch 11–14 · Modern physics and electronics
steps.body:
- E = hν = 1240/λ(nm) eV; K_max = hν − φ₀ = eV₀; p = h/λ
- de Broglie λ = h/mv = h/√(2mK); electron 1.227/√V nm
- Closest approach d = 2kZe²/K; Bohr r = 0.529n²/Z Å; E = −13.6Z²/n² eV; v ∝ Z/n
- 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²); lines n(n − 1)/2
- R = 1.2A^(1/3) fm; 1 u = 931.5 MeV; E_b = ΔM c²; N = N₀e^(−λt); T½ = 0.693/λ
- nₑnₕ = nᵢ²; Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV; half-wave ripple ν, full-wave 2ν

steps.title: Units cheat-sheet
steps.body: Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m · nm = 10⁻⁹ m · fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m · eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J · MeV = 1.6×10⁻¹³ J · μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m/A · ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² F/m · h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s

quiz.q: Magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “f_o/f_e”. Reasoning: Angular magnification. A choice like “f_e/f_o” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: YDSE fringe width in water (n = 4/3) compared with air is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “smaller”. Reasoning: β/n. A choice like “larger” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Photon energy for 1240 nm is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1 eV”. Reasoning: 1240/1240. A choice like “12.4 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Radius of the 2nd Bohr orbit of hydrogen is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2.12 Å”. Reasoning: 4 × 0.529. A choice like “4.76 Å” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: 1 u equals
quiz.why: The correct answer is “931.5 MeV”. Reasoning: Energy equivalent. A choice like “1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “100 Hz”. Reasoning: 2ν. A choice like “200 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

lessons.title: Mock paper 1 (mixed chapters)

scenes.text: Saturday morning: Ankit sits a timed mock paper at home with the phone in another room.
He gives 1 minute per MCQ, skips any that take longer, and returns later.
He checks answers only after finishing — and learns more from his mistakes than from his correct answers.

steps.title: How to use this mock
steps.body: Attempt the 8 questions below in 12 minutes without notes. Then read every explanation, including for the questions you got right. Mark each wrong answer as: concept gap, formula slip, unit error or careless reading.

steps.title: Board exam strategy
steps.body:
- Read the whole paper in the first 10–15 minutes; start with sections you are strongest in.
- For derivations, draw a labelled diagram, state assumptions, then derive step by step — marks are given per step.
- Box the final answer with units.
- For numericals, write the formula first (it earns marks even if arithmetic slips).

steps.title: JEE/NEET strategy
steps.body:
- Use elimination: check units/dimensions and limiting cases (what if θ = 0? r → ∞?).
- NEET penalises wrong answers: guess only when you can rule out two options.
- Keep 10% of time to recheck marked questions.

steps.title: Avoid these
steps.body:
- Not converting cm/μC/mA to SI.
- Copying the sign convention halfway through optics problems.
- Reading 'NOT' or 'incorrect' in the question too fast.

steps.title: Disclaimer
steps.body: Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by CBSE, NTA or any exam provider. Check the official syllabus and exam guide for the current pattern.

activity.prompt: Mock-paper discipline checklist
items: Every wrong answer categorised (concept / formula / unit / careless)
Formula sheet re-read for those chapters

quiz.q: Two point charges repel with 9 N at 1 m. At 3 m the force is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1 N”. Reasoning: 9/9. A choice like “27 N” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor in parallel are in series with 2 Ω across 8 V. Current from the source:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2 A”. Reasoning: R = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. A choice like “1 A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A proton enters B = 0.5 T at 10⁶ m/s perpendicular. Radius (m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg):
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2.1 cm”. Reasoning: r = 1.67×10⁻²¹/(0.8×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 0.021 m. A choice like “0.21 m” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 200-turn coil of area 0.01 m² rotates at 50 rad/s in B = 0.2 T. Peak emf:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “20 V”. Reasoning: 200 × 0.2 × 0.01 × 50. A choice like “40 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A convex lens of f = 10 cm forms a real image at 30 cm. Object distance:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “15 cm”. Reasoning: 1/30 − 1/u = 1/10 ⇒ u = −15 cm. A choice like “30 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: In YDSE, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m, λ = 500 nm. Fringe width:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “0.5 mm”. Reasoning: λD/d. A choice like “1 mm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Light of 248 nm on a metal of φ₀ = 3 eV. Stopping potential:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2 V”. Reasoning: 5 eV − 3 eV. A choice like “8 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Binding energy per nucleon of a nucleus with ΔM = 0.5 u and A = 60:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “7.76 MeV”. Reasoning: 0.5 × 931.5/60. A choice like “465.8 MeV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

lessons.title: Mock paper 2 (mixed chapters)

scenes.text: In her first mock, Pooja scored 52%. Optics and EMI were her weakest.
She revised those formula sheets and redid every wrong question.
This second mock is her chance to see the improvement.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: 8 questions, 12 minutes, no notes. Several questions are assertion–reason and case-based, as in recent board papers. Then study the explanations.

steps.title: Assertion–reason method
steps.body:
1. Judge the assertion alone: true or false?
2. Judge the reason alone.
3. Only if both are true, ask: does the reason *explain* the assertion (does 'because' make sense)?

steps.title: Case-based questions
steps.body: Read the case once fully, underline numbers and units, then answer each sub-question independently — one mistake should not cascade.

steps.title: Last-minute warnings
steps.body:
- In AC questions check whether a value is rms or peak.
- In modern physics check eV vs J.
- In capacitor questions check whether the battery stays connected.

activity.prompt: Compare your two mock scores. Which chapter improved most, and which still needs work? Write your three-day plan.
activity.hint: Be specific: chapter, topic, and how many questions you will practise each day.

quiz.q: Assertion: Inside a charged conducting shell E = 0. Reason: All charge resides on the outer surface.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: Gauss's law with zero enclosed charge. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 10 μF capacitor charged to 100 V stores energy
quiz.why: The correct answer is “0.05 J”. Reasoning: ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 10⁴. A choice like “5 J” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Case: An LCR circuit has L = 0.4 H and C = 10 μF. Resonant angular frequency:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “500 rad/s”. Reasoning: 1/√(4×10⁻⁶) = 500. A choice like “1000 rad/s” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A transformer with Nₚ : Nₛ = 1 : 20 is fed 230 V. Output voltage:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4600 V”. Reasoning: × 20. A choice like “230 V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Critical angle for n = √2 is
quiz.why: The correct answer is “45°”. Reasoning: sin i_c = 1/√2. A choice like “60°” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Unpolarised light through two polaroids at 45°: fraction transmitted
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1/4”. Reasoning: ½ × cos²45°. A choice like “0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Energy of an electron in the 3rd orbit of hydrogen:
quiz.why: The correct answer is “−1.51 eV”. Reasoning: −13.6/9. A choice like “−0.85 eV” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A full-wave rectifier's output on 60 Hz mains has ripple frequency
quiz.why: The correct answer is “120 Hz”. Reasoning: Twice input. A choice like “60 Hz” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

sources: NCERT Class 12 Physics (topic reference, own wording)

questions.q: SI unit of electric flux is
questions.why: The correct answer is “N m²/C”. Reasoning: E × area. A choice like “V” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Unit of inductance is
questions.why: The correct answer is “henry”. A choice like “tesla” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.

questions.q: Which EM wave has the highest frequency?
questions.why: The correct answer is “gamma rays”. Reasoning: Shortest wavelength. A choice like “X-rays” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Majority carriers in n-type Ge are
questions.why: The correct answer is “electrons”. Reasoning: Donor electrons. A choice like “holes” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The potential at the centre of a charged conducting sphere (radius R, charge Q) is
questions.why: The correct answer is “kQ/R”. Reasoning: Same as surface. A choice like “kQ/R²” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A cell of 2 V, r = 0.5 Ω gives what current through 3.5 Ω?
questions.why: The correct answer is “0.5 A”. Reasoning: 2/4. A choice like “0.57 A” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Field at the centre of a 50-turn coil of radius 5 cm carrying 2 A:
questions.why: The correct answer is “1.26×10⁻³ T”. Reasoning: μ₀NI/2R = 4π×10⁻⁷ × 100/0.1. A choice like “2.5×10⁻³ T” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Image by a plane mirror is
questions.why: The correct answer is “virtual, erect, same size”. Reasoning: Basic property. A choice like “real, inverted” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: A capacitor blocks DC but passes AC. Reason: X_C = 1/ωC decreases with frequency.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true; reason explains”. Reasoning: At ω = 0, X_C → ∞. A choice like “Both true; reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Equivalent of 3 μF, 6 μF in series, in parallel with 4 μF:
questions.why: The correct answer is “6 μF”. Reasoning: 2 + 4. A choice like “13 μF” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron at 25 V is
questions.why: The correct answer is “0.245 nm”. Reasoning: 1.227/5. A choice like “0.049 nm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A 2 m rod moves at 5 m/s perpendicular to 0.3 T on rails with R = 6 Ω. Power dissipated:
questions.why: The correct answer is “1.5 W”. Reasoning: ε = 3 V; P = ε²/R = 1.5 W. A choice like “9 W” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A prism of 60° and n = √2 gives minimum deviation
questions.why: The correct answer is “30°”. Reasoning: sin((60 + D)/2) = √2 × 0.5 ⇒ 45° ⇒ D = 30°. A choice like “60°” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Two coherent sources with intensity ratio 1 : 9. I_max : I_min =
questions.why: The correct answer is “4 : 1”. Reasoning: (1 + 3)²/(3 − 1)² = 16/4 = 4. A choice like “9 : 1” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
